title: Gcp Accelerateagentdevelopmentwithantigravityandagentscli Dev Understanding
text: Antigravity and agents cli in the ADK development workflow Antigravity and agents cli in the ADK development workflow In this lesson, you'll learn how to utilize the local Agent Development Kit (ADK) 2.0 ecosystem by leveraging Antigravity (opens in a new tab), Google’s agentic IDE, alongside agents cli , the lifecycle toolchain. Together, these tools form a powerful local development platform that allows you to shift your focus away from wrestling with complex API syntax and toward designing high level agent logic, while also understanding how Antigravity and agents cli work together as your local ADK development platform. Throughout the course, you'll build an ambient agent that runs in response to events rather than through chat, performing its tasks in the background and involving a person only when necessary. You'll work with an example of an agent that handles expense reports, routing each transaction, screening for risk before the LLM runs, and pausing for human review when needed. This process requires juggling multiple elements simultaneously, including your design intent, the ADK API, a growing codebase, and a test harness. Antigravity (opens in a new tab) lifts that load by writing and editing ADK code straight from your natural language design, while agents cli supplies the domain knowledge it needs to target the ADK 2.0 API correctly from the start. Together, they keep your attention on what the agent should do and why not on how to wire up a graph. The vibecoding model and the architect role Building ADK agents with Antigravity follows a rapid prototyping practice called vibecoding. You act as the architect. In natural language, you describe the agent's purpose, routing rules, and security requirements. Antigravity writes the code. You review the output, verify the structure, and direct the next step. If you want to build a graph based ADK 2.0 agent with custom routing, a pre LLM security screen, and human in the loop pauses without holding the full ADK API reference in your head, vibecoding gives you that. You keep the high level design in focus and delegate the implementation. For the expense agent, you describe the business rule and the routing outcome, and Antigravity produces the corresponding graph structure edge conditions, the LLM agent node, and the RequestInput human in the loop step. The most effective architectural prompts are specific, behavioral, and explicit about boundary conditions. A vague prompt "build an expense agent" produces a generic agent. A specific one names the routing threshold, what each branch does, and which parts should never touch the LLM. Prompt example I'm building an ambient expense approval agent as an ADK 2.0 graph workflow. An expense report arrives as a JSON event with amount, submitter, category, description, and date. Apply one rule: under $100, auto approve instantly with no LLM involved. At $100 or more, send to an LLM reviewer for risk analysis, then pause the workflow for a human to approve or reject. Keep the dollar threshold and routing in Python code the model is only for the risk judgment. After Antigravity generates the graph, ask it to explain what it built before moving on: "Walk me through the graph you wired up step by step, highlighting the code I should be paying attention to." This explanation is your verification step. Read it against your design and push back on any discrepancy "the threshold should be $100 or more, not strictly over $100, please correct the edge condition" before moving to the next prompt. Spec Driven Development (SDD) Before writing any prompts, write a formal specification for the agent you're building. This practice is called Spec Driven Development (SDD) and reflects a fundamental shift in what the developer's role actually is. Your job is to write high quality blueprints. Antigravity's job is to turn those blueprints into code. Benefits of the SDD Approach A direct consequence: the code itself is disposable. If the spec is solid, you can regenerate the entire codebase at any point, swap languages, restructure the project, or discard a broken branch and restart without losing the design. There's no twelve hours spent debugging a single function. There's no hesitation about deleting generated output and starting over when requirements change. A good spec acts as an Architectural North Star for the entire build session. It prevents context fragmentation the failure mode where the agent loses the plot as it works from outdated file snapshots and partial in session context. Store the spec as a checked in file in your project, for example at \specs/expense agent.md\ . Antigravity reads it directly. You don't have to re explain the design at each step in the conversation. A production grade spec for the expense agent covers four elements. Select each item to learn more. Full technical design The routing rules, state transitions, tool signatures, and security constraints. Be specific name the $100 threshold, each branch outcome, and which paths must bypass the LLM entirely. Background The "why" behind the design. When Antigravity knows the intent, it can reason forward to the next step without waiting for another prompt. Visual aids and version numbers Include diagrams and pin every library version. Without explicit pins, the agent defaults to versions from its training cutoff. Scenarios What correct behavior looks like, what failure looks like, and the edge cases. BDD style Gherkin syntax works especially well here. Gherkin is a plain language format from Behavior Driven Development that structures each scenario as a Scenario / Given / When / Then block — describing the starting state, the trigger, and the expected outcome. It forces State → Action → Outcome thinking and leaves no ambiguity about what correct behavior means: Defining behavior with Gherkin scenarios In SDD, your specification should include Gherkin scenarios. This provides Antigravity with a clear "Definition of Done" for the agent's logic. Example: Expense agent specification Include the following scenarios within your specs/expense agent.md file to ensure the agent logic handles thresholds and security requirements correctly. Gherkin scenarios eliminate ambiguity about what correct behavior means. They also map directly to the evaluation dataset you'll build in a later lesson the same scenarios that guide Antigravity during the build become the test cases that grade the agent once it's running. Use the chat interface for high level orchestration only: " Review \specs/expense agent.md\ and implement Scenario 2. Confirm which files you changed." The spec does the heavy lifting; the prompt is the pointer to it. https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud training/cls html5 courses/P AACLID I/content/assets/text%20notes.png This gives you a stable reference to compare against Antigravity's output and prevents the most common failure mode in vibecoding: accepting generated code that's close to your intent but not exactly right, and discovering the gap only after several more build steps have compounded on top of it. The tradeoff is sustained attention, not less expertise. A misconfigured routing edge or a missing security node is easy to miss in generated code if you're not reading it as carefully as you would code you wrote yourself. Read every response the LLM gives you. When a detail is wrong, correct it specifically. Antigravity: Google's agentic development platform Antigravity is Google's agentic IDE, which also contains CLI, available on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It runs on Gemini, Claude, and other models. The model handles all code generation, file edits, and terminal commands. You don't switch between a chat interface and an editor. Antigravity does both. It has two main surfaces: editor view, and the manager surface. Click each tab to learn more. Editor View Manager Surface The editor view is a full featured IDE with AI completions, inline suggestions, and direct file manipulation. You can write code yourself, ask Antigravity to edit a specific function, or hand it a multi step task and let it execute. The manager surface lets you spawn and observe multiple agents working on tasks asynchronously. You can send one agent to research the ADK evaluation API while you review the graph workflow the previous step produced. Each subagent reports back when its task is done. Antigravity operates with bounded access by design. It works within the project folder you open. Its file reads, writes, and terminal commands are scoped to that workspace. When Antigravity needs to do something outside that scope install a global tool, access a credential file it asks for explicit permission first. This keeps the agent's actions visible and predictable during a multi step build where it would otherwise be easy to lose track of what the agent has changed. Antigravity tracks progress through Artifacts: tangible deliverables it produces so you can verify work without reading raw tool call logs. Artifacts include task lists, implementation plans, generated files, screenshots, and test output summaries. When Antigravity builds an ADK workflow, the generated agent.py, pyproject.toml, and Makefile each appear as Artifacts. You inspect them, run them, and reference them in follow up prompts: Continue from the agent.py you just generated. Before the high value expense reaches the LLM reviewer, add a security checkpoint that scrubs SSNs and credit card numbers from the description and routes any prompt injection attempt straight to human review, bypassing the model entirely. Referencing a previous Artifact by name keeps the context precise and prevents Antigravity from re generating something you've already verified. Out of the box, Antigravity can write general Python. It doesn't know the ADK 2.0 graph API, the RequestInput pattern for human in the loop steps, or the agents cli project layout. Without that context, it produces syntactically correct code that uses the wrong API surface often the 1.x SequentialAgent and LlmAgent patterns, which don't support the graph routing or session based state management you need for an ambient agent. Installing agents cli loads the domain specific skill files that fix this. Those skills are what keeps the generated code aligned with the current ADK surface. Antigravity workflow https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud training/cls html5 courses/P AACLID I/content/assets/graph.svg Solid arrows show active interactions. The dashed arrow shows the ADK skills loading into Antigravity automatically at startup. agents cli: the ADK lifecycle toolchain agents cli is the command line toolchain for building ADK agents and deploying them to the agent platform. Its most important function for Antigravity users is the skills system: a single setup command installs seven domain specific skill files into \ /.agents/skills/\ . Every supported coding agent on your machine scans that directory at startup and loads those files automatically. ADK 2.0 introduced a graph Workflow API: function nodes, typed edges, and \RequestInput\ for human in the loop pauses. Without the skills, Antigravity defaults to 1.x patterns whenever the prompt is ambiguous or session context is lost mid session. The \google agents cli adk code\ skill provides the 2.0 reference that keeps generated code on the correct API surface throughout the build. Up next, you'll install agents cli, see what each of the seven skills provides, and learn the session start pattern that loads the right skills at the beginning of each Antigravity build session.

title: Gcp Build With The Managed Agents Api On Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
text: Course introduction Welcome to the course Build with the Managed Agents API on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform . In this course, you'll learn to build and run enterprise agents on the Managed Agents API, the managed agent runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. You'll learn why a real business task needs an agent rather than a chat model. You'll examine how the platform splits into a control plane that defines agents and a data plane that runs them. You'll learn how to assemble an agent from a definition, a sandboxed environment, mounted data, tools, and skills. And you'll learn how to run it with background interactions, a streamed reason act loop, resilient typed results, and state that persists across turns. You then put that model to work in a hands on lab, where you build, run, and harden a retail merchandising agent for Cymbal Retail from an empty project to a production shaped deployment. By the end, you'll be able to design, build, and operate a managed agent of your own. The focus of this course is on eliminating security configuration drift and operational risk caused by unmanaged agent sprawl to deliver fully compliant, auditable, and secure zero trust AI environments and achieve a drastic reduction in deployment time.1 This course is designed for Security Teams, Cloud Architects, and AI Platform Engineers planning to scale their AI capabilities with centralized governance. Participants should have a strong understanding of networking primitives (VPC, DNS) and foundational knowledge of Identity and Access Management (IAM). In this course, you will learn to: https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud training/cls html5 courses/P BDMGFD A/content/assets/objective3.png ✓ Build managed, secure, isolated agents leveraging Google infrastructure using the Agents API. ✓ Interact with the Agents API to manage the control plane and with the Interactions API to work with the data plane. ✓ Extend agents with mounted data, skills, tools and MCP servers. ✓ Run agents using background interactions, a streamed reason act loop, resilient typed results, and multi turn state. ✓ Apply the security model and operational practices that secure an agent for production. The need for an agent in a sandbox In this lesson, you'll learn why a real business task demands secure infrastructure, when to choose a managed runtime over a developer framework, and what the platform's secure sandbox gives you. The hero task and the infrastructure it demands Let's use an example scenario to learn the various concepts in this course. Imagine a category manager at Cymbal Retail asks: "Umbrella sales dropped 18% last quarter in the Northeast. Pull the Q3 sales, find the five worst declining products, check current inventory, and tell me whether it's a demand problem or a stock problem." Answering it means reading data from storage, running an analysis over it, and checking a live inventory system, each step depending on the one before. To do that work, an agent needs real infrastructure: somewhere to run code, access to Cymbal's data, a way to reach a live inventory system, and credentials to use it. https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud training/cls html5 courses/P BDMGFD A/content/assets/sandbox%20environment.png For an enterprise, each of those is also a security question where the data sits, what the agent can touch, and what it can reach on the network. That is the task this course builds an agent to answer, and the reason it starts from secured infrastructure rather than from code. From a developer framework to a managed runtime Agents built with code using agentic frameworks such as ADK are great for the flexibility they offer. You start with code and you can run it and deploy it anywhere. However, enterprises think about security first. They need a secure environment where they can limit what an agent can do and who has access to that agent. With agentic frameworks you develop an app and think about infrastructure later. The Managed Agents API changes that. It starts with a standard, isolated Linux sandbox, and then you add functionality on top. In this secure, fully managed execution container, custom agents can reason, plan workflows, execute bash commands, and read or write files out of the box. The choice depends on where you start. Choose a developer framework when you want full control of the runtime and the freedom to deploy anywhere. Choose the managed runtime when you want a secure, isolated foundation and would rather add your agent's logic on top than build and operate that infrastructure yourself. What the sandbox provides Every sandbox environment provides the following core systems and controls: Persistent file system Bash terminal Preloaded toolchain Network isolation Extensible integrations MCP credentials scoping Data scoping for Cloud Storage and Skill Registry mounts Project access Select the markers on the architecture diagram to discover how the Managed Agents API isolates your project and securely connects to external resources. image 1. Persistent file system Securely persists files, agent logic, and execution state across multi turn interactions. 2. Bash terminal Provides a secure environment for executing terminal commands, running custom scripts, and processing local files. 3. Preloaded toolchain The sandbox ships with Python 3.11 (including pandas, numpy, and the google genai SDK), Node 20, and common command line tools, so the agent can analyze data with no setup. Any packages it installs at run time with pip or npm persist in the environment. 4. Network isolation You can explicitly declare a network allowlist to let the agent access public internet resources or download external libraries. 5. Extensible integrations Supports importing custom capabilities dynamically, including standard web APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. 6. MCP credentials scoping Header configurations for MCP servers, which contain backend authentication tokens, are transmitted only when accessing the specific MCP endpoints defined in your configuration. 7. Data scoping for Cloud Storage and Skill Registry mounts When you attach external data sources from Google Cloud Storage or Skill Registry, the environment is provided with downscoped authorization tokens designed to access only the specific directories or skills specified in the agent configurations. 8. Project access To run an interaction, a caller needs the right Identity and Access Management role on the project: the aiplatform.user (opens in a new tab) role to run interactions, and the aiplatform.admin (opens in a new tab) role to create, update, or delete agents. The security boundary image Diagram: the security boundary. Project IAM controls who can call; the platform service account reads your data on your behalf with a downscoped token; the sandbox runs with no credentials of its own, and no egress until you open it. These standard parameters govern the sandbox execution and lifecycle: Sandbox Environment Agents operate within a fully managed sandbox environment, utilizing the Antigravity harness for orchestration. Sandbox Time to Live (TTL) The sandbox environment has a standard time to live (TTL) of 7 days. Each new interaction automatically resets this timer to ensure active agents remain available. Agent Configuration Persistence The backend persistently stores agent configurations, which remain until an explicit DELETE request is sent to the Agents API. Agent Collaboration Multiple agents can share the same environment when the same env\ id is provided during interaction. Module introduction In this module, you'll learn why enterprises build agents on secure, isolated infrastructure first and add capability on top. You'll explore how the Managed Agents API on Agent Platform (opens in a new tab) takes that approach, separates defining an agent from running one, and keeps your data and credentials contained. There are two ways to build an agent. The code first Approach With a developer framework such as the Agent Development Kit (ADK), you start from code: you build the agent first and decide how to secure and host its infrastructure later. The infrastructure first approach The Managed Agents API inverts that order. It starts with a secure, isolated runtime, and you add the agent's logic on top. The enterprise perspective For an enterprise that must answer "where does our data go, and what can this agent reach?" before anything ships, starting from secured infrastructure is the point. By the end of this module, you understand that trade off, how the platform is organized, and the security model you build on. By the end of this module, you'll be able to: Choose between developer frameworks and infrastructure frameworks for building agents. Secure the infrastructure, identity and network access controls around your agent. Configure the Agents API to manage the control plane and execute interactions with the data plane. Distinguish between the infrastructure managed by the Agents API and the custom logic you must provide. image Interaction with the agent in a sandbox In this lesson, you'll learn how the platform splits into a control plane and a data plane, and what it runs for you versus what you provide. The two planes: control and data There are two distinct APIs that divide the interaction with the agent. The Agents API, which is responsible for creating and configuring the agent, and the Interactions API, which is responsible for managing the agent at runtime in a conversation. Agents API The Agents API is the control plane. You use it to define an agent once, as a durable cloud resource with a name. The definition holds the agent's persona, its tools, and its environment. It persists until you delete it, the way a virtual machine or a storage bucket persists. You create, read, update, and delete agents here. Interactions API The Interactions API is the data plane. You use it to run the agent. Each interaction references an agent by name, binds an environment, and drives the reason act loop to completion. An interaction is ephemeral: it exists for one run. So you define an agent once on the control plane, then run it many times on the data plane. In code, those are two different calls against the same named agent: image Long running operations in agent creation Creating an agent doesn't return the agent immediately. It returns a long running operation (LRO), a handle to work the platform is doing in the background. You poll that handle until it reports done, then read the finished agent. Long running operations appear whenever the platform performs complex tasks, so it helps to recognize the pattern early. What the platform runs for you That reason act loop needs infrastructure. Click each button to expand the items and learn more. Orchestrator An orchestrator is essential for managing the steps of the reason act loop and determining when to halt the process. It ensures seamless coordination and decision making throughout the workflow. Secure Sandbox A secure, stateful sandbox is necessary to execute code and store intermediate files safely. This environment provides isolation and security for the operations performed by the agent. Credential Management Proper methods are required to securely provide credentials to the systems accessed by the agent. This prevents unauthorized access and ensures the confidentiality of sensitive information. Network Control Controlling the agent's network access is crucial to limit its reach and ensure security. Implementing restrictions helps mitigate potential risks and unauthorized activities. Combining these manageable components forms a comprehensive platform. The Managed Agents API: Structure and functionality The Managed Agents API draws a clean boundary around that work. You provide the intent: the system instruction that gives the agent its persona and rules, the tools it's allowed to use, and the bounds of its environment. The environment is the sandbox the agent runs in, plus the data and network access it's allowed. The platform provides the runtime: it runs the reason act loop, manages state, dispatches each tool call, and provisions and tears down the sandbox. The practical effect is that a question like Cymbal's becomes a matter of configuration and instruction, not infrastructure. You describe the agent and the data it can see. The platform runs the loop that reads, computes, checks inventory, and decides. image Diagram: the capability stack. You provide the intent at the top; the platform runs everything below the boundary. Defining the agent: configuration, environment, and data In this lesson, you’ll learn how to define an agent on the control plane as a durable resource. This definition includes setting up the agent's persona and rules using system\ instruction, defining its isolated execution environment using base\ environment, and attaching necessary data from a Cloud Storage source so the agent has a workspace and files to process. Define the agent and create it An agent definition is small. It is a short collection of fields. The id names the resource, and it's the one field you can't change later, because it becomes the resource name. The base\ agent selects the platform's foundation agent to run on. You also set a description , a system\ instruction that gives the agent its persona and rules, the tools it may use, and a base\ environment that bounds its runtime. Creating the agent follows the long running operation pattern , where create returns an operation handle you poll until it finishes. You call create, and the platform hands back that operation, not the agent. You poll until it reports done, then read the agent from the result. Always check for an error, because an operation can report done and still carry an error instead of an agent. The SDK does this polling for you and returns the created agent directly, so you don't write the loop by hand; over REST, you poll the operation yourself. Once created, the agent is a normal cloud resource with a full lifecycle. You can read it, list the agents in a project, update its mutable fields, and delete it when you're done. The definition persists until you delete it, separate from any run. image Diagram: the agent lifecycle. Create moves through an operation you poll; the active agent can be updated, and persists until you delete it. The execution environment The agent needs somewhere to run, and you attach that with its base\ environment . The agent definition establishes the environment, every interaction inherits the same sandbox unless a particular run overrides it. Setting the environment type to remote requests a managed, isolated Linux container. The platform provisions it lazily, at the first interaction, rather than at create time, so defining the agent is cheap. Inside that container, the agent can run code and read and write files from the start. The environment carries two more things you'll use constantly. The sources list says what to mount into the sandbox, and only two source types are valid: a Cloud Storage bucket, or a skill from the registry. The network allowlist controls what network destinations the sandbox may reach. It's closed by default. During development you can open it fully, and in production you tighten it to the specific domains the agent needs. Mount your data To give the agent your data, you add a Cloud Storage source to the environment. A source names the bucket and a target path to mount it at, conventionally /.agent/data . Once mounted, your files appear in the sandbox as ordinary files. The agent reads them with its file system tool and processes them with code execution, for example by running a data analysis library over a set of sales records. A source is just three fields: type, source, and target. The detail that's easy to miss is access. The sandbox doesn't read your private bucket using your personal account level credentials. Instead, the platform reads the bucket as its per project service account (P4SA). You must grant that service account read access on the bucket. Note: If you skip the service account grant, the agent still creates successfully and the mount still appears, but the read fails at run time as a file not found error inside the interaction. That makes it a confusing failure to debug after the fact, so grant the access when you mount the bucket. Extend agent capabilities with tools and skills In this lesson, you’ll learn how to extend your agent's capabilities by providing it with external actions and reusable procedures. You’ll learn how to differentiate between tools, which are actions the agent can choose to take, and skills, which are mounted directories of files and scripts that extend the agent's logic, like report templates or reusable procedures. You’ll also cover the three distinct kinds of tools including built in and external systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how to package and mount skills from the Skill Registry. Give the agent tools Tools are the actions the agent can choose to take while it runs, in the reasoning loop covered in the next lesson. There are three distinct kinds, and it helps to keep them separate. Click each button to expand the items and learn more. Built in tools Built in tools run inside the managed sandbox. Two of them, code execution and the file system, are always on, so the agent can run code and read files with no setup. Two more, web search and reading a web page, are opt in: they are only invoked if you include them in the tool list. When the search tools run, their citations come back in a separate annotations block. That block is a distinct section of the response that lists the sources, which gives you clean provenance for a decision. External systems External systems connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for exposing tools to a model. You declare an MCP connection on the agent, with the tool type mcp\ server, a name, and a URL. Authentication tokens expire, so you keep them out of the durable definition. You supply a fresh token at run time, where the interaction time form of the connection injects it. Local functions Local functions are functions in your own application. You pass a function to the SDK, the model asks you to run it, you run it in your process, and you return the result on the next turn. Use this when the logic must stay in your code rather than in the sandbox or a remote service. Each tool is a small entry in the agent's tools list: You decide which tools to offer; the model decides which to use, with what arguments, and in what order. Give the agent skills The three kinds above are tools, which are actions. A skill is different: it's a folder of files and scripts that the agent reads and runs, such as a report template or a reusable procedure. A skill is a directory anchored by a required file named SKILL.md , with optional scripts, references, and assets alongside it. To publish a skill, you package the directory, encode it, and create it in the Skill Registry. The registry is the one regional surface in this API. Agents and interactions live in the global location, but skills live in a specific region. You create a skill there, and because creation is a long running operation, you poll it to completion just as you do for agents. Mount a skill Before you mount a skill, you first need to find it. Select each tab to learn more. The registry supports search functionality, allowing you to describe your requirements and receive ranked matches. Additionally, it provides a listing of all available skills within the project and region. To mount a skill, you add a skill registry source to the agent's environment. This is done at a target location, such as /.agent/skills , ensuring the skill is accessible to the agent. Skills are versioned, with every creation or update generating a new version. You reference these versions using a skill\ versions path. This ensures clarity and control over the skill's state. In production, you pin a specific version so a skill update can't silently change the agent's behavior. During development, you let it track the latest version. image Diagram: The assembled agent is a single control plane resource that links together the sandbox, your mounted data, its tools, and a mounted skill. With data, tools, and a skill in place, the agent definition is fully assembled on the control plane. The whole configuration exists before a single interaction runs. In the next lesson, you move to the data plane, the execution layer where interactions actually run, and run it. Module introduction In this module, you'll learn how to build an agent with the Agents API on the control plane: how you define it, give it an environment and data, and extend it with tools and skills. The control plane is the management layer where you define and configure agents as durable resources, before any of them run. Everything here happens before the agent runs. You assemble the whole configuration first, as a durable resource, so that when you finally run an interaction the agent already has its workspace, its data, and its capabilities in place. By the end of this lesson, you can describe each part of an agent's definition and the choices you make when you assemble one. By the end of this module, you'll be able to: Design and deploy a durable agent configuration, managing the long running lifecycle and creation operations. Explain how the base execution environment and mounted data sources function together to establish a working workspace for an agent. Integrate tools and skills to extend an agent. Defining the agent: configuration, environment, and data In this lesson, you’ll learn how to define an agent on the control plane as a durable resource. This definition includes setting up the agent's persona and rules using system\ instruction, defining its isolated execution environment using base\ environment, and attaching necessary data from a Cloud Storage source so the agent has a workspace and files to process. Define the agent and create it An agent definition is small. It is a short collection of fields. The id names the resource, and it's the one field you can't change later, because it becomes the resource name. The base\ agent selects the platform's foundation agent to run on. You also set a description , a system\ instruction that gives the agent its persona and rules, the tools it may use, and a base\ environment that bounds its runtime. Creating the agent follows the long running operation pattern , where create returns an operation handle you poll until it finishes. You call create, and the platform hands back that operation, not the agent. You poll until it reports done, then read the agent from the result. Always check for an error, because an operation can report done and still carry an error instead of an agent. The SDK does this polling for you and returns the created agent directly, so you don't write the loop by hand; over REST, you poll the operation yourself. Once created, the agent is a normal cloud resource with a full lifecycle. You can read it, list the agents in a project, update its mutable fields, and delete it when you're done. The definition persists until you delete it, separate from any run. image Diagram: the agent lifecycle. Create moves through an operation you poll; the active agent can be updated, and persists until you delete it. The execution environment The agent needs somewhere to run, and you attach that with its base\ environment . The agent definition establishes the environment, every interaction inherits the same sandbox unless a particular run overrides it. Setting the environment type to remote requests a managed, isolated Linux container. The platform provisions it lazily, at the first interaction, rather than at create time, so defining the agent is cheap. Inside that container, the agent can run code and read and write files from the start. The environment carries two more things you'll use constantly. The sources list says what to mount into the sandbox, and only two source types are valid: a Cloud Storage bucket, or a skill from the registry. The network allowlist controls what network destinations the sandbox may reach. It's closed by default. During development you can open it fully, and in production you tighten it to the specific domains the agent needs. Mount your data To give the agent your data, you add a Cloud Storage source to the environment. A source names the bucket and a target path to mount it at, conventionally /.agent/data . Once mounted, your files appear in the sandbox as ordinary files. The agent reads them with its file system tool and processes them with code execution, for example by running a data analysis library over a set of sales records. A source is just three fields: type, source, and target. The detail that's easy to miss is access. The sandbox doesn't read your private bucket using your personal account level credentials. Instead, the platform reads the bucket as its per project service account (P4SA). You must grant that service account read access on the bucket. Note: If you skip the service account grant, the agent still creates successfully and the mount still appears, but the read fails at run time as a file not found error inside the interaction. That makes it a confusing failure to debug after the fact, so grant the access when you mount the bucket. Extend agent capabilities with tools and skills In this lesson, you’ll learn how to extend your agent's capabilities by providing it with external actions and reusable procedures. You’ll learn how to differentiate between tools, which are actions the agent can choose to take, and skills, which are mounted directories of files and scripts that extend the agent's logic, like report templates or reusable procedures. You’ll also cover the three distinct kinds of tools including built in and external systems using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how to package and mount skills from the Skill Registry. Give the agent tools Tools are the actions the agent can choose to take while it runs, in the reasoning loop covered in the next lesson. There are three distinct kinds, and it helps to keep them separate. Click each button to expand the items and learn more. Built in tools Built in tools run inside the managed sandbox. Two of them, code execution and the file system, are always on, so the agent can run code and read files with no setup. Two more, web search and reading a web page, are opt in: they are only invoked if you include them in the tool list. When the search tools run, their citations come back in a separate annotations block. That block is a distinct section of the response that lists the sources, which gives you clean provenance for a decision. External systems External systems connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for exposing tools to a model. You declare an MCP connection on the agent, with the tool type mcp\ server, a name, and a URL. Authentication tokens expire, so you keep them out of the durable definition. You supply a fresh token at run time, where the interaction time form of the connection injects it. Local functions Local functions are functions in your own application. You pass a function to the SDK, the model asks you to run it, you run it in your process, and you return the result on the next turn. Use this when the logic must stay in your code rather than in the sandbox or a remote service. Each tool is a small entry in the agent's tools list: You decide which tools to offer; the model decides which to use, with what arguments, and in what order. Give the agent skills The three kinds above are tools, which are actions. A skill is different: it's a folder of files and scripts that the agent reads and runs, such as a report template or a reusable procedure. A skill is a directory anchored by a required file named SKILL.md , with optional scripts, references, and assets alongside it. To publish a skill, you package the directory, encode it, and create it in the Skill Registry. The registry is the one regional surface in this API. You create a skill there, and because creation is a long running operation, you poll it to completion just as you do for agents. Mount a skill Before you mount a skill, you first need to find it. Select each tab to learn more. The registry supports search functionality, allowing you to describe your requirements and receive ranked matches. Additionally, it provides a listing of all available skills within the project and region. To mount a skill, you add a skill registry source to the agent's environment. This is done at a target location, such as /.agent/skills , ensuring the skill is accessible to the agent. Skills are versioned, with every creation or update generating a new version. You reference these versions using a skill\ versions path. This ensures clarity and control over the skill's state. In production, you pin a specific version so a skill update can't silently change the agent's behavior. During development, you let it track the latest version. image Diagram: The assembled agent is a single control plane resource that links together the sandbox, your mounted data, its tools, and a mounted skill. With data, tools, and a skill in place, the agent definition is fully assembled on the control plane. The whole configuration exists before a single interaction runs. In the next lesson, you move to the data plane, the execution layer where interactions actually run, and run it. Module introduction Run and operate the agent In this module, you'll learn how an agent runs on the data plane, the part of the platform that actually executes the runs. You'll explore how a run executes, how to follow its reasoning, how to get reliable typed results, how state carries across turns, and how to reshape and secure the agent for production. The agent you assembled previously hasn't done anything yet. Now you run it. You discover why agent runs happen in the background, how the reason act loop unfolds as a stream of steps, and how one assembled agent is really a family of reusable blueprints. By the end of this module, you'll be able to: Perform synchronous background runs Create interactions with reliable, typed results Persist state across turns and create blueprints from a codebase Apply the security model and operational practices that secure an agent for production. Execute the agent and handle results In this lesson, you'll learn how to run your assembled agent on the platform's data plane, starting with the difference between synchronous model runs and required background agent runs. You'll then explore the reason act loop, how to watch its stream of steps, and how to get reliable, typed, machine readable results from the agent's final output. Run the agent in the background An agent run is asynchronous, and you must mark the call as a background run. An agent task can take minutes, for example while it runs a data analysis. A synchronous connection held open that long would drop. The platform requires the background path. The call returns immediately with a status of in progress and an identifier, and you check that identifier until the status becomes completed. If you forget the background flag on an agent run, the platform rejects the call. Two choices matter when you start a run. 1. You capture the identifier the call returns, because it's your only handle to the asynchronous run. 2. You also choose whether to store the interaction. Storing it makes the run retrievable by the identifier later. It also lets you chain the run into a multi turn conversation, which the rest of this lesson relies on. The reason act loop and its events Internally, an interaction is a list of steps, and each step has a type. A model output step is the agent reasoning and planning its next move. A function call step is the agent choosing one tool and its arguments. A function result step is the platform running that tool and feeding the output back into the agent's context. That observe step, where the result flows back in, is exactly what makes this an agent and not a fixed pipeline. The loop repeats think, act, observe until the task is resolved. It ends with the agent's final answer, which is the last model output step that actually contains text. The very last step can be empty, so you scan backward for the last non empty one rather than trusting the final step without verification. For a customer question, the agent reads the sales file, runs a ranking computation, checks live inventory for the worst SKUs, classifies each one, and creates the final verdict. You constrain which tools are available; the model owns the order it uses them in. image Diagram: the reason act loop in action. The model plans, calls a tool, reads the result, and repeats until it states the verdict. Reading the answer requires caution, because the run can end with an empty step: You can watch this happen live by streaming the run. Streaming returns server sent events, a simple stream of messages the platform pushes as work happens. The run opens with a created event that carries the identifier. Each step brings a start event, then delta events that stream the content, then a stop event. A final completed event ends the stream. A single consumer function can handle every event type, which is the one piece of streaming code you reuse everywhere. Reliable, typed results Because an agent run executes on the platform, not on your machine, it survives a dropped connection. The work continues server side whether or not you're still connected. If you stored the interaction, nothing is lost when a laptop sleeps or a proxy cuts the stream. You have two ways to finish: poll the run by its identifier until it reports completed, or reconnect the stream and re attach to the same events. The pattern you ship in production tries the live stream first and falls back to polling on any drop, because the run never stopped. You can also make the result machine readable. By default the agent returns prose, which a person can read but another system can't easily consume. When you pass a response format, a typed schema for the output, the platform constrains the final answer to valid structured data that matches your schema. You parse it directly into typed fields, so the verdict can drive a dashboard instead of sitting in a paragraph. Stream the run When you stream the run, its completed event carries a usage block: the total tokens it consumed, broken out by input and output. It also includes a count of thought tokens, which measures how much the agent reasoned. This usage is attached to the streaming completed event, not the polled run, so capture it from the stream. On long investigations, watch the thought token count, because it's a direct signal of cost. State across turns and blueprints In this lesson, you'll learn how to maintain state across multiple turns by reusing the conversation and workspace environment. You'll also discover how to leverage a single agent definition to create a family of reusable blueprints by modifying its sources and tools. State across turns By default, each interaction starts completely new: a fresh conversation and a fresh, empty sandbox (the isolated file system the agent works in). To continue a conversation and keep the same workspace, you pass two independent handles on the next run. The first handle continues the conversation. You pass the previous interaction's identifier, and the agent regains the dialogue so far, including its earlier verdict and the specific SKUs it found. The second handle reuses the workspace. You pass back the environment identifier captured from the first run, and the agent re attaches to the same sandbox. The mounted data, the mounted skills, and any intermediate files the agent wrote are all still there. The two handles are independent, so you can keep one without the other. Note: The classic multi turn mistake is to pass a fresh environment routinely on the second turn. That gives the agent a new, empty sandbox, discards the first turn's work, and pays the cost of provisioning again. To continue work, reuse the captured environment identifier rather than requesting a new environment. It helps to name the three scopes that state persists in. Click each button to expand the items and learn more. Iteration Scope Iteration scope refers to the agent's working context for a single turn of the loop. This scope is transient and resets with each iteration. Interaction Scope Interaction scope encompasses the sandbox file system used during a single run. Files written in one step are accessible in subsequent steps of the same run. Environment Scope Environment scope represents the outer workspace that persists across multiple runs. This persistence occurs only when the environment identifier is explicitly reused. image Diagram: the three nested state scopes. Iterations share one interaction's sandbox files; the environment contains the interaction and persists across runs when you reuse its identifier. One codebase, many blueprints, hardened for production Once you've assembled one agent, you've effectively built a group of related agents. The body of the definition, the identifier, base agent, description, and instruction, stays constant. Only two fields move: the sources you mount and the tools you offer. A skill is a packaged, reusable capability you mount as a source for the agent to use. From those two fields you get several reusable blueprints: An agent grounded on your stored data. An agent driven by a single packaged skill. An agent integrated with a live external system. An agent that mounts a whole library of skills. A composite that combines all of them. There's no special composite setting; composition is just longer sources and tools lists. So the design question becomes simple: what does this agent need to reach? Secure and harden for production In this lesson, you'll learn the security model the platform enforces, how its design keeps your data and credentials contained, and how to harden an agent for production. For an advanced engineer, this is the material that lets you explain the platform's security posture to a customer with confidence. The security model The platform's security model rests on one idea: your personal credentials never enter the sandbox where the agent runs code. Three layers enforce it. Click each tab to learn more. Project access is managed through Identity and Access Management. A caller requires the aiplatform.user role to execute interactions and the aiplatform.admin role to create, update, or delete agents. These roles define two key personas: those who can run an agent and those who can modify one. When an agent accesses your data or utilizes a skill, it operates through a per project service account (P4SA). This account uses a downscoped token limited to the specific source, ensuring your credentials remain secure. Your credentials are never duplicated into the sandbox environment. The containerized environment operates without ambient or privileged credentials. Additionally, its network egress is disabled by default, enhancing security. This containment also covers external systems. When you attach an MCP connection with an authentication header, the platform sends that header only to the endpoint you declared, never to other hosts the agent can reach. How the platform contains your data A natural question from any enterprise customer is: "If the agent runs code, what stops it from leaking our data?" The design answers that on several fronts, and you should be able to walk a customer through each one. Click each button to expand the items and learn more. No ambient credentials The sandbox holds no standing access to your project, so code running inside it can't reach buckets, repositories, or files you didn't explicitly mount. Downscoped, per source tokens Each mounted bucket or skill is read with a token limited to that one source, so mounting one bucket gives no path to another. Closed egress by default The network allowlist starts empty, so even code that wanted to send data out has nowhere to send it until you approve specific domains. Scoped tool credentials An MCP authentication header travels only to its declared endpoint. Explicit data paths Data leaves the sandbox only through paths you explicitly opened. This ensures a secure posture when evaluating the risks of running agents against customer data. Harden for production Hardening the agent for production is mostly applying the security model from earlier in this lesson. You replace the wide open development allowlist with an explicit list of the domains the agent actually needs, which you apply as an update to the agent's environment. Updating an agent is REST only, so you send a PATCH that resends the base\ environment with the narrowed allowlist: Domain level allowlisting is the production goal, but the current release accepts only {"domain": "\ "} and rejects a specific host with INVALID\ ARGUMENT : Only domain '\ ' is supported now. Learn the pattern now; expect that response until fine grained allowlisting ships. You design around the platform's limits, such as identifier length and the page size for listing. And you operate defensively: Rely on the result accessor, the call that returns the run's output and raises an error instead of a half formed object when create fails. Log the usage block from each run as cost and latency telemetry. Keep the parsed stream of steps as an execution log. That execution log is what answers the question "why did the agent decide this?", because it shows the exact tool results the agent saw before its final answer. You've now traced an agent from an idea to a hardened, multi turn deployment. In the lab, you build and run one end to end. 1. An enterprise customer worries about an agent leaking sensitive data from their repositories. How does the platform ensure that code running inside the sandbox cannot access files that were not explicitly mounted? ✅ Answer: The sandbox operates with no ambient credentials and reads sources with downscoped tokens. 2. When does the platform provision the isolated Linux container for an agent? ✅ Answer: When a user first interacts with the agent. 3. A developer connects an agent to an external system using the Model Context Protocol. Where should the developer supply the required authentication token? ✅ Answer: At the time the interaction runs. 4. A developer creates an agent and mounts a Cloud Storage bucket, but the agent fails to read the files at run time. What step did the developer likely miss? ✅ Answer: They neglected to grant the project service account read access to the bucket. 5. An organization wants to define a durable agent resource that stores the agent's name, persona, and tools. Which component of the platform is responsible for this task? ✅ Answer: The Agents API serves as the control plane for defining and persisting the agent configuration. 6. Your company requires a solution that prioritizes security and isolation before any code is written. Which approach fits these requirements? ✅ Answer: Use the Managed Agents API to start with a secure, isolated runtime and add agent logic on top. 7. An agent needs to access external libraries and public internet resources securely. How does the sandbox environment support this requirement? ✅ Answer: You declare a network allowlist to explicitly permit the agent to access specific public internet resources. 8. A developer wants to build a multi turn conversation where the agent remembers the files it wrote during the first turn. What does the developer pass to the second interaction to ensure the agent uses the same workspace? ✅ Answer: The environment identifier captured from the first run. 9. An engineer triggers an agent to perform a complex data analysis that takes several minutes to finish. Why must the engineer mark this call as a background run? ✅ Answer: The platform closes synchronous connections that stay open too long.

A Layer 4 (L4) NLB handles traffic based on network level information like IP addresses and port numbers, and does not inspect the content of the traffic. There are several ways you can load balance on Google Cloud. Set Up Application Load Balancers GSP155 Google Cloud self paced labs Overview In this hands on lab you learn how to set up a Layer 7 (L7) application load balancer on Compute Engine virtual machines (VMs). L7 load balancers can understand HTTP(S) protocols, allowing them to make routing decisions based on parameters like URL, headers, cookies, and the content of the request. This allows for improved application performance and responsiveness. There are several ways you can load balance on Google Cloud. This lab takes you through the setup of the following load balancers: Application Load Balancer You are encouraged to type the commands yourself, which can help you learn the core concepts. Many labs include a code block that contains the required commands. You can easily copy and paste the commands from the code block into the appropriate places during the lab. Use an Internal Application Load Balancer GSP041 Google Cloud self paced labs Overview The internal Application Load Balancer is essential for building robust, secure, and easily manageable internal applications that power your business operations. This lab explores how to distribute network traffic within your private cloud network without exposing your virtual machines (VMs) directly to the public internet, which keeps your services secure and efficient. In this lab you build a simplified, but very common, architectural pattern: A "Web Tier" (public facing website) that needs to ask another internal service for help. An "Internal Service Tier" (a prime number calculator) that performs specific tasks and is distributed across multiple machines. This setup ensures that even if one part of your internal service gets busy or goes down, the overall system keeps running smoothly, because the load balancer automatically directs requests to healthy machines. What you'll do In this lab, you learn how to perform the following tasks: Learn about the components that make up an Internal Load Balancer. Create a group of backend machines (prime number calculator). Set up internal load balancer to direct internal traffic to the backend machines. Test the internal load balancer from another internal machine. Set up a public facing web server that uses the internal load balancer to get results from the internal "prime number calculator" service. Prerequisites Basic familiarity with Google Cloud Compute Engine: Understanding what a Virtual Machine (VM) instance is. Basic concepts of networking: What an IP address is. Basic Unix/Linux command line: How to type commands in a terminal. Some knowledge about VPCs (Virtual Private Clouds): Understanding that your Google Cloud resources live in a private network. text: Introduction to APIs in Google Cloud GSP294 Google Cloud self paced labs Overview APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are software programs that give developers access to computing resources and data. Companies from many different fields offer publicly available APIs so that developers can integrate specialized tools, services, or libraries with their own applications and codebase. This lab reviews the architecture and basic functioning of APIs. This also provides hands on practice, where you configure and run Cloud Storage API methods in Google Cloud Shell. Taking this lab helps you understand the key principles of API communication, architecture, and authentication. You also gain practical experience with APIs, which you can apply to future labs or projects. APIs what and why The ability to access data and computing resources greatly increases a developer's efficiency. It is much easier to use an API than to build every single program, method, or dataset from scratch. APIs are built on the principle of abstraction—you don't need to understand the inner workings or complexities of an API to use it in your own environment. APIs are built with the developer in mind and often don't offer a graphical user interface (GUI). However, there are exceptions to this standard. Google has released a new tool called APIs Explorer, which allows you to explore various Google APIs interactively (be sure to check out the APIs Explorer: Qwik Start lab afterwards if you are interested in learning more.) Cloud APIs Google offers APIs that can be applied to many different fields and sectors. APIs are often used in web development, machine learning, data science, and system administration workflows. However, these are only a handful of use cases. By exploring AnyAPI, for example, you see that there are many APIs available. When Qwiklabs provisions a new Google Cloud Project for a lab instance, it enables most APIs behind the scenes so you can work on the lab's tasks right away. If you create your own projects outside of Qwiklabs, you must enable certain APIs yourself. As you gain proficiency as a Google Cloud user, you use more APIs in your workflow. Experienced users integrate and use Cloud APIs in their local environments almost exclusively, rarely using the Cloud Console to run tools and services. Dozens of Hands on Labs are available that give you practice with various Google APIs in different languages. In this lab, you explore the API library to see what Google APIs are available. Objectives In this lab, you learn about: Google APIs API architecture HTTP protocol and methods Endpoints REST (Representational State Transfer) and RESTful APIs JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) API authentication services Prerequisites This is an introductory level lab. This assumes little to no prior knowledge of APIs or experience using Google APIs. Familiarity with shell environments and command line interface tools is recommended, but not required. API architecture APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are a set of methods that allow programs to communicate with each other. To communicate effectively, programs must adhere to a clear protocol that governs the transfer and interpretation of data. The internet is the standard communication channel that APIs use to transmit requests and responses between programs. Web based APIs use the client server model as the underlying architecture for exchanging information. The client is a computing device that makes a request for some computing resource or data, and the server has data and/or computing resources stored on it, which interprets and fulfills the client's request. HTTP protocol and methods Since APIs use the web as a communication channel, many of them adhere to the HTTP protocol, which specifies rules and methods for data exchange between clients and servers over the internet. APIs that utilize the HTTP protocol use HTTP request methods (also known as "HTTP verbs") for transmitting client requests to servers. The most commonly used HTTP request methods are GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. GET is used by a client to fetch data from a server, PUT replaces existing data or creates data if it does not exist, POST is used primarily to create new resources, and DELETE removes data or resources specified by the client on a server. Endpoints APIs use HTTP methods to interact with data or computing services hosted on a server. These methods are useless if there isn't a way to access specific resources with consistency. APIs utilize communication channels called endpoints so that clients can access the resources they need without complication or irregularity. Endpoints are access points to data or computing resources hosted on a server and they take the form of an HTTP URI. Endpoints are added to an API's base URL to create a path to a specific resource or container of resources. Additionally, query strings can be added to endpoints to pass in variables that may be needed to complete an API's request. REST and RESTful APIs APIs that utilize the HTTP protocol, request methods, and endpoints are referred to as RESTful APIs. RESTful APIs live on the server, acting as an implementer for client requests. This model defines a framework of endpoints (nouns) that HTTP methods (verbs) act on, and APIs use this framework to fulfill requests. To summarize, RESTful APIs utilize the client server model, adhere to the HTTP protocol, utilize HTTP request methods, and utilize endpoints to access specific resources. Authenticate and authorize the Cloud Storage JSON/REST API Authentication and authorization Authentication and authorization are two terms that are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same thing. Authentication refers to the process of determining a client's identity. Authorization refers to the process of determining what permissions an authenticated client has for a set of resources. Authentication identifies who you are, and authorization determines what you can do. There are three types of authentication/authorization services that Google APIs use. These are "API Keys", "Service accounts", and "OAuth". An API uses one of these authentication services depending on the resources it requests and from where the API is called from. API keys API keys are secret tokens that usually come in the form of an encrypted string. API keys are quick to generate and use. Oftentimes, APIs that use public data or methods and want to get developers up and running use API keys to quickly authenticate users. In Google Cloud terms, API keys identify the calling project making the call to an API. By identifying the calling project, API keys enable usage information to be associated with that project, and they can reject calls from projects that haven't been granted access or enabled by the API. OAuth OAuth tokens are similar to API keys in their format, but they are more secure and can be linked to user accounts or identities. These tokens are used primarily when APIs give a developer the means to access user data. While API keys give developers access to all of an API's functionality, OAuth client IDs are all based on scope; different privileges are granted to different identities. Service Accounts A service account is a special type of Google account that belongs to your application or a virtual machine (VM) instead of to an individual end user. Your application assumes the identity of the service account to call Google APIs, so that the users aren't directly involved. You can use a service account by providing its private key to your application, or by using the built in service accounts available when running on Cloud Functions, Google App Engine, Compute Engine, or Google Kubernetes Engine. Publishing APIs with Apigee X GSP843 Google Cloud self paced labs Overview APIs are designed to be consumed by app developers, who leverage APIs to provide unique experiences for their users. Google Cloud's Apigee API Platform can be used to publish APIs and make them available for app developers to consume. In this lab, you create an Apigee API proxy, which requires API key verification to restrict access to the API. You create API products to provide different levels of service for internal and external application developers. You use a Quota policy to limit the number of calls for each specific application. You create a CORS policy to add Cross Origin Resource Sharing functionality to the API, which allows it to be called from web applications. You then create a developer portal and publish the API products for app developers to consume. What you'll learn In this lab, you learn how to perform the following tasks: Verify an API key to restrict access to an API and track application usage Create API products to provide different levels of access for different types of app developers Use the Quota policy to limit the number of calls for a particular application based on attached API product Add Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) functionality to an API to allow cross origin API calls from web applications Create a developer portal and publish the API products Setup and requirements Before you click the Start Lab button Read these instructions. Add CORS to the API proxy In this task, you add CORS (cross origin resource sharing) to the bank v1 proxy. CORS is a protocol that uses HTTP headers to indicate to browsers whether it is safe to access restricted resources from a separate domain. By default, cross domain requests are forbidden by the same origin security policy. The same origin policy protects browser users from unknowingly sharing session information with bad actors. The same origin policy means that a web page served from www.example.com could not, by default, make a call to APIs at api.example.com because the host name is different. CORS can be used to allow this kind of cross origin access. You will need CORS in the bank API for the developer portal. An Apigee developer portal has a domain name of \ .apigee.io , and the API is accessed via a different domain. Securing APIs with Apigee X GSP844 Google Cloud self paced labs Overview Apigee is a platform for developing and managing APIs. Apigee can help you secure access to your APIs and rate limit access to them. Apigee also provides features used to secure internal access to API data. In this lab, you create an API that requires OAuth tokens for access. You use the SpikeArrest policy to limit the rate of API calls by application, and you use private variables and data masking to hide sensitive data from users who debug API traffic. An OAuthV2 policy using the VerifyJWTAccessToken operation enforces verification of access tokens at runtime, allowing only applications with a valid OAuth access token to access the API. Note: 5 requests per minute is used to facilitate testing the SpikeArrest limits in this lab are typically too low for real world scenarios. UseEffectiveCount set to false specifies that the SpikeArrest policy is using the Token Bucket algorithm. The traffic is smoothed by dividing the rate into smaller intervals. 5 requests per minute means 1 request per one fifth of a minute, or 1 request every 12 seconds. When a second request comes into a message processor less than 12 seconds after the previous one, it may be rejected. Change the SpikeArrest policy configuration to: Like the previous policy, the configuration specifies that the maximum allowed rate of requests is 5 per minute . However, this policy specifies an Identifier , which maintains the SpikeArrest rate separately for each client\ id . The client ID is populated by the OA VerifyToken policy, and it is unique per developer application. UseEffectiveCount set to true specifies that the rate count is maintained for all traffic within the region. The policy maintains a counter of requests received per period, which is a minute long when using a rate of requests per minute . The rate calculation is based on a sliding window. A sliding window example, with the rate of 48 and 5. For this example shown above, assume we are using a rate of 50 requests per minute. The counters use a period of one minute, although the counter period would be one second if the rate had been specified per second. Assume that we are 10 seconds into the current minute, represented by the arrow. The previous minute had 48 requests, and the current period had 5 requests so far. To allow another request, the rate would need to be less than 50 requests per minute. The calculated rate is: request\ rate = (48 \ (60 10)/60) + 6 = 46 Since only 10 seconds out of 60 have elapsed in the current period, the other 50 seconds are calculated using the previous period's rate. 5/6 of 48 is 40. If a request were allowed, the count for the current period would be 5 + 1, or 6. The request rate calculation of 46 indicates that the request is allowed, because the request rate is less than 50 requests per minute. 6. Click Save Save as new revision . 7. The contents of your logs should typically include proxy flow variables that would help you debug any issues. For example, the variable publishmessage.failed will be true if the Pub/Sub message was not sent. Labels can also be added to the logged message to categorize the message contents. Deploy the API 1. Click Save . If you are notified that the proxy was saved as a new revision, click Save as new revision . 2. Click Deploy . 3. For Environment select eval . 4. For Service Account , specify the service account's email address: 5. Click Deploy and Confirm . Wait for the deployment to complete. Click Check my progress to verify the objective. Add the MessageLogging policy Test the API 1. In Cloud Shell, if your SSH connection has closed, open the SSH connection to your test VM: If asked to authorize, click Authorize . 2. Call the deployed services v1 API proxy in the eval environment: The category supplied (invalid category) does not have a corresponding Pub/Sub topic. 3. From the Navigation menu (Navigation menu icon), navigate to Monitoring Logs Explorer . 4. In the Query box, enter the following query: 5. Click Run query . 6. Expand the log entry in the Query Results pane, and then expand the jsonPayload . Expanding the log entry shows the logged JSON message and other metadata. The jsonPayload should resemble this: publishFailed is true because there wasn't a topic created for this category. Well designed logs can help find issues in your API proxies and backend services. You called the Cloud Natural Language API by using a ServiceCallout policy, leveraging the service account authentication provided by Apigee. You used the PublishMessage policy to publish a message to a Pub/Sub topic. Finally, you used the MessageLogging policy to log a message to Cloud Logging.
