Cloud IAM – Custom Roles Overview IAM grants access via roles (collections of permissions), not individual permissions. Predefined roles : managed/updated by Google. Custom roles : user defined, not auto updated — support least privilege design. Permission Format e.g. compute.instances.list, compute.instances.stop Custom Role Scope Created at project or organization level (not folder level). Usable only within the project/org that owns them. Required Permissions to Manage Custom Roles iam.roles.create Roles that grant this: Project Owner IAM Role Administrator (roles/iam.roleAdmin) Organization Role Administrator (roles/iam.organizationRoleAdmin) View only: IAM Security Reviewer (roles/iam.securityReviewer) Common Commands Create Custom Roles Using YAML File role definition.yaml: Using Flags List Custom Roles Update Custom Roles Via YAML (with etag) Via Flags Disable a Custom Role Disabled roles grant no permissions even if assigned. Delete / Restore a Custom Role Best Practices Use custom roles only when predefined roles are insufficient Keep permissions minimal Prefer DISABLED / DEPRECATED over immediate deletion Document role intent clearly 7. Service Accounts & Roles – Fundamentals Overview Service accounts : special Google accounts for applications/VMs (not humans), used for secure API/resource access. Permissions assigned via IAM roles, same as user accounts. Service Account Format Types User Managed Created/managed by users Defaults: Compute Engine default SA: PROJECT NUMBER compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com App Engine default SA: PROJECT ID@appspot.gserviceaccount.com Google Managed Created/owned by Google, used internally e.g. Google APIs Service Account: PROJECT NUMBER@cloudservices.gserviceaccount.com ⚠️ Do not remove or modify these. Role Types Recap Primitive: Owner, Editor, Viewer Predefined: service specific, Google managed Custom: user defined Roles can be assigned to users, groups, or service accounts . Create a Service Account & Grant Roles Service accounts act both as an identity (what it can do) and a resource (who can impersonate it). Example: BigQuery via Service Account Create SA bigquery qwiklab with roles: BigQuery Data Viewer BigQuery User Create VM bigquery instance (e2 medium, Debian 12), attach this SA, enable BigQuery API scope. Install Dependencies (on VM) Query BigQuery Using Service Account Credentials Key Takeaways Service accounts = secure identities for workloads Apply least privilege roles Prefer predefined roles when available Avoid Editor/Owner unless necessary Never delete Google managed service accounts 8. VPC Network Peering Overview VPC Network Peering enables private connectivity between two VPC networks (same or different projects/orgs) using internal IPs, entirely over Google's network. Benefits Low latency (private) Improved security (no public IP exposure) Reduced cost (no internet egress charges) Useful for SaaS architectures across orgs Key Characteristics Networks remain independent No transitive peering CIDR ranges must not overlap Full mesh VM to VM connectivity Supports Internal Load Balancers Lab Setup Two projects (project A, project B), each with one custom VPC + VM. Peering must be configured bidirectionally. Task 1: Create Custom VPCs Project A Project B Task 2: Configure VPC Peering Peer network a → network b (project A) Connection name: peer ab Network: network a Peer project: PROJECT ID 2 Peer network: network b Status: INACTIVE (waiting for reverse peering) Peer network b → network a (project B) Connection name: peer ba Network: network b Peer project: PROJECT ID 1 Peer network: network a Status: ACTIVE ✅ Routes are exchanged automatically once both sides are configured. Verify Routes Should show routes for 10.0.0.0/16, 10.8.0.0/16, and peering next hops. Task 3: Test Connectivity Get internal IP of vm a SSH into vm b, run: ✅ Successful ICMP responses confirm peering works. Traffic Supported After Peering VM ↔ VM (full mesh) VM ↔ Internal Load Balancer Private RFC1918 IPs only Best Practices Avoid CIDR overlap Use explicit firewall rules Peering must be configured on both sides Use Shared VPC if centralized control is needed Comparison | Feature | VPC Peering | VPN | Public IP | | | | | | | Latency | Low | Medium | High | | Security | High | Medium | Low | | Encryption | Internal | Yes | No | | Cost | Low | Medium | High | 9. Identity Aware Proxy (IAP) – Cloud Run Authentication Overview IAP protects applications by: Authenticating users via Google Identity Allowing access only to authorized users Injecting verified user identity headers into requests ✅ Minimal/no in app authentication code required. Architecture Flow Task 1: Deploy Cloud Run App & Enable IAP Console → Security → Identity Aware Proxy → enable IAP for the Cloud Run service. Grant access: add user as principal with role IAP Secured Web App User . ✅ Only authorized users can access the app afterward. Task 2: Access User Identity Information IAP injects these headers: | Header | Description | | | | | X Goog Authenticated User Email | User email | | X Goog Authenticated User ID | Persistent unique ID | Read Identity (Python/Flask) ⚠️ Spoofing Risk If IAP is disabled or bypassed, these headers can be forged: The app cannot detect spoofing without cryptographic verification. Task 3: Cryptographic Verification (Secure Method) Uses the signed JWT header X Goog IAP JWT Assertion (signed by Google private keys). Enable Verified Identity Verified Identity Code (Simplified) Grant IAP Permission to Invoke Cloud Run Behavior Summary | Scenario | Result | | | | | IAP ON + Verified | ✅ Secure identity | | IAP OFF | ❌ No identity | | Header spoof attempt | ❌ Rejected (with verification) | Best Practices Always use cryptographic verification for sensitive apps Never trust raw headers without IAP Use IAP for internal tools, admin dashboards, SaaS apps, Cloud Run/GKE/App Engine Key Takeaways IAP = Authentication + Authorization Minimal app code required JWT verification prevents spoofing 10. Cloud KMS – Getting Started Overview Cloud KMS lets you: Create/manage encryption keys Encrypt/decrypt sensitive data Control access via IAM Audit key usage via Cloud Audit Logs Key Concepts KeyRing : logical grouping of CryptoKeys; cannot be deleted; scoped to a location. CryptoKey : actual encryption key; cannot be deleted. Task 1: Create Storage Bucket Task 2: Review Sample Data Task 3: Enable Cloud KMS Task 4: Create KeyRing & CryptoKey Task 5: Encrypt & Decrypt Data Task 6: Configure IAM Permissions | Role | Purpose | | | | | roles/cloudkms.admin | Manage keys | | roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter | Encrypt & decrypt | Task 7: Encrypt Multiple Files (Backup Script) Task 8: View Audit Logs Cloud Overview → Activity → Log Explorer Resource type: Cloud KMS Key Ring View: key creation, encrypt/decrypt actions, IAM changes Best Practices Use IAM least privilege Rotate keys periodically Prefer Cloud Storage CMEK for production Monitor audit logs regularly Key Takeaways Cloud KMS secures sensitive data centrally IAM controls key usage Audit logs give full visibility 11. Private Kubernetes (GKE) Cluster Overview A private GKE cluster: No public IPs on nodes Private control plane endpoint VPC peered communication Uses defined CIDR ranges for master, nodes, pods, services Key Characteristics Master endpoint not reachable from public internet Nodes have private IPs only Requires IP aliasing Admin access via Master Authorized Networks Task 1: Set Region/Zone Task 2: Create Private Cluster (Auto Subnet) Cluster name: private cluster Master CIDR: 172.16.0.16/28 Machine type: e2 medium Task 3: View Subnet & Secondary Ranges Primary range → Nodes Secondary ranges → Pods, Services privateIpGoogleAccess = true → nodes access Google APIs privately Task 4: Enable Master Authorized Networks Access Cluster from VM Task 5: Clean Up Task 6: Private Cluster with Custom Subnet Create Custom Subnet Create Private Cluster Using Custom Subnet Authorize External Access Again Network Access Summary | Component | Access | | | | | Master | Private + authorized CIDR only | | Nodes | Private IP only | | Pods | Secondary IP range | | Services | Secondary IP range | Best Practices Always use Master Authorized Networks Avoid overlapping CIDR ranges Use custom subnets for production Combine with Private Google Access 12. Automated scoring validates each task. Global constraints : Use specified region/zone; all resources must use prefix orca . Required permissions: Task 2: Create Service Account Dedicated SA, used only by the GKE cluster Name: orca service account Task 3: Bind IAM Roles to Service Account (Least Privilege) Built in roles: Plus the custom storage role from Task 1. to events (e.g., file upload, pub/sub) | Cloud Functions | | You need fine control over infra/networking | GKE (Kubernetes) | | Long running or background processing | Cloud Run / GKE | | Monolith app you want to scale easily | App Engine Flexible | | Microservices with moderate complexity | Cloud Run / GKE | 🎯 Visual Summary When you see Google Cloud Pub/Sub being used with Cloud Run or Cloud Functions , it’s usually because of how these services are designed compared to Kafka or gRPC. ⚖️ Why Pub/Sub instead of Kafka or gRPC in Cloud Run / Cloud Functions? 1. Cloud Functions / Cloud Run are serverless & event driven They scale to zero when idle and spin up on demand. Pub/Sub integrates natively: push or pull events trigger the function automatically. You don’t need to manage connections, brokers, or workers → Pub/Sub handles delivery + retries. 👉 With Kafka , you’d need a long running consumer to poll a topic. Cloud Functions don’t stay alive for that. 2. gRPC is synchronous, but Functions are async gRPC works best for low latency, always on microservices talking directly. Cloud Functions are short lived, ephemeral , designed for event triggers (not open streams). Using gRPC would require the function to stay active to handle requests → not cost efficient in serverless. 3. Pub/Sub fits the “fire and forget” event model Functions usually react to events : New file uploaded to GCS → Pub/Sub event → Cloud Function processes it. API request → Publish to Pub/Sub → Function scales out and handles jobs. Pub/Sub guarantees at least once delivery , retries, dead letter topics. Kafka could do this too, but in GCP: Kafka = extra infra (self manage or use Confluent Cloud). Pub/Sub = fully managed, integrated with IAM, billing, and Cloud Run triggers. 4. Simplicity and ecosystem integration Pub/Sub integrates directly with: Cloud Storage Cloud Run Cloud Functions BigQuery, Dataflow, Firestore, etc. Kafka has richer features for event streaming, but is heavier and overkill for lightweight serverless event triggers. ✅ When to choose what (Rule of Thumb) Pub/Sub + Cloud Run/Functions Event driven workloads. Serverless scale to zero needed. Native GCP ecosystem integration. Example: “Process every uploaded image asynchronously.” Kafka + Kubernetes (GKE, VM based microservices) Large scale event streaming with high throughput. Need replay, ordering guarantees, stream processing (Flink, ksqlDB). Example: “Process billions of user activity logs for analytics.” gRPC between microservices Real time request/response, streaming APIs. Low latency, strongly typed communication. Example: “Payment service calling fraud detection service.” ⚡ So in short: 👉 In Cloud Run/Functions , Pub/Sub is used because it’s event driven, managed, and integrates natively with ephemeral, scale to zero workloads . Kafka and gRPC don’t fit as neatly into that serverless model. Perfect 👍 — here’s an ASCII flow diagram (Markdown) showing how Pub/Sub, Kafka, and gRPC typically integrate with Cloud Run / Cloud Functions vs Microservices . ✅ Key Takeaway Pub/Sub + Cloud Functions/Run → Event driven, serverless, auto scaling, scale to zero. Kafka → High throughput, persistent streaming backbone, needs long running consumers. gRPC → Real time RPC between always on microservices, tightly coupled schema. Choosing between Cloud Functions and Cloud Run depends on the nature of your application, workload, and requirements. Let’s break it down carefully: 1. Cloud Functions Type: Serverless Functions (FaaS – Function as a Service) Trigger based: Automatically runs in response to events (HTTP requests, Pub/Sub messages, Firestore changes, etc.) Execution: Short lived tasks (typically <9 minutes) Scaling: Fully automatic, scales from 0 to N instances depending on demand Deployment: Simple – just upload your code Language support: Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Ruby, .NET, etc. Best for: Event driven tasks Lightweight APIs or microservices Backend for mobile or web apps that respond to triggers Tasks that don’t need custom runtime or OS level control Pros: No server management Pay only for actual execution time Easy to integrate with other Google Cloud services Cons: Limited execution time Limited control over the runtime environment Harder to handle complex workflows or long running processes 2. Cloud Run Type: Serverless Containers Trigger based: Can handle HTTP requests directly Execution: Can run long lived tasks Scaling: Automatically scales from 0 to N instances based on traffic Deployment: Deploy a container (Docker or OCI) – any language, any library, any binary Best for: HTTP based microservices Applications that need custom dependencies or libraries Workloads that require long running processes or larger memory/CPU Migrating existing containerized apps to serverless Pros: Full control over runtime and environment Supports long running services Can run any programming language or framework via container Can respond to high traffic spikes Cons: Slightly more complex deployment (requires Docker/containers) Billing is per instance time (even when idle instances exist, but scales to zero when no traffic) Decision Guide | Criteria | Cloud Functions | Cloud Run | | | | | | Execution Type | Short, event driven | Long running HTTP services | | Runtime Flexibility | Limited (predefined languages) | Fully customizable (any container) | | Scaling | Automatic, instant | Automatic, may have small startup latency | | Deployment Complexity | Very simple | Moderate (containerization needed) | | Cost | Pay per execution | Pay per instance runtime | | Use Case Examples | Pub/Sub triggers, webhook, CRON | REST APIs, microservices, backend apps | 🧩 1. Google Compute Engine (GCE) — Virtual Machines (IaaS) 💡 Think of this as: “Your own server in the cloud.” ✅ You can run: DevOps tools : Jenkins, SonarQube, Nexus, GitLab Runner Databases : MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB Middleware : Apache, Nginx, Tomcat, WebLogic Container runtimes : Docker, containerd Security tools : Vault, ELK Stack (Elastic, Logstash, Kibana) Networking / Infra agents : Prometheus, Grafana, Consul, etc. Custom enterprise apps (legacy or modern) 🧠 Basically: Anything you can install on a Linux/Windows VM — including full control of OS, packages, and networking. 🚀 2. App Engine (GAE) — Platform as a Service (PaaS) 💡 Think of this as: “Just deploy your code — Google handles the rest.” ✅ You can run: Web APIs and apps written in: Python , Java , Node.js , Go , PHP , .NET , Ruby REST APIs, backend web services Lightweight microservices Websites or dashboards ❌ Not suitable for: Jenkins, SonarQube, or tools needing full OS access Custom binaries or background daemons 🧠 It’s code only deployment , not infrastructure level — good for developers , not sysadmins. 🐳 3. Cloud Run — Serverless Containers (CaaS) 💡 Think of this as: “Deploy any container easily, without managing servers.” ✅ You can run: Docker containers with any runtime or language Microservices built with Spring Boot, Flask, Express.js, etc. APIs or backend tasks (HTTP based) Event driven jobs using Pub/Sub triggers Lightweight tools like: API wrappers, webhook receivers, schedulers, CI helpers ❌ Not suitable for: Stateful apps (like Jenkins master or databases) Long running background services (timeout limits) 🧠 Great for stateless containerized workloads with scaling to zero. ☸️ 4. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — Managed Kubernetes 💡 Think of this as: “You manage apps inside containers, Google manages the cluster.” ✅ You can run: Microservices architecture Jenkins (in containers) SonarQube , Apigee hybrid gateway , ELK stack Custom container workloads Message processing apps using Pub/Sub , Kafka, RabbitMQ ML pipelines using TensorFlow Serving, Kubeflow ❌ Not ideal for: Tiny single function apps — overhead is higher Purely serverless use cases (Cloud Run fits better) 🧠 GKE gives you container orchestration power with scaling, networking, and resilience — ideal for modern DevOps teams. ⚙️ 5. Cloud Functions — Serverless Functions (FaaS) 💡 Think of this as: “Run small pieces of code when something happens.” ✅ You can run: Event driven logic , e.g.: Triggered by Pub/Sub , Cloud Storage , HTTP , or Firestore Lightweight APIs CI/CD triggers Data processing tasks ❌ Not suitable for: Stateful or long running jobs Jenkins, Docker, or anything needing an OS 🧠 Use for automation, glue code, and backend triggers — not for full applications. 🧱 Summary Table | GCP Service | Type | Control Level | Examples You Can Run | Ideal For | | | | | | | | Compute Engine | IaaS | Full (VM level) | Jenkins, SonarQube, Docker, DBs, ELK | Traditional apps, infra tools | | App Engine | PaaS | Limited | Web APIs, Dashboards | Code only apps | | Cloud Run | CaaS | Medium | Dockerized APIs, microservices | Stateless containers | | GKE (Kubernetes Engine) | Managed K8s | High | Jenkins agents, Apigee hybrid, Microservices | Container orchestration | | Cloud Functions | FaaS | Minimal | Event driven code, triggers | Serverless automation | ⚡ Example Use Case Mapping | Tool / Service | Best Place to Run | | | | | Jenkins | Compute Engine (VM) or GKE | | SonarQube | Compute Engine or GKE | | Docker | GCE, GKE, or Cloud Run | | Kubernetes | GKE (native) | | Apigee | Managed by GCP (Apigee X) or GKE (Apigee hybrid) | | Pub/Sub | It’s a service (not hosted), can trigger Cloud Functions / Run | | Grafana / Prometheus | GCE or GKE | | Databases (Postgres/MySQL) | Cloud SQL (managed) or GCE (self hosted) | ✅ Rule of Thumb: If you have simple event driven logic or lightweight API endpoints → Cloud Functions If you need full control, long running tasks, or complex services → Cloud Run Stack Trace https://googlecloudplatform.github.io/spring cloud https://opentelemetry.io/ Google Cloud Dataflow is a serverless, managed stream and batch processing service built on Apache Beam that automatically scales resources and handles complex data engineering tasks. Google Cloud Dataproc is a managed Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark service that provides managed clusters for big data processing using open source tools, requiring more manual infrastructure management than Dataflow. The choice depends on factors like the need for serverless operation (Dataflow) versus fine grained cluster control (Dataproc), specific ecosystem tools needed (Beam vs. Hadoop/Spark), and operational preferences. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Choose Dataflow if you need: • Serverless Operation: Dataflow is fully serverless, meaning you don't have to manage underlying infrastructure like clusters. [2, 3] • Unified Batch and Streaming: It provides a single framework (Apache Beam) for building both batch and streaming data processing pipelines. [1, 2] • Automatic Scaling: Dataflow dynamically scales resources up or down based on job demand, optimizing performance and cost. [2, 6, 7] • Simplified Development: Focus on the logical computation of your pipeline rather than the specifics of how data is processed on a particular runner. [2, 8] Choose Dataproc if you need: • Open Source Hadoop/Spark Expertise: You or your team are already familiar with and want to use Apache Spark, Hadoop, or other tools in the Hadoop ecosystem. [3, 4, 8] • Fine grained Cluster Control: You require more control over the underlying infrastructure and cluster configuration for specific workloads. [2, 5] • Specific Tool Integration: Your workflow relies on tools beyond the Apache Beam ecosystem, such as Hive, Pig, or Flink, which are readily available in Dataproc. [4, 8] • Cost Optimization: Dataproc allows for managing clusters, including the ability to turn them off when not in use and utilize preemptible instances for cost savings. [2, 5] Key Differences Summarized | Feature | Dataflow | Dataproc | | | | | | Underlying Technology | Apache Beam | Apache Spark, Hadoop, etc. | | Operational Model | Serverless and fully managed | Managed service for Hadoop/Spark clusters | | Infrastructure Management | Largely automated | Requires more cluster and infrastructure management | | Workload Focus | Unified batch and stream processing | Batch, streaming, querying, machine learning with Hadoop/Spark tools | | Scaling | Automatic, dynamic, and granular | Cluster based, with autoscaling policies available | AI responses may include mistakes. text: Git & GitHub Q\&A and Commands Git & GitHub Q\&A and Commands <details <summary <strong 1. You can use Git without GitHub , but GitHub requires Git to manage repositories. </details <details <summary <strong 2. Push Contents to an Existing Repo</strong </summary m → message M → Move (force rename) u → Upstream tracking Common Git commands Check local changes: git status Fetch remote changes (without merge): git fetch Pull remote changes and merge: git pull </details <details <summary <strong 4. Navigate Directories in Git Bash</strong </summary Go home directory: cd or cd Go up one directory: cd .. Go back to previous directory: cd Go to root: cd / Navigate multiple levels: cd /folder/subfolder/ Example: </details <details <summary <strong 5. Remove Files/Folders</strong </summary Rename files: </details <details <summary <strong 6. Branch Management</strong </summary Create a new branch: Create and switch to new branch: ✅ Difference git checkout b → older, multifunction command (used for branches + files) git switch c → newer, clearer command dedicated to branch switching 💡 Both commands do the same thing : 👉 create branch + move HEAD to it immediately Check branch origin: Compare two branches: </details <details <summary <strong 8. SSH Key Generation for GitHub</strong </summary Generate SSH key: Press enter to accept default file location. Enter a passphrase or leave blank. Add generated public key (id ed25519.pub) to GitHub at https://github.com/settings/ssh/new. List .ssh folder: </details <details <summary <strong 9. Pushing to Codeberg (or other Git hosting)</strong </summary Push existing repo: </details <details <summary <strong 10. Using Git in IDE (e.g., IntelliJ)</strong </summary Clone repository via VCS Git paste clone URL Clone. Switch branches via bottom right corner branch icon. Use Ctrl+Shift+R to find/replace in project. Use commit tab to select files, commit and push. </details <details <summary <strong 11. NPM Commands</strong </summary Install packages with offline mode and no audit: Show npm config: Update npm globally: List globally installed packages: Show outdated packages: </details <details <summary <strong 12. Git Pull vs Fetch</strong </summary | Command | Description | Use case | | | | | | git fetch | Downloads changes from remote but does not merge into your working branch. | Review changes before merging. Safer. | | git pull | Downloads changes and immediately merges into your current branch. | Quick update and merge. More convenient. | Summary: Fetch = get changes only Pull = get + merge changes Use fetch to review first, pull to update fast. </details Sure! Here’s a step by step Git beginner tutorial in a clear, friendly way: <details <summary <strong Step 1: Install Git</strong </summary Download Git from git scm.com and install it on your computer. After installation, you can use Git via command line (Git Bash on Windows) or GUI tools like GitHub Desktop. </details <details <summary <strong Step 2: Configure Git</strong </summary Open your terminal or Git Bash and set your identity so Git knows who you are: This info will appear in your commits. </details <details <summary <strong Step 3: Create a New Repository</strong </summary To create a new Git repository in an existing folder: This starts tracking files in that folder. </details <details <summary <strong Step 4: Stage and Commit Changes</strong </summary 1. Add files to the staging area (preparing them for commit): 2. Commit your changes with a message: Each commit is like a snapshot of your project. </details <details <summary <strong Step 5: Connect to a Remote Repository</strong </summary If you want to push your code to GitHub or any Git server: Replace the URL with your repo URL. </details <details <summary <strong Step 6: Push Changes to Remote</strong </summary Send your commits to the remote server: The u sets the upstream branch so next pushes can be done simply by git push. </details <details <summary <strong Step 7: Pull Latest Changes</strong </summary To update your local repo with changes from remote: This fetches and merges remote changes. </details Great! Here’s a clear, friendly explanation of branching and merging in Git with collapsible sections: <details <summary <strong What is a Branch?</strong </summary A branch is a separate line of development in your project. Think of it like a parallel universe where you can try new features or fixes without affecting the main code. The default branch is usually called main or master. </details <details <summary <strong Why Use Branches?</strong </summary To work on new features independently. To fix bugs safely. To experiment without breaking the stable code. To collaborate with others without conflict. </details <details <summary <strong How to Create and Switch Branches</strong </summary 1. Create a new branch: 2. Switch to the new branch: Or combine both in one command: From Git 2.23+, you can also use: </details <details <summary <strong Check Which Branch You Are On</strong </summary The current branch will be highlighted with a . </details <details <summary <strong Make Changes and Commit on Your Branch</strong </summary Just like usual: These commits stay isolated on your branch. </details <details <summary <strong Merging Branches</strong </summary When your feature or fix is ready, merge your branch into another branch (usually main): 1. Switch to the branch you want to merge into: 2. Merge the feature branch: This will bring all the commits from feature branch into main. </details <details <summary <strong Resolving Merge Conflicts</strong </summary Sometimes Git can’t automatically merge files because of conflicting changes. You will see conflict markers like <<<<<<, ======, . You need to manually edit the files to resolve conflicts. After fixing, add and commit: </details <details <summary <strong Deleting a Branch After Merge</strong </summary If you no longer need the feature branch: If the branch is not merged and you want to force delete: </details Awesome! Here’s a clear and friendly explanation of Git Rebase with collapsible markdown: <details <summary <strong What is Git Rebase?</strong </summary Git rebase is a way to reapply commits from one branch onto another base commit . Instead of merging branches with a merge commit, rebase rewrites history by moving your branch’s commits on top of another branch. It helps keep a clean, linear commit history . </details <details <summary <strong Why Use Rebase?</strong </summary To keep commit history simple and linear. To avoid unnecessary merge commits. To update your feature branch with the latest changes from the main branch before merging. Makes reviewing history easier. </details <details <summary <strong How to Use Rebase</strong </summary Suppose you’re working on feature branch and want to update it with the latest main branch changes: 1. Checkout your feature branch: 2. Rebase on top of main: This takes your feature commits and reapplies them after the latest commits from main. </details <details <summary <strong What Happens During Rebase?</strong </summary Git temporarily saves your commits. Resets your branch to point at the target branch (main). Reapplies your commits one by one on top of main. If there are conflicts, Git pauses and asks you to resolve them. </details <details <summary <strong Resolving Conflicts During Rebase</strong </summary Git will stop on a conflicted commit and show which files have conflicts. Fix the conflicts manually. Stage the resolved files: Continue the rebase: To abort the rebase and go back to the original state: </details <details <summary <strong Rebase vs Merge</strong </summary | Feature | Merge | Rebase | | | | | | History | Creates a merge commit, keeps branch structure | Rewrites commits to create linear history | | Commit Graph | Branching and merging shown | Linear commit history | | Conflict Handling | Conflicts handled once during merge | Conflicts may need to be resolved multiple times during rebase | | Use Case | Good for preserving full history | Good for clean history before merging feature branches | </details <details <summary <strong When NOT to Rebase</strong </summary Don’t rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared/public repository — it rewrites history and can cause problems for others. Safe to rebase only your local branches or branches that nobody else is using yet. </details

title: Graphql Quarkus Guide
text: GraphQL in Quarkus: Complete Beginner to Advanced Guide Table of Contents 1. Basic Part 2. Intermediate Part 3. Advanced Part Basic Part What is Quarkus? Simple Explanation: Imagine you're building a web application (like a bookstore website). Traditionally, Java applications take a long time to start (20 30 seconds) and use a lot of computer memory (500MB 1GB). Quarkus is a modern Java framework that changes this completely. Think of it like this: Traditional Java App : Like starting a big diesel truck takes time to warm up, uses lots of fuel Quarkus App : Like starting an electric car instant start, very efficient Key Benefits for Beginners: 1. Super Fast Startup Your application starts in less than 1 second (instead of 20 30 seconds) 2. Low Memory Usage Uses only 50 100MB of RAM (instead of 500MB 1GB) 3. Live Reload Change your code and see results immediately without restarting 4. Easy to Learn Uses familiar Java concepts you already know 5. Cloud Ready Perfect for modern cloud deployments (AWS, Google Cloud, etc.) Real World Analogy: If you're building a food delivery app: Traditional Java : Opening a full restaurant expensive, slow to set up Quarkus : Running a food truck quick to start, efficient, can serve customers immediately Why It Matters: For Development : You save time because your app restarts instantly when you make changes For Production : You save money because it uses less server resources For Users : Your app responds faster and handles more requests What is GraphQL? Simple Explanation: GraphQL is a way for your frontend (website or mobile app) to ask your backend (server) for exactly the data it needs nothing more, nothing less. Real World Analogy: Imagine you're at a restaurant: Traditional REST API (Old Way): You: "I want the lunch combo" Waiter brings: Burger, fries, drink, salad, dessert You: "But I only wanted the burger and fries..." Problem: You got too much (over fetching) Or: You: "I want a burger" Waiter: "Okay!" (brings burger) You: "Now I want fries" Waiter: "Okay!" (brings fries) You: "Now I want a drink" Problem: Too many trips (multiple requests) GraphQL (New Way): You: "I want a burger and fries, no drink, no salad" Waiter brings: Exactly burger and fries Result: You get exactly what you want in one trip! Visual Example: Why GraphQL is Better (Especially for Mobile Apps): 1. Saves Data Mobile users don't download unnecessary data 2. Faster One request instead of many 3. Flexible Different screens can ask for different data 4. Easy to Understand You see exactly what data you're getting Simple Example: Let's say you're building a book store app: With GraphQL, you ask for ONLY what you need: With REST, you'd get ALL the book data even if you don't use it! How GraphQL Works in Quarkus Simple Explanation: Quarkus makes it super easy to build GraphQL APIs. Instead of writing lots of configuration, you just write simple Java classes with special annotations (markers), and Quarkus automatically creates the GraphQL API for you. The Stack (What's Working Behind the Scenes): What This Means for You: You don't need to learn GraphQL syntax deeply You just write normal Java code Quarkus converts it to GraphQL automatically You get a working GraphQL API with very little code Setting Up GraphQL in Quarkus (Step by Step for Beginners) What We're Doing: We need to tell Quarkus that we want to use GraphQL. We do this by adding "dependencies" think of these as ingredients for a recipe. Understanding Dependencies: When you cook, you need ingredients. When you code, you need dependencies (libraries of pre written code). Step 1: Add Dependencies If you're using Maven (build tool like a recipe manager): Add this to your pom.xml file: What each dependency does: 1. quarkus smallrye graphql The core GraphQL engine (Required) This is like getting the stove and oven for your kitchen 2. quarkus smallrye graphql ui A web interface to test your API (Optional but very helpful) This is like having a food tasting area where you can try your dishes If you're using Gradle (another build tool): Add this to your build.gradle file: Same dependencies, just different syntax! Basic Configuration (Setting Up Your API) What is Configuration? Configuration is like setting up the rules for your app where should it run, what features should be enabled, etc. Where to configure: Create or edit a file called application.properties in your project's src/main/resources folder. Understanding Each Setting: Real World Example: Imagine you're setting up a store: root path = The address of your store (123 Main Street) ui.enable = Should you have a showroom? (Yes for testing) cors.origins = Which delivery services can pick up orders (your frontend apps) print data fetcher exception = Should employees see detailed error logs? (Yes during setup, maybe not when open to public) What You'll See: After configuration, you can: 1. Send GraphQL queries to: http://localhost:8080/graphql 2. Test your API visually at: http://localhost:8080/graphql ui Creating Your First GraphQL API (Complete Walkthrough) What We're Building: A simple bookstore API where you can: Get a list of all books Get a specific book by its ID Add a new book Delete a book Think of it like this: We're building a library system where: Books are stored in memory (like index cards) We can view, add, and remove books Everything is accessible through GraphQL Step 1: Create a Book Model (What is a Book?) What is a Model? A model is like a blueprint or template. It defines what a "Book" looks like in our system. Real World Analogy: Think of a library card catalog. Each card has: ID number Book title Author name Number of pages Price That's exactly what we're creating in code! Why Do We Need Getters and Setters? Getters : Like asking "What's the book's title?" Setters : Like saying "Change the book's title to 'New Title'" This is a Java best practice for controlling access to data Step 2: Create the GraphQL API Resource What is a Resource? A Resource is where you define what operations people can do with your data. It's like the librarian who handles all the requests. Operations We'll Create: 1. Query Reading data (like asking "What books do you have?") 2. Mutation Changing data (like saying "Add this new book" or "Remove that book") What Just Happened? We created a complete GraphQL API! Here's what each part does: 1. Storage : We store books in a simple list (in real apps, this would be a database) 2. ID Counter : Automatically generates unique IDs for new books 3. getAllBooks() : Returns all books (like viewing the entire library catalog) 4. bookById() : Finds one specific book (like looking up a book by its barcode) 5. addBook() : Creates a new book (like the librarian adding a new book to the collection) 6. deleteBook() : Removes a book (like removing a book from the library) Key Concepts: @Query = Operations that READ data (don't change anything) @Mutation = Operations that WRITE/CHANGE data (add, update, delete) @Name = Gives a parameter a specific name in GraphQL Step 3: Understanding the Generated GraphQL Schema What is a Schema? A schema is like a menu at a restaurant it shows what's available and how to order it. The Magic Part: You don't write the schema! Quarkus looks at your Java code and automatically creates the GraphQL schema for you. The Generated Schema: Based on our Java code above, Quarkus automatically creates this: Understanding the Symbols: ! = Required (must provide this) No ! = Optional (can skip this) [Book!]! = A list that's never null, containing books that are never null Book = Might return null (book might not exist) How Java Types Convert to GraphQL Types: Real World Example: Imagine a restaurant menu: Testing Your GraphQL API (Multiple Ways) Now that we've built our API, let's test it! There are several ways to do this. Method 1: Using GraphQL UI (Easiest for Beginners) What is GraphQL UI? It's a visual, interactive playground where you can test your API without writing code. Think of it like a test kitchen where you can try out your recipes. Step by Step: 1. Start your Quarkus application 2. Open your web browser Go to: http://localhost:8080/graphql ui You'll see a nice interface with: Left side: Where you type queries Right side: Where you see results Middle: A "Play" button to run your query 3. Try Your First Query (Get all books) Type this in the left panel: Click the Play button ▶️ What you'll see: What just happened? You asked for all books You specified you want: id, title, author, and price GraphQL returned exactly those fields! 4. Try Getting One Specific Book Result: Notice: We only asked for title and author, so we only got those! 5. Try Adding a New Book (Mutation) Result: What happened? You created a new book It was assigned ID: 3 (automatically) The new book was added to the list 6. Try Deleting a Book Result: true means it was successfully deleted! Method 2: Using cURL (Command Line) What is cURL? A command line tool to send HTTP requests. Good for automated testing or scripts. Getting All Books: What each part means: curl = The command X POST = We're sending a POST request http://localhost:8080/graphql = Where to send it H "Content Type: application/json" = We're sending JSON d '...' = The data we're sending (our GraphQL query) Adding a Book: Note: In cURL, you need to escape quotes with \" Method 3: Using Postman (GUI Tool) What is Postman? A popular application for testing APIs with a nice graphical interface. Steps: 1. Open Postman 2. Create a new POST request 3. URL: http://localhost:8080/graphql 4. Headers: Add Content Type: application/json 5. Body (raw, JSON): 6. Click Send Understanding the Request/Response Flow Here's what happens when you send a query: Key Points: 1. Client sends a query Asks for specific data 2. Quarkus receives it HTTP layer handles the request 3. GraphQL engine parses Understands what you're asking for 4. Validates Checks if your query is valid 5. Executes your code Calls your @Query or @Mutation method 6. Filters results Only returns fields you asked for 7. Sends response Returns formatted JSON This all happens in milliseconds! Understanding GraphQL Annotations (The Special Markers) What are Annotations? Annotations are special markers in Java that start with @. They give instructions to the framework about how to handle your code. Think of them as sticky notes that say "Hey Quarkus, treat this in a special way!" Real World Analogy: Imagine you're writing a cookbook: @Recipe Marks something as a recipe @Ingredient Marks something as an ingredient @Step Marks something as a cooking step In GraphQL/Quarkus, we use similar markers! Complete Guide to GraphQL Annotations Complete Example Using Multiple Annotations What the Generated GraphQL Schema Looks Like: Benefits of Using Annotations: 1. Self Documenting Your API documentation is in your code 2. Type Safety Compiler checks your code 3. Less Boilerplate No need to write schema files separately 4. Maintenance Change code once, schema updates automatically Quick Reference Table | Annotation | Use On | Purpose | Example | | | | | | | @GraphQLApi | Class | Mark as GraphQL API | @GraphQLApi public class BookResource | | @Query | Method | Read data | @Query public List<Book getBooks() | | @Mutation | Method | Change data | @Mutation public Book addBook() | | @Name | Parameter | Name a parameter | @Name("id") Long bookId | | @Description | Any | Add documentation | @Description("A book") | | @NonNull | Field/Parameter | Make required | @NonNull String title | | @DefaultValue | Parameter | Set default | @DefaultValue("10") Integer limit | | @Ignore | Field | Exclude from schema | @Ignore private String internal | | @DateFormat | Field | Format dates | @DateFormat("yyyy MM dd") | | @NumberFormat | Field | Format numbers | @NumberFormat("00.00") | This covers all the basic annotations you need to build GraphQL APIs in Quarkus! Intermediate Part What You'll Learn in This Section: Now that you understand the basics, we'll explore more realistic scenarios: How to connect related data (like authors and their books) Working with real databases instead of in memory lists Handling large datasets with pagination Adding security to protect your API Dealing with errors gracefully Real World Context: The basic part taught you to build a simple bookstore. The intermediate part teaches you to build a real bookstore with: Multiple related tables (authors, books, reviews) Actual database storage User authentication Professional error handling Think of it as moving from a lemonade stand to a real store! Understanding Data Relationships (How Things Connect) What Are Relationships? In the real world, data is connected. For example: An Author writes many Books A Book has one Author A Book has many Reviews A Review is written by one User This is called "relationships" how different pieces of data relate to each other. Visual Example: One to Many Relationship (Beginner's Guide) What is One to Many? One author has many books One book has many reviews One customer has many orders Real World Analogy: Think of a family tree: One parent → Many children One teacher → Many students One company → Many employees Let's build an Author to Books relationship! Step 1: Create the Author Model What We're Building: An Author who can have multiple books. Each author has: An ID (unique identifier) A name An email A list of books they've written Step 2: Update the Book Model What Changed: Books now need to remember which author wrote them. We add an authorId field. Step 3: Create a Book Service What is a Service? A service is a helper class that handles specific tasks. In this case, it manages book related operations. Why Use a Service? Separation of Concerns : GraphQL resource focuses on handling requests, service focuses on business logic Reusability : Multiple parts of your app can use the same service Testability : Easier to test business logic separately Step 4: Create the Author GraphQL Resource The Magic Part Field Resolvers: This is where GraphQL really shines. We can define HOW to get an author's books. Understanding the Generated GraphQL Schema What Gets Generated: How to Use This in Practice Example 1: Get all authors with their books What Happens Behind the Scenes: Response: Example 2: Get just author names and book count The Beauty of GraphQL: Even though we CAN get books, we don't have to! The books() method is only called if you ask for books in your query. This saves processing time and database queries! Understanding @Source (The Field Resolver Pattern) What is @Source? @Source is special annotation that tells GraphQL: "This method provides data for a field on a parent object" Real World Analogy: Imagine you're at a restaurant: Parent Object = Your main dish (Author) Field Resolver = Side dishes you can add (books, bookCount) @Source = The waiter asking "Which main dish is this side for?" The Pattern: Why This is Powerful: 1. Lazy Loading : Books are only fetched if requested 2. Computed Fields : Can calculate fields that don't exist in the model 3. Clean Separation : Business logic separate from data models 4. Flexibility : Easy to add new fields without changing the model More Examples: These all become queryable fields in GraphQL! Input Types (Grouping Related Data) What Are Input Types? When creating or updating complex data, instead of passing many individual parameters, we group them into an "Input Type" like filling out a form. Real World Analogy: Imagine registering for a website: Bad Way (Many individual fields): This is messy with 8 parameters! Good Way (Grouped input): Much cleaner and organized! Step 1: Create the Input Class What We're Building: An input type for creating books with all necessary information grouped together. Step 2: Create a Nested Input Type (Advanced) What if we want to create a book AND its author in one mutation? We can nest input types! Step 3: Use Input Types in Mutations Generated GraphQL Schema How to Use Input Types Example 1: Create a simple book Example 2: Update only some fields Example 3: Create book with new author (nested) Benefits of Input Types: 1. Organization : Related fields grouped together 2. Reusability : Same input type can be used in multiple mutations 3. Type Safety : GraphQL validates the structure 4. Clarity : Clear what data is needed 5. Flexibility : Easy to add new fields without breaking existing code 6. Documentation : Self documenting with descriptions When to Use Input Types: ✅ Use input types when: Creating or updating complex objects Multiple related fields Same data structure used in multiple mutations Want to group optional fields ❌ Don't need input types when: Simple operations with 1 2 parameters Single primitive value (just pass it directly) Example: deleteBook(id: 5) no need for input type Interfaces and Unions (Advanced Type Relationships) What Are These? Sometimes different types of objects share common fields, or you need to return different types from the same query. That's where interfaces and unions come in. Interfaces: Shared Fields Across Types What is an Interface? An interface is like a contract that says "All types implementing this interface MUST have these fields." Real World Analogy: Think about vehicles: Interface : Vehicle (all vehicles have: id, manufacturer, year) Implementations : Car, Truck, Motorcycle (each has additional specific fields) All vehicles share common properties, but each type has unique ones too. GraphQL Example: Implementing the Interface: Using the Interface: Generated GraphQL Schema: How to Query: What are fragments? ... on Book is called an "inline fragment". It means: "If this Node is actually a Book, also give me these Book specific fields." Unions: Multiple Possible Types What is a Union? A union represents a value that could be one of several different types. Unlike interfaces, union types don't share common fields. Real World Analogy: Search results on Amazon: You search for "apple" Results could be: Books, Electronics, Food, or Clothing Each result type is completely different But they all appear in the same search results list GraphQL Example: Implement the Union: Use the Union: Generated Schema: How to Query Unions: Response: Comparison: Interface vs Union When to Use Each: Use Interface when: Types share common fields (id, createdAt, etc.) Types are related conceptually You want to query common fields without fragments Example: Different types of users (Admin, Regular, Guest) Use Union when: Types are completely different No common fields except maybe id Representing mixed results Example: Search results, activity feeds, notifications Example Activity Feed (Union): Example User Types (Interface): Error Handling (Dealing with Problems Gracefully) Why Error Handling Matters: Things go wrong in applications: User enters invalid data Database is down Book doesn't exist User doesn't have permission Good error handling tells users WHAT went wrong and HOW to fix it. Bad Error Handling: User thinks: "What? What went wrong? What do I do now?" Good Error Handling: User thinks: "Ah, I used the wrong ID. Let me fix that." Approach 1: Custom Exceptions (Recommended for Simple Cases) What Are Custom Exceptions? You create your own error types that are specific to your application. Creating Custom Exceptions: Understanding Exception Types: Using Custom Exceptions: What Users See (Error Response): When an error occurs, GraphQL returns this format: Understanding the Error Response: Approach 2: Error Payload Pattern (Recommended for Production) What is Error Payload? Instead of throwing exceptions, you return a structured response that includes both the result AND any errors. This is more GraphQL friendly. Benefits: Partial success possible (some operations succeed, some fail) Better for batch operations Client can handle errors programmatically More information can be included Creating Error Types: Using the Error Payload: Generated Schema: How to Use (Client Side): Response (With Errors): Response (Success): Error Handling Best Practices When to Use Each Approach: Use Exceptions when: Fatal errors (database down, etc.) Authentication failures Single operation queries Simple CRUD operations Use Error Payload when: Form validation Batch operations Complex business rules Need to return partial success Want better client side error handling Working with Real Databases (Panache Introduction) What We've Done So Far: We've been storing data in memory (Lists). When you restart the app, all data is lost. What We Need: A real database that persists data permanently! What is Panache? Panache is Quarkus's way of making database work super easy. It's like a simplified version of Hibernate (Java's most popular database framework). Real World Analogy: Traditional Hibernate : Like learning to drive a manual transmission car powerful but complex Panache : Like driving an automatic much easier, does the complex stuff for you What Panache Does: Connects to databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc.) Converts Java objects to database tables automatically Provides simple methods to save, find, update, delete data No need to write SQL queries! Step 1: Add Panache Dependencies Add to your pom.xml: What Each Dependency Does: Step 2: Configure Database Connection Add to application.properties: ⚠️ IMPORTANT WARNING: Understanding the Connection URL: Step 3: Create Entity Classes (Database Tables) What is an Entity? An entity is a Java class that represents a database table. Each instance of the class is a row in the table. Real World Analogy: Think of a spreadsheet: Entity Class = The column headers (what fields exist) Entity Instance = A row of data Database Table = The entire spreadsheet Creating a Book Entity: What Gets Created in the Database: Creating an Author Entity: Understanding Relationships: Step 4: Using Panache's Built in Methods The Magic of PanacheEntity: By extending PanacheEntity, your entity gets FREE methods: Understanding @Transactional: Step 5: Repository Pattern (Professional Approach) What is a Repository? A repository is a class dedicated to database operations. It separates database logic from GraphQL logic. Why Use Repositories? Cleaner Code : GraphQL resource doesn't worry about database details Reusability : Same repository used by multiple resources Testability : Easy to test database operations separately Maintainability : All database queries in one place Creating a Book Repository: Using the Repository: Panache Query Methods Reference: This gives you a complete, production ready database setup with Panache! Setup Panache Entity with Panache Repository Pattern GraphQL with Panache Pagination (Handling Large Datasets) What is Pagination? When you have thousands or millions of records, you can't send them all at once. Pagination splits data into manageable chunks (pages). Real World Analogy: Think of Google search results: You search for "cats" Google doesn't show all 10 billion results at once It shows 10 results per page You click "Next" to see more Why Pagination Matters: There are TWO main pagination approaches: Offset Based and Cursor Based. Approach 1: Offset Based Pagination (Simple but Limited) How it Works: Like page numbers in a book: Page 1: Items 1 10 Page 2: Items 11 20 Page 3: Items 21 30 Concepts: Limit : How many items per page (e.g., 10) Offset : How many items to skip (e.g., skip 20 to get page 3) Visual Example: Step 1: Create Connection Type Step 2: Implement in GraphQL Resource Step 3: Query with Offset Pagination Response: Get Second Page: Pros and Cons of Offset Pagination: Approach 2: Cursor Based Pagination (Professional, Scalable) How it Works: Like a bookmark in a book: Instead of page numbers, you use a "cursor" (bookmark) Cursor points to the last item you saw Next page starts after that cursor Real World Analogy: Think of your social media feed: You scroll down See 20 posts App remembers the last post you saw (cursor) Loads 20 more posts AFTER that one No page numbers, just "load more" Why Cursor Based is Better for Large Data: Step 1: Create Cursor Types Step 2: Implement Cursor Pagination Step 3: Query with Cursor Pagination First Page (no cursor): Response: Next Page (use endCursor from previous page): Visual Flow: Choosing the Right Pagination Strategy Performance Comparison: Both pagination strategies are now fully explained and ready to use! Offset Based Pagination Cursor Based Pagination Authentication and Authorization (Securing Your API) What's the Difference? Real World Example: Authentication : You log in to Netflix with your email/password Authorization : Your "Basic" plan can't watch in 4K (only Premium can) Setting Up JWT Authentication What is JWT? JWT (JSON Web Token) is like a digital passport that proves who you are. How JWT Works: Step 1: Add JWT Dependency Step 2: Configure JWT Step 3: Generate Keys (One Time Setup) You need a public/private key pair. Run these commands: Place publicKey.pem in src/main/resources/META INF/resources/ Step 4: Create a User Model Step 5: Using JWT in GraphQL Understanding @RolesAllowed: Step 6: Extracting JWT Information Custom Security Context (Alternative Approach) When to Use: If you want more control over authentication/authorization logic. Step 1: Create Security Context Step 2: Use Custom Security Context Field Level Security What is Field Level Security? Sometimes you want to hide certain fields based on who's asking. Example: Regular users can see book title and price Only owners can see sales statistics Only admins can see internal notes Implementation: Query Result Based on Role: Response for Regular User: Response for Owner/Admin: Security Best Practices This covers authentication and authorization comprehensively for beginners! JWT Authentication Custom Security Context Source/DataFetcher Pattern Generated Schema: Reactive GraphQL Advanced Part What You'll Learn in This Section: Now we're moving into professional, production grade topics: Solving performance problems (N+1 queries) Real time updates with WebSockets Building distributed systems with Federation Optimizing for speed and scale Testing strategies Deploying to production Who Should Read This: You've mastered the Basic and Intermediate parts You're building a production application You need to handle high traffic You want to optimize performance You're working on a team with multiple services Real World Context: This section takes your hobby project and makes it enterprise ready. Think of it as upgrading from a food truck to a restaurant chain! The N+1 Problem and DataLoader Solution What is the N+1 Problem? One of the most common performance issues in GraphQL. Let's understand it with a story. The Problem (Illustrated): Imagine you run a bookstore and a customer asks: "Show me all authors and their books" Bad Approach (N+1 Queries): Why This is Bad: 3 authors = 4 queries 100 authors = 101 queries 10,000 authors = 10,001 queries! 😱 Each database query takes time. This adds up FAST! Visual Representation: Understanding DataLoader What is DataLoader? DataLoader is a tool that batches multiple requests into one. Instead of asking for data one item at a time, it collects all requests and asks for everything at once. Real World Analogy: Without DataLoader: Each request is separate very slow! With DataLoader: One batch request super fast! Implementing DataLoader in Quarkus Step 1: Add DataLoader Dependency Step 2: Create a DataLoader Registry Producer Step 3: Update Repository to Support Batch Loading Step 4: Use DataLoader in GraphQL Resource Step 5: Configure DataLoader in Application How DataLoader Works (Behind the Scenes) The Batching Process: Key Concepts: 1. Batching Window : DataLoader waits a tiny moment (1 2ms) to collect requests 2. Single Query : All collected IDs are fetched in one database query 3. Order Preservation : Results must be returned in same order as requested IDs 4. Per Request : Each GraphQL request gets its own DataLoader (no cache between requests) Advanced DataLoader Features Feature 1: Caching DataLoader can cache results within a single request: When This Helps: Feature 2: Custom Cache Key Feature 3: Max Batch Size Prevent batches from getting too large: If you request 250 authors, it will make 3 batches: Batch 1: IDs 1 100 Batch 2: IDs 101 200 Batch 3: IDs 201 250 Creating a Reusable DataLoader Class For better organization: Performance Comparison Scenario: Fetch 100 books with their authors When DataLoader Makes the Biggest Difference: DataLoader is essential for production GraphQL APIs it can turn a slow, unusable API into a fast, responsive one! Custom Scalars Register Scalar: Usage: Subscriptions (Real Time Updates with WebSockets) What are Subscriptions? Subscriptions allow your client to receive real time updates from the server when data changes. Instead of repeatedly asking "Any updates?", the server pushes updates to you automatically. Real World Analogy: Traditional Queries (Polling): Subscriptions (Push Notifications): Use Cases for Subscriptions: For detailed implementation and advanced subscription patterns, please refer to the full GraphQL documentation. Subscriptions use WebSockets to maintain persistent connections between client and server. Advanced Subscription with Filters: Client Subscription (JavaScript): Federation Support Performance Optimization Query Complexity Limiting Field Level Caching Query Result Caching Testing GraphQL APIs REST Assured Testing Integration Testing with TestContainers Native Compilation Build Native Image: Monitoring and Metrics Custom Metrics: Health Check: OpenAPI Integration Production Architecture Best Practices Deployment Kubernetes Deployment Docker Build Conclusion GraphQL in Quarkus provides: 1. Developer Experience Annotation based, auto generated schema, hot reload 2. Performance Fast startup, low memory, native compilation support 3. Cloud Native Kubernetes ready, reactive support, observability 4. Production Ready Security, caching, monitoring, testing support 5. Standards Based MicroProfile GraphQL, familiar Java patterns Key Advantages: Supersonic startup times (< 1 second) Minimal memory footprint (< 100MB) Native compilation for containers Excellent developer experience Full GraphQL feature support Quarkus makes GraphQL development in Java modern, efficient, and enjoyable while maintaining production grade quality and performance.

title: Hibernate
text: Hibernate Interview Questions (Easy Interview Ready Answers) 1️⃣ What is Hibernate? Why do we use it? Hibernate is an ORM (Object Relational Mapping) framework for Java that simplifies database operations. Instead of writing SQL manually, Hibernate converts Java objects into database records and vice versa. Why use Hibernate? Reduces JDBC boilerplate code Database independent Automatic table mapping Caching support Transaction management Better performance optimization Example No need to write: 2️⃣ What is ORM (Object Relational Mapping)? ORM is a technique that maps: | Java Object | Database Table | | | | | Class | Table | | Object | Row | | Field | Column | Example Mapped to: Interview Answer ORM maps Java objects to database tables so developers can work with objects instead of writing SQL. 3️⃣ Hibernate vs JDBC | Feature | JDBC | Hibernate | | | | | | SQL Writing | Manual | Automatic | | Boilerplate Code | More | Less | | Caching | No | Yes | | ORM Support | No | Yes | | Database Independent | No | Yes | | Performance Tuning | Manual | Built in | | Learning Curve | Easy | Moderate | Interview Answer JDBC is low level database access whereas Hibernate is an ORM framework built on top of JDBC. 4️⃣ Explain Hibernate Architecture Components Configuration Reads: SessionFactory Heavy object Created once Session Lightweight Used for CRUD operations Transaction Manages commit and rollback. 5️⃣ What is Session and SessionFactory? SessionFactory Thread safe Created once per application Stores metadata and cache Session Represents a database connection Used for CRUD operations Interview Answer SessionFactory creates Session objects. Session is used to interact with the database. 6️⃣ Hibernate Object States 1. Transient Object created but not saved. 2. Persistent Associated with Session. 3. Detached Session closed but object still exists. Flow 7️⃣ Difference Between get() and load() | Feature | get() | load() | | | | | | Database Hit | Immediate | Lazy | | Returns | Object | Proxy | | Record Not Found | null | Exception | | Performance | Slower | Faster | get() load() Interview Answer get() immediately fetches data. load() returns a proxy object and fetches data lazily. 8️⃣ Hibernate Caching Caching reduces database hits. Level 1 Cache Enabled by default Session scoped Only first query hits DB. Level 2 Cache SessionFactory scoped Shared across sessions Examples: Ehcache Hazelcast Infinispan Interview Answer L1 cache is session level and default. L2 cache is application level and shared across sessions. 9️⃣ save() vs persist() vs saveOrUpdate() | Method | Returns | Insert | Update | | | | | | | save() | ID | Yes | No | | persist() | void | Yes | No | | saveOrUpdate() | void | Yes | Yes | save() persist() saveOrUpdate() 🔟 What are Hibernate Annotations? Annotations replace XML configuration. Common Annotations Example: 1️⃣1️⃣ What is HQL? HQL = Hibernate Query Language Works on entities, not tables. HQL SQL Interview Answer HQL uses Java entity names whereas SQL uses database tables. 1️⃣2️⃣ What is Criteria API? Used to build dynamic queries programmatically. Advantages Type safe Dynamic query generation Object oriented 1️⃣3️⃣ Lazy vs Eager Loading Lazy Loading Data loaded only when needed. Query Execution Triggers DB call. Eager Loading Loads immediately. Interview Answer Lazy loading improves performance by fetching data only when required. 1️⃣4️⃣ What is N+1 Select Problem? Suppose: 1 Department 100 Employees Hibernate fires: Total = 101 Queries Solution JOIN FETCH EntityGraph Interview Answer N+1 occurs when Hibernate fires one query for parent data and N queries for children. JOIN FETCH solves it. 1️⃣5️⃣ merge() vs update() | Feature | update() | merge() | | | | | | Existing Persistent Object | Exception | Works | | Returns New Object | No | Yes | | Safe | No | Yes | update() merge() Interview Answer merge() is safer because it copies detached object state into a managed entity. 1️⃣6️⃣ Hibernate Inheritance Strategies Single Table One table for all classes. ✅ Fast ❌ Many null columns Joined Separate tables. ✅ Normalized ❌ More joins Table Per Class Each class has its own table. ✅ Independent tables ❌ UNION queries 1️⃣7️⃣ What is a Transaction in Hibernate? A group of operations executed as one unit. ACID Atomicity Consistency Isolation Durability Rollback: 1️⃣8️⃣ What is a Proxy Object? A placeholder object used for lazy loading. Hibernate returns proxy. Actual data loads only when: is accessed. 1️⃣9️⃣ What are Named Queries? Predefined reusable queries. Usage: Benefits Reusable Better readability Compiled at startup 2️⃣0️⃣ GeneratorType and ID Strategies Hibernate generates primary keys automatically. AUTO Hibernate decides. IDENTITY Uses auto increment. SEQUENCE Uses DB sequence. TABLE Stores IDs in separate table. UUID Example: 2️⃣1️⃣ Hibernate Relationships One to One One to Many Many to One Many to Many 2️⃣2️⃣ Cascade Types Used to propagate operations. ALL Includes everything. PERSIST Save child with parent. MERGE Merge child too. REMOVE Delete child too. REFRESH Reload from DB. DETACH Detach child objects. 2️⃣3️⃣ What is Dirty Checking? Hibernate automatically detects object changes. No explicit update needed. At commit: generated automatically. Interview Answer Dirty Checking automatically tracks changes in persistent entities and updates the database during transaction commit. 2️⃣4️⃣ What is Hibernate Interceptor? Allows interception of entity lifecycle events. Examples: Use cases: Audit logging Tracking changes Security validation Example: 2️⃣5️⃣ Difference Between Hibernate and JPA | Feature | JPA | Hibernate | | | | | | Type | Specification | Implementation | | Vendor | Java Standard | Hibernate Team | | APIs | Standard APIs | Extra Features | | Portability | High | Lower | | Dependency | Interface | Concrete Framework | Example JPA Hibernate Interview Answer JPA is the standard specification, while Hibernate is the most popular implementation of JPA. Quick Interview Revision (30 Seconds) ✅ Hibernate = ORM framework ✅ SessionFactory = Heavy, singleton ✅ Session = DB interaction ✅ States = Transient → Persistent → Detached ✅ get() = Immediate DB hit ✅ load() = Proxy/Lazy ✅ Cache = L1(Session), L2(Application) ✅ HQL = Query entities, not tables ✅ Lazy Loading preferred over Eager ✅ N+1 solved by JOIN FETCH / EntityGraph ✅ Dirty Checking = Auto update changed entities ✅ JPA = Specification, Hibernate = Implementation ✅ merge() safer than update() ✅ Cascade propagates parent operations to child entities ✅ Proxy objects enable lazy loading ✅ Hibernate sits on top of JDBC and simplifies persistence operations. Hibernate Concepts Explained <details open <summary <strong 1. Eager vs Lazy Loading</strong </summary What is it? Lazy Loading: Delay fetching related entities until they are actually accessed. Eager Loading: Fetch related entities immediately with the parent entity. Why use? Lazy loading improves performance when related data is not always needed. Eager loading is useful when you always need related entities. | Feature | Lazy Loading | Eager Loading | | | | | | When data loads | On first access to related entity | Immediately with parent entity | | Default usage | @OneToMany, @ManyToMany (lazy by default) | @OneToOne, @ManyToOne (eager by default) | | Annotation syntax | fetch = FetchType.LAZY | fetch = FetchType.EAGER | | Performance | Faster initial load, but possible N+1 queries | Slower initial load, fewer queries | | Use case | Large collections, optional relations | Small relations always required | Example: </details <details open <summary <strong 2. SessionFactory</strong </summary Responsible for creating Hibernate Session objects. Thread safe and heavy weight, usually one per application/database. Holds metadata and configuration of ORM mapping. Use at app startup, keep for the app lifecycle. Sessions created by SessionFactory are used to perform DB operations (save, update, delete). </details <details open <summary <strong 3. Data Connection Setup and Configuration</strong </summary Configure hibernate.cfg.xml or application.properties with DB URL, username, password, dialect. Example properties for Spring Boot: Hibernate uses these configs to establish DB connection and manage sessions. </details <details open <summary <strong 4. Stored Procedures vs Prepared Statements</strong </summary | Feature | PreparedStatement | Stored Procedure | | | | | | Definition | Precompiled parameterized SQL query | Precompiled SQL logic stored in DB | | Use case | Dynamic queries with parameters | Complex operations, multiple queries | | Security | Prevents SQL injection by parameterization | Can enhance security via controlled access | | Performance | Good for repeated queries | Optimized execution in DB engine | | Portability | Portable across DBs | Often DB specific syntax | | Java usage | Connection.prepareStatement(sql) | Connection.prepareCall("{CALL proc(?)}") | Example PreparedStatement: Example Stored Procedure call: </details <details open <summary <strong 5. Cascading in Hibernate</strong </summary Cascading controls how operations on a parent entity propagate to its related child entities. Useful to keep DB consistent without manual handling of each related entity. | Cascade Type | Description | | | | | ALL | All operations (persist, merge, remove, etc.) cascade to children | | PERSIST | Persist operation cascades | | MERGE | Merge operation cascades | | REMOVE | Remove (delete) operation cascades | | DETACH | Detach operation cascades | | REPLICATE | Replicate operation cascades | | SAVE UPDATE | Save or update cascades | Example: Use cascade carefully—deleting a parent can delete all children! </details <details open <summary <strong 6. Hibernate get() vs load()</strong </summary | Feature | get() | load() | | | | | | Behavior | Immediately hits DB, returns entity or null if not found | Returns proxy, hits DB only on property access | | When to use | When you want to fetch immediately and check if entity exists | When you expect entity exists and want lazy loading | | Exception | Returns null if not found | Throws ObjectNotFoundException if entity missing | Example get(): Example load(): </details Dirty checking Hibernate Dirty Checking (Simple Interview Ready Explanation) What is Dirty Checking? Dirty Checking is a Hibernate feature that automatically detects changes made to an entity and updates the database without calling save() or update() explicitly. Simple Flow Real Life Example Imagine Hibernate is a teacher checking an answer sheet. You change: When the transaction ends, Hibernate compares: Since they are different, Hibernate says: No need to call save(). Example Code Hibernate automatically executes: Internal Steps 1. Load Entity Hibernate stores: 2. Modify Entity Now: 3. Transaction Commit Hibernate compares: Difference found → Entity is Dirty 4. Execute Update Why is it Called "Dirty"? In Hibernate terminology: Example: Now the entity is Dirty because its state differs from the original snapshot. When Does Dirty Checking Happen? Usually during Flush . Flush occurs: ✅ Before Transaction Commit ✅ Before some JPQL/HQL queries ✅ When manually calling Do We Need save() Every Time? New Entity Required because Hibernate doesn't know about the object yet. Existing Entity Inside a transaction: ❌ No need for save() ✅ Dirty Checking handles it. Performance Impact Memory Cost Hibernate stores: So memory usage increases. CPU Cost At commit time Hibernate compares: For many entities this comparison takes CPU time. Optimization Techniques 1. Read Only Transaction Use for: Benefit: ✅ No snapshot creation ✅ No dirty checking ✅ Better performance 2. Detach Entity After detach: Hibernate ignores it. No update SQL generated. 3. Immutable Entity Use for: Hibernate will never perform dirty checking. 4. Dynamic Update By default Hibernate updates all columns: Even if only email changed. Use: Now Hibernate generates: Only changed columns are updated. Interview Answer (30 Seconds) Dirty Checking is a Hibernate feature that automatically detects changes made to managed entities inside a transaction. When an entity is loaded, Hibernate stores a snapshot of its original state. During flush or transaction commit, it compares the current entity with the snapshot. If any field has changed, Hibernate automatically generates and executes the required UPDATE statement without explicitly calling save() or update(). Baeldung Hibernate Guide: A practical walkthrough for configuring and verifying dirty tracking behavior inside standard spring applications. Hibernate vs JPA</strong </summary | Criteria | Hibernate | JPA | | | | | | Nature | Full featured ORM framework | Java specification (standard API) | | Features | Advanced features (multi tenancy, caching) | Basic ORM features | | Portability | Less portable due to proprietary features | Portable across JPA providers | | Ecosystem | Mature, large community | Part of Java EE ecosystem | | Implementation | Can be used standalone or as JPA provider | Needs a provider like Hibernate, EclipseLink | Choose Hibernate if: You want advanced ORM features Working with legacy Hibernate projects Need vendor specific extensions Choose JPA if: You want standardization and portability Building Java EE / Jakarta EE apps Prefer simpler API <details open <summary Use Hibernate as JPA provider for best of both worlds.</summary </details </details <details open <summary <strong 8. Connection Pooling in Java</strong </summary Manages a pool of database connections for reuse. Improves app response time by avoiding connection creation overhead.
