text: Java 8 Streams vs Collections — Enhanced Guide (with DSA Interview Questions) 📺 Video Explanation | 🔗 Original source: java2novice.com This is an enhanced version of the original notes. New material added: A "Missing Points" section covering Collectors and Stream methods the original skipped (teeing, filtering, flatMapping, mapping, Stream.generate/iterate, Files.lines, Comparator.nullsFirst, common pitfalls, etc.) A full DSA Interview Questions section — 20 classic coding interview problems solved with Streams, each with a plain loop equivalent for comparison. A Do's & Don'ts cheat sheet for using Streams safely in interviews and production code. Table of Contents 1. Stream API Overview 2. Key Differences: Collections vs Streams 3. flatMap, Stream.concat, mapMulti 4. Intermediate vs Terminal Operations 5. ForkJoinPool & Parallel Streams 6. Collectors Reference 7. 🆕 Missing/Additional Points 8. Java Features 8 → 21 9. 🆕 DSA Interview Questions Using Streams 10. 🆕 Streams Do's and Don'ts 🌊 Stream API Overview In Java, Collections and Streams serve different purposes: | Collections | Streams | | | | | Purpose : Store and manage groups of objects like List, Set, Map, etc. | Purpose : Process data in a functional and declarative manner using filter, map, reduce, etc. | | Data Storage : In memory storage with CRUD operations. | Data Processing : Pipeline based processing; does not store data. | | Mutability : Collections can be modified. | Immutability : Streams are immutable; operations return new streams. | | Iteration : External iteration (e.g., for each). | Iteration : Internal iteration handled by the stream API. | | Performance : Varies with collection type (e.g., ArrayList vs LinkedList). | Performance : Efficient, especially with parallel streams. | | Thread Safety : Some are thread safe (Vector, Hashtable), others are not. | Thread Safety : Streams are not thread safe unless explicitly handled. | | 🆕 Reusability : Collections can be iterated repeatedly. | 🆕 Reusability : A stream can only be consumed once — reuse throws IllegalStateException. | | 🆕 Nullability : Elements can be null (depending on collection type). | 🆕 Nullability : Most stream operations are hostile to null; prefer Optional. | Stream API Using collections framework in Java, a developer has to use loops and make repeated checks. Another concern is efficiency; as multi core processors are available at ease, a Java developer has to write parallel code processing that can be pretty error prone. To resolve such issues, Java 8 introduced the concept of stream that lets the developer to proccess data declaratively and leverage multicore architecture without the need to write any specific code for it. forEach() to iterate each element of the stream. map() used to map each element to its corresponding result. filter() used to eliminate elements based on a criteria. sorted() Used to sort the stream ⚖️ Key Differences Collections are for storing and manipulating data. Streams are for processing data. Streams are lazy , stateless , and functional . Collections are eager , stateful , and imperative . Streams support easy parallelism (parallelStream()). 💡 Example Comparison <details open <summary <strong 📚 Collections Example</strong </summary </details <details open <summary <strong 🚀 flatMap & mapMultiStreams Example</strong </summary 1. flatMap in streams flatMap is used when one element produces zero, one, or many elements , and you want a single flattened stream . map → one to one flatMap → one to many (then flatten) Result : ["a", "b", "c", "d"] Without flatMap, you'd get a Stream<Stream<String , which is almost never what you want. 2. flatMap vs Stream.concat Stream.concat(a, b) only merges two streams . For many streams, flatMap scales much better than nested concat calls: Efficiency note : flatMap isn't magically faster for two streams, but for dynamic or large numbers of streams , it's more memory friendly, easier for the JVM to optimize, and cleaner for parallel execution. 3. mapMulti (Java 16+) mapMulti is a more efficient alternative to flatMap when you don't need intermediate streams and want fine grained control over output. Filtering + mapping in one step is where mapMulti really shines: 4. When to use what | Method | Best for | Notes | | | | | | flatMap | One to many transformations | Clean, expressive | | Stream.concat | Merging two streams | Doesn't scale well | | mapMulti | High performance flattening | Java 16+, fewer allocations | Benchmarks: flatMap vs mapMulti (indicative) | Operation | flatMap | mapMulti | | | | | | Throughput | baseline | 1.3x – 2x faster | | Allocations | high | near zero | | GC pressure | noticeable | minimal | You'll mostly see benefits with large streams, hot code paths, and elements that produce few outputs. If each element explodes into thousands of outputs, the difference shrinks. Rule of thumb: mapMulti ≈ flatMap without the stream tax Real world examples JSON tag extraction: Graph traversal (edges → neighbors): This matters in recommendation engines, dependency graphs, call graphs, and social networks — graphs are often wide , and flatMap creates one stream per node while mapMulti stays flat and cache friendly. Parallel stream behavior flatMap under .parallel() creates substreams per thread and pulls elements via nested spliterators — this can increase contention and reduce work stealing efficiency. mapMulti avoids nested streams entirely: each thread pulls input and emits output directly, leading to better chunking and less synchronization. mapMulti is safe in parallel streams IF you don't mutate shared state and only call out.accept(...) — the same rule as map/flatMap. Final guidance: Default → flatMap (clarity) Performance sensitive paths → mapMulti Two streams only → Stream.concat Parallel + high volume → strongly prefer mapMulti </details 🧱 Stream Operations: Intermediate vs Terminal Intermediate operations (lazy, return a stream) Terminal operations (eager, return a result) 🔁 Intermediate Operations <details <summary <strong Intermediate Operations</strong </summary | Method | Description | Example | | | | | | filter(Predicate<T ) | Filters elements by condition. | stream.filter(x x 5) | | map(Function<T, R ) | Transforms elements. | stream.map(x x 2) | | flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R ) | Flattens nested streams. | stream.flatMap(x Stream.of(x, x 2)) | | distinct() | Removes duplicates. | stream.distinct() | | sorted() | Sorts elements. | stream.sorted() | | peek(Consumer<T ) | Performs action for debugging. | stream.peek(System.out::println) | | limit(long) | Truncates stream size. | stream.limit(5) | | skip(long) | Skips first n elements. | stream.skip(3) | | 🆕 takeWhile(Predicate<T ) | Takes elements while true (Java 9+, stops at first false). | stream.takeWhile(x x < 10) | | 🆕 dropWhile(Predicate<T ) | Drops elements while true, then takes the rest (Java 9+). | stream.dropWhile(x x < 10) | | 🆕 mapMulti(BiConsumer) | Push based one to many mapping (Java 16+), avoids intermediate streams. | stream.mapMulti((x, out) out.accept(x)) | | 🆕 boxed() | Converts IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream to boxed Stream<Integer etc. | IntStream.range(0,5).boxed() | | 🆕 mapToObj / mapToInt / mapToLong / mapToDouble | Converts between primitive and object streams. | IntStream.range(0,5).mapToObj(String::valueOf) | </details ✅ Terminal Operations <details <summary <strong Terminal Operations</strong </summary | Method | Description | Example | | | | | | forEach(Consumer<T ) | Performs action on each element. | stream.forEach(System.out::println) | | toArray() | Converts stream to array. | Object[] arr = stream.toArray() | | reduce(BinaryOperator<T ) | Reduces elements to single value. | stream.reduce((a, b) a + b) | | collect(Collector<T, A, R ) | Collects results into container. | stream.collect(Collectors.toList()) | | min(Comparator<T ) / max(...) | Finds min/max elements. | stream.min(Comparator.naturalOrder()) | | count() | Counts number of elements. | stream.count() | | anyMatch(...) / allMatch(...) / noneMatch(...) | Matches based on conditions. | stream.anyMatch(x x 10) | | findFirst() / findAny() | Finds first/any element. | stream.findFirst() | | iterator() / spliterator() | Provides stream iterator. | stream.iterator() | | isParallel() / parallel() / sequential() / unordered() | Stream configuration. | stream.parallel() | | 🆕 toList() | Shortcut for collect(Collectors.toList()) (Java 16+), returns unmodifiable list. | stream.toList() | </details 🧩 Summary | Feature | Collections | Streams | | | | | | Data Handling | Stores data | Processes data | | Mutability | Mutable | Immutable | | Evaluation | Eager | Lazy | | Iteration | External | Internal | | Use Case | CRUD operations | Data transformation | | Parallelism | Manual | Easy with parallelStream() | ⚙️ ForkJoinPool, Stream & ParallelStream — Summary <details <summary <strong ForkJoinPool and Stream / ParallelStream (internal working)</strong </summary 1️⃣ ForkJoinPool Overview Introduced in Java 7 for parallel, divide and conquer tasks. Uses work stealing algorithm — idle threads "steal" tasks from others. Backbone for parallel streams and CompletableFuture . 2️⃣ ForkJoinPool vs Threads vs ExecutorService | Feature | Thread | ExecutorService | ForkJoinPool | | | | | | | Creation | Manual (new Thread) | Managed pool | Specialized pool | | Work Model | 1 task/thread | Queued tasks | Split–merge recursive tasks | | Best For | Simple async jobs | Batch tasks | CPU bound parallel compute | | Example | new Thread() | Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5) | new ForkJoinPool() | 3️⃣ Still Used in Java 21? ✅ Yes — powers parallelStream(), CompletableFuture, some structured concurrency APIs. Java 21 also has Virtual Threads for I/O bound concurrency. | Feature | ForkJoinPool | Virtual Threads | | | | | | Model | Work stealing | Lightweight threads | | Best For | CPU bound parallel compute | Massive I/O concurrency | | Threads | Few (≈ CPU cores) | Thousands possible | 4️⃣ Stream Internals Internally uses Spliterator (splits data), PipelineHelper/Sink (chains ops), and StreamOpFlags (manage properties like ORDERED, DISTINCT). 5️⃣ Parallel Stream — How It Works 1. Spliterator divides source into chunks. 2. Tasks submitted to ForkJoinPool.commonPool() . 3. Threads process chunks in parallel. 4. Results are merged (joined). 6️⃣ Stream vs ParallelStream | Feature | stream() | parallelStream() | | | | | | Execution | Single thread | Multi thread (ForkJoinPool) | | Thread Pool | Main thread | ForkJoinPool.commonPool() | | Ordering | Maintained | May reorder | | Performance | Small / simple | Large, CPU bound | | Best For | Small data | Large data, heavy CPU tasks | 7️⃣ When to Use Parallel Streams ✅ Use when: data is large, CPU bound, no shared mutable state. ❌ Avoid when: task is I/O bound, order must be preserved, shared state causes race conditions. 🆕 Common pitfall : calling parallelStream() inside a web request handler that already runs on a limited thread pool can starve ForkJoinPool.commonPool() for the whole JVM (all parallel streams share it by default). For per task pools, wrap the call in a custom ForkJoinPool: ✅ In Short | Concept | Description | | | | | ForkJoinPool | Core parallel engine (split + join tasks) | | Stream | Sequential lazy pipeline | | ParallelStream | Same pipeline, but split across ForkJoinPool threads | | Spliterator | Splits source data | | Still used in Java 21? | ✅ Yes — for parallel compute (CPU tasks) | | Virtual Threads | 🚀 New in Java 21 — for I/O bound concurrency | </details 📦 Collectors from java.util.stream <details <summary <strong 1–24: Common Collector Methods</strong </summary Collecting Joining Strings Counting & Summarizing Grouping & Partitioning Reducing Post processing Min / Max </details 🆕 Missing Points — Additional Stream & Collector Features The original notes covered the essentials but skipped several collectors and stream methods that come up often in real code and interviews. <details open <summary <strong 🆕 25. <code Collectors.mapping()</code — transform before a downstream collector</strong </summary Used inside groupingBy to map each element before collecting it into the group. </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 26. <code Collectors.filtering()</code — filter inside a downstream collector (Java 9+)</strong </summary Unlike stream().filter() before groupingBy, filtering() keeps groups that would otherwise disappear (with an empty list) instead of dropping them. </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 27. <code Collectors.flatMapping()</code — flatten inside a downstream collector (Java 9+)</strong </summary </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 28. <code Collectors.teeing()</code — combine two collectors into one result (Java 12+)</strong </summary Runs two collectors over the same stream and merges their results — great for computing multiple aggregates in a single pass. </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 29. <code groupingBy</code with a custom Map supplier</strong </summary By default groupingBy returns a HashMap (unordered). Pass a supplier to control the map type — e.g. TreeMap for sorted keys. </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 30. <code Stream.generate()</code vs <code Stream.iterate()</code </strong </summary Both create infinite streams — always pair with limit(). </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 31. Primitive stream summary stats in one call</strong </summary </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 32. <code Files.lines()</code — stream a file line by line</strong </summary Always use try with resources — Files.lines() opens a file handle that must be closed. </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 33. <code Comparator</code helpers often forgotten</strong </summary </details <details <summary <strong 🆕 34. Common Stream pitfalls / interview gotchas</strong </summary A stream can only be consumed once. Calling a terminal operation twice throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. peek() should not be used for side effects in production code — it's meant for debugging; the JVM may optimize it away or not call it at all if the pipeline is short circuited. Collectors.toMap() throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys unless you supply a merge function: Collectors.toMap(k, v, (a,b) b). parallelStream() isn't always faster — for small collections, the overhead of splitting/merging can be worse than sequential processing. Order isn't always preserved in parallel streams unless the source is ordered and you avoid unordered operations like forEach (use forEachOrdered instead). Stream.of() is not lazy about the source array , but every intermediate op still is — nothing runs until a terminal operation is invoked. Autoboxing cost : prefer IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream over Stream<Integer for numeric heavy pipelines to avoid boxing overhead. </details 📘 Java Features from 8 to 21 (LTS) <details <summary <strong Java Features from 8 to 21 (LTS) with Examples</strong </summary 🔗 References: Reflectoring | Pretius ☕ Java 8 (2014) ✅ Lambda Expressions ✅ Stream API ✅ New Date Time API ☕ Java 9 (2017) ✅ Lambda Expressions & Stream API</strong </summary Conciseness : Replace one method anonymous classes with compact expressions Functional Style : Ideal for use with Streams, Predicates, Functions Readability : Focus on "what" rather than "how" </details <details <summary <strong 2. Method References</strong </summary | Syntax | Example | | | | | Class::staticMethod | Stream.of("a","b").forEach(System.out::println); | | instance::instanceMethod | list.sort(String::compareToIgnoreCase); | | Class::instanceMethod | Stream.of("a","b").map(String::toUpperCase) | | Class::new | Supplier<List<String s = ArrayList::new; | </details <details <summary <strong 3. Default & Static Methods in Interfaces</strong </summary </details <details <summary <strong 4. Optional API — full cheat sheet</strong </summary | Method | Description | Example | | | | | | of(T value) | Returns an Optional with a non null value; throws NPE if null | Optional<String opt = Optional.of("Hello"); | | ofNullable(T value) | Returns Optional containing value if non null, else empty | Optional<String opt = Optional.ofNullable(possibleNull); | | empty() | Returns an empty Optional | Optional<String opt = Optional.empty(); | | isPresent() | Checks if a value is present | if(opt.isPresent()) { ... } | | isEmpty() | Checks if Optional is empty (Java 11+) | if(opt.isEmpty()) { ... } | | ifPresent(Consumer<? super T ) | Executes action if value is present | opt.ifPresent(System.out::println); | | ifPresentOrElse(Consumer, Runnable) | Executes action if present, else emptyAction (Java 9+) | opt.ifPresentOrElse(System.out::println, () System.out.println("No value")); | | get() | Returns value if present, else throws NoSuchElementException | String s = opt.get(); | | orElse(T other) | Returns value if present, else other | String s = opt.orElse("Default"); | | orElseGet(Supplier<? extends T ) | Returns value if present, else invokes supplier | String s = opt.orElseGet(() "Generated"); | | orElseThrow() | Returns value if present, else throws NoSuchElementException | String s = opt.orElseThrow(); | | orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X ) | Returns value if present, else throws custom exception | String s = opt.orElseThrow(() new RuntimeException("Missing")); | | map(Function<? super T,? extends U ) | Transforms value if present, wraps in Optional | Optional<Integer len = opt.map(String::length); | | flatMap(Function<? super T, Optional<U ) | Transforms value, avoids nested Optional | Optional<Integer len = opt.flatMap(s Optional.of(s.length())); | | filter(Predicate<? super T ) | Returns Optional if value matches predicate, else empty | opt.filter(s s.length() 3); | | stream() | Converts Optional to Stream (Java 9+) | opt.stream().forEach(System.out::println); | Key notes: use map for transformations, flatMap to avoid nested Optionals; prefer orElseGet for expensive default computations; use ifPresentOrElse instead of manual isPresent() checks. </details <details <summary <strong 5. Stream Operations: map() vs flatMap()</strong </summary </details <details <summary <strong 6. @SafeVarargs</strong </summary Suppresses unchecked warnings related to generic varargs . Can only be applied to final methods, static methods, and constructors. </details 🆕 DSA Interview Questions Using Streams Classic coding interview problems solved the "stream way," each paired with a plain loop version so you can compare readability and explain trade offs in an interview. 1. Find the first non repeated character in a string 2. Find duplicate elements in a list 3. Group anagrams together 4. Word frequency count (case insensitive) 5. Find the second highest number in a list 6. Reverse a string using streams 7. Check if a string is a palindrome 8. Flatten a nested list 9. Sort a Map by its values 10. Find the longest word in a list 11. Sum of digits of a number 12. Fibonacci sequence (first N terms) using Stream.iterate 13. Find all prime numbers up to N (Sieve style filter) 14. Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted list 15. Find all pairs in an array that sum to a target (two sum, all pairs) 16. Count vowels and consonants in a string 17. Find the intersection of two lists 18. Kth largest element in an array 19. Convert a list of objects into a Map grouped and counted (e.g. employees per department) 20. Check if two strings are anagrams 🆕 Streams Do's and Don'ts (Interview Cheat Sheet) ✅ Do Use streams for readable, declarative transformations of collections (filter → map → collect pipelines). Prefer Collectors.toMap with a merge function when duplicate keys are possible. Use IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream for numeric heavy work to avoid boxing. Use Collectors.groupingBy + downstream collectors (counting(), mapping(), averagingX()) instead of manual loops for aggregation problems — interviewers like seeing this fluency. Explain time complexity even when using streams — a stream pipeline doesn't change the underlying algorithmic complexity (e.g. sorted() is still O(n log n)). Know the plain loop equivalent of any stream solution you write — interviewers often ask you to convert one to the other. ❌ Don't Don't use streams for simple, single pass loops where a for loop is clearer and just as short. Don't mutate external state inside map/filter/forEach lambdas (breaks referential transparency, breaks parallel safety). Don't chain parallelStream() reflexively "for performance" — measure first; overhead often outweighs benefit for small/medium collections. Don't reuse a stream after a terminal operation — build a new one instead. Don't nest streams three or four levels deep purely to be "clever" — readability matters more than showing off syntax in an interview. Attribution Original content adapted from java2novice.com, tutorialspoint.com, reflectoring.io, and pretius.com. DSA question set, "Missing Points" section, and Do's/Don'ts cheat sheet are new additions for this enhanced guide.

text: Java Java Interview Question Bank Java Interview Questions 1 Java Interview Questions 2 Java Go through Points JDK, JRE, and JVM Jdk Jre Jvm ✅ Tree Structure (Relationship) ✅ JVM (Java Virtual Machine) • JVM is a virtual machine that runs Java bytecode (.class files). • It is platform dependent (Windows JVM ≠ Linux JVM). 📌 Main Responsibilities • Converts bytecode → machine code • Memory management (Heap, Stack, GC) • Security • Execution engine 📌 Components of JVM • Class Loader • Runtime Data Areas (Heap, Stack, Method Area, PC Register) • Execution Engine • Garbage Collector 📌 Use Required to run Java programs ✅ JRE (Java Runtime Environment) • Environment to run Java applications • Contains JVM + standard libraries 📌 Includes • JVM • Core Java libraries (API) • Supporting files 📌 Does NOT include ❌ Java compiler (javac) ❌ Development tools 📌 Use ✅ Needed only to run Java applications ❌ Cannot develop or compile Java code ✅ JDK (Java Development Kit) • Complete package for Java development • Contains JRE + development tools 📌 Includes • JRE • Compiler (javac) • Java launcher (java) • Debugger • Documentation tools • Packaging tools (jar) 📌 Use ✅ Required to develop, compile, debug, and run Java programs ✅ Quick Comparison Table Component Purpose Used For JVM Executes bytecode Running Java JRE JVM + Libraries Running Java apps JDK JRE + Dev tools Developing Java apps ✅ One‑Line Summary (Easy to Remember) • JVM → runs Java bytecode • JRE → JVM + libraries to run Java • JDK → JRE + tools to develop Java If you want, I can also: • Explain JVM internal memory areas with diagram • Give interview answers • Show real world analogy • Explain JDK vs JRE after Java 11 Core Design Principles SOLID 🚀 Primary Main Features of Java <details <summary Java main features</summary 1. Platform Independent 2. Object Oriented Programming Language Abstraction Encapsulation Inheritance Polymorphism 3. Simple 4. Robust 5. Secure 6. Distributed 7. Multithreading 8. Portable Java's Main Features (with Examples) 1. Platform Independent Write once, run anywhere. Java code compiles to bytecode, which runs on any OS with a JVM. Example: 2. Object Oriented Uses classes and objects. Supports Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism. Example: 3. Simple Easy syntax, no pointers, automatic memory management. Example: 4. Robust Strong memory management, exception handling, type checking. Example: 5. Secure No explicit pointer, runs in JVM sandbox, bytecode verification. Example: // Applets run in restricted environment 6. Distributed Supports networking, RMI, and web applications. Example: 7. Multithreaded Can run multiple threads (tasks) at once. Example: 8. Portable Java programs run the same on any platform with JVM. Example: // Bytecode runs on Windows, Mac, Linux </details 🧩 Class Loaders in Java Version Summary Table | Java Version | Class Loaders | | | | | Java 1.0 – 1.1 | Bootstrap, Custom | | Java 1.2 – 8 | Bootstrap, Extension, Application | | Java 9+ | Bootstrap, Platform, Application | <details <summary Class Loaders explanation</summary Loads .class files into JVM memory in a strict parent first order. 1. Three Types of Class Loaders 2. Loading Phases All 3 loaders go through these same 3 phases. | Phase | What Happens | | | | | Loading | Reads .class file, creates Class object in heap | | Verify | Checks bytecode is valid and safe | | Prepare | Allocates memory for static variables with default values | | Resolve | Replaces symbolic references with direct memory references | | Initialization | Runs static blocks, assigns actual values to static variables | 3. Delegation Model When a class is requested, loaders do not load it directly — they ask their parent first. How loadClass() works internally Why delegation matters Prevents duplicate class loading Prevents security issues — core classes like String and Object cannot be overridden Ensures consistency — same class loaded once across the JVM 4. Quick Reference | Loader | Source | Written In | Example | | | | | | | Bootstrap | rt.jar / JAVA HOME/lib | Native C/C++ | String.class | | Platform | JAVA HOME/lib/ext | Java | javax.crypto. | | Application | Classpath | Java | com.myapp.Main | 5. Get Class Loader Programmatically getParent() returns null for Bootstrap — it has no Java parent. Key Rule Delegation always goes up first (App → Platform → Bootstrap), then down only if not found. Bootstrap loads first — your code loads last. Custom Class Loader (All Versions) Used in: Application servers (Tomcat, WebLogic) Plugin systems OSGi Hot deployment Quick Reference Interview One‑Liners ✅ Bootstrap Class Loader is not a Java object Extension Class Loader removed in Java 9 Java 9 introduced Platform Class Loader Delegation model ensures security Multiple class loaders allow same class name | Loader | Loads | Written In | | | | | | Bootstrap | java.lang. , java.util. , java.io. | Native C/C++ | | Platform | javax. , crypto, XML, security | Java | | Application | Your .class files, classpath JARs | Java | </details 🆔 Identifiers in Java <details <summary Java Identifiers and Keywords</summary Identifiers start with alphabets, underscore , or dollar $. Case sensitive. Keywords cannot be used as identifiers . Some Java Keywords | Keyword | Usage | | | | | class | Declare a class | | public | Accessibility modifier | | static | Belongs to class rather than instance | | void | Method returns nothing | | main | Entry point of Java program | | new | Create new object | | if, else | Conditional statements | | for, while, do | Loop constructs | | return | Exit method and optionally return value | | try, catch, finally | Exception handling blocks | | throw, throws | Exception declaration and throwing | Java Identifiers (Short & Simple) Identifiers are names for variables, methods, classes, etc. Rules: Must start with a letter (A Z, a z), underscore , or dollar sign $. Can contain digits (0 9) after the first character. Case sensitive (MyVar ≠ myvar). Cannot use Java keywords (like class, int). Examples: Common Java Keywords: class, public, static, void, if, else, for, while, return, try, catch, throw, throws </details <details <summary Variables in Java</summary Local: Inside method body; cannot be static. Instance: Inside class body; each object has its own copy. Static: Shared across all instances; memory allocated once when class loads. </details 🏷️ What is a Class? A class is a blueprint or template from which objects are created. It contains data (fields) and behaviors (methods). Object class is the parent (superclass) of every class — automatically, even if you don't write extends Object | Method | What it does | | | | | toString() | Text representation of the object | | equals(obj) | Checks if two objects are equal | | hashCode() | Returns a hash number for the object | | getClass() | Returns the class name at runtime | | clone() | Copies the object | | finalize() | Called before garbage collection | Every class you ever write automatically gets those 6 methods. You can override them to customize behaviour. Always create the object with new before using it. Stack holds the reference (variable name). Definition: A HAS A relationship represents composition or aggregation — one class contains another class as a member. It means “has a” or “contains a” relationship. ➡️ Example Here: Car has an Engine. The HAS A relationship exists between Car and Engine. ✅ We can write: 🧠 Conceptually: One class uses or contains another class. It’s composition if the contained object’s lifetime depends on the container. Example: A Car’s Engine exists only as long as the Car exists. It’s aggregation if they can exist independently. But how tightly one class owns the other defines whether it’s: Composition (strong ownership) Aggregation (weak ownership) ⚙️ 1. Composition — Strong HAS A relationship Definition: When one class owns another class completely — the contained object cannot exist independently of the container. Lifetime is dependent: If the container object is destroyed, the contained object is also destroyed. ➡️ Example: Car has an Engine ✅ Explanation: Car creates the Engine object. If the Car object is destroyed → its Engine object also ceases to exist. Engine’s lifecycle is tied to Car. Diamond (♦) denotes composition (from UML). ⚙️ 2. Aggregation — Weak HAS A relationship Definition: When one class uses another class without owning it . The contained object can exist independently . Lifetime is independent: If the container is destroyed, the contained object still exists elsewhere. ➡️ Example: Department has Employees ✅ Explanation: Employee objects are created outside the Department. Department just uses a reference to them. Even if the Department is deleted, employees can exist independently. Deserialization reconstructs the object from the byte stream. Use writeObject() and ObjectOutputStream for serialization. Use readObject() and ObjectInputStream for deserialization. Only classes implementing java.io.Serializable can be serialized. 1. What is Serialization? Serialization is the process of converting an in memory Java object into a byte stream (or some other transferable format like JSON, XML, etc.). The reverse process is deserialization — converting the byte stream back into an object. 2. Why do we need to serialize if an object is already in memory (which is bytes anyway)? Good question. Yes, technically objects in memory are stored as bytes in the JVM heap. But: That representation is JVM specific , tied to memory layout, references, garbage collector, etc. You cannot take those raw JVM bytes and write them to a file or send them over a network — another JVM (or another language) won’t know how to interpret them. Serialization converts the object into a standardized format that can be: Saved to disk Sent over a network Reconstructed later 3. Why Serialization is Needed (Use Cases) 1. Persistence Save an object’s state to a file/database and restore it later. Example: storing user sessions. 2. Communication (Distributed Systems) Send objects over the network (e.g., between microservices). Example: Spring Boot → JSON serialization for REST APIs. 3. Caching Objects are serialized to store in Redis, Hazelcast, or another distributed cache. 4. Deep Copying Serialize → Deserialize to create a true deep copy of an object. 4. Analogy Think of an object in memory like a house : Inside, things are structured in a very specific way (JVM internal representation). If you want to move the house elsewhere (send object to another system), you can’t just “copy the ground and bricks” — that won’t make sense. Instead, you serialize it into blueprints (bytes in standard format) , send/store them, and then rebuild the house (deserialize) elsewhere. ✅ Summary : Objects in memory are already bytes , but only meaningful to the current JVM . Serialization makes those objects portable and reconstructible , independent of the JVM’s internal representation. Transient Keywor Fields marked transient are not serialized . Reactive Programming emerged to overcome the limitations of traditional thread per request architectures by using: Non blocking I/O Event driven processing Reactive Streams Asynchronous execution pipelines Popular reactive frameworks include: Project Reactor RxJava Spring WebFlux Virtual Threads, introduced through Project Loom in Java 21+ , take a different approach. Instead of avoiding blocking operations, they make blocking inexpensive by introducing lightweight JVM managed threads. This represents one of the biggest architectural shifts in modern Java development. Reactive Programming Core Principles Reactive programming is built around: Non blocking I/O Event driven execution Publisher Subscriber model Backpressure aware streams Functional composition Common Reactive Types Mono Represents zero or one result. Flux Represents multiple results. Reactive Architecture Instead of blocking a thread while waiting for I/O, the request is suspended and resumed when the data becomes available. Example Everything executes asynchronously through a reactive pipeline. Virtual Threads What Are Virtual Threads? Virtual Threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than directly by the operating system. Introduced through: They allow developers to continue using the familiar thread per task programming model while supporting very high concurrency. Key Idea Traditional Threads: Virtual Threads: Thousands or even millions of virtual threads can run on a relatively small number of OS threads. How Virtual Threads Work When a virtual thread encounters a blocking operation: the JVM: 1. Unmounts the virtual thread from its carrier thread 2. Frees the underlying OS thread 3. Resumes execution when the operation completes This scheduling is completely transparent to developers. Virtual Thread Architecture The application still appears synchronous even though the JVM is efficiently managing execution. Example This is standard blocking code. With virtual threads, the same code can scale significantly better without rewriting it into reactive chains. The Architectural Shift Reactive programming emerged because traditional Java applications faced several challenges. Problems in Traditional Systems Thread Explosion OS threads are expensive. Large thread counts consume: Memory CPU resources Scheduling overhead Blocking Operations Operations such as: Database Calls File Reads Network Requests External APIs cause threads to sit idle while waiting. High I/O Wait Times Systems often spend more time waiting than computing. Reactive programming solved this by eliminating blocking. Old Mindset This was the foundation of reactive architectures. New Mindset Virtual Threads introduce a different philosophy: Instead of avoiding blocking entirely, the JVM makes blocking efficient. This fundamentally changes how modern Java applications can be designed. Where Virtual Threads Win 1. Simple Programming Model Reactive code often requires: which can become difficult to read and debug. Virtual threads allow traditional sequential programming. Example Easy to read. Easy to maintain. Easy to debug. 2. Minimal Code Changes Most existing applications can benefit from virtual threads with very little modification. Examples: Spring Boot MVC JDBC RestTemplate Feign Clients Legacy Libraries can continue to work. 3. Existing Drivers Continue Working A major advantage is compatibility. Existing blocking technologies work immediately: JDBC Drivers Hibernate JPA Apache HTTP Client Legacy SDKs No special reactive driver is required. 4. Easier Developer Adoption Most Java developers already understand: Virtual Threads preserve familiar programming models. The learning curve is significantly smaller. Example Enterprise Scenario A Spring Boot service performs: With Virtual Threads: Existing code stays mostly unchanged JDBC works immediately Blocking HTTP clients still work Scalability increases significantly This is why many modern Spring applications are moving toward Virtual Threads. Where Reactive Programming Still Wins Virtual Threads do not replace Reactive Programming entirely. There are workloads where Reactive remains superior. 1. Streaming Systems Examples: Kafka Consumers Kafka Streams Server Sent Events (SSE) WebSocket Streams Reactive pipelines naturally model continuous data streams. 2. Heavy Backpressure Scenarios Reactive Streams include: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers. This remains a major advantage. 3. Real Time Event Processing Applications processing: Millions of events Continuous streams Real time analytics often benefit more from reactive architectures. 4. High Frequency Data Pipelines Examples: Financial trading Telemetry ingestion IoT systems Sensor streams Reactive frameworks offer sophisticated stream processing capabilities. Example: Without @Override, this compiles but results in a new method (overloading) instead of overriding. 3️⃣ Why it matters If you omit @Override , and accidentally change: method name (typo), parameter list, or return type, ...you’ll create a new method , not an override. That can silently break polymorphism — your child class won’t behave as intended. Example: Even though the method names are the same, this is overloading , not overriding — because parameter types differ. If you had used @Override, the compiler would’ve caught this mistake. ⚠️ Special Cases | Case | Behavior | | | | | Parent method is static | Child method with same name hides it, not overrides it. | | Parent method is private | Child method is new , not visible to parent; no overriding. | | Parent method is final | Cannot be overridden — compile time error. | | Parent method return type changed covariantly | Allowed (if subtype of parent’s return). | 🧠 In summary | With @Override | Without @Override | | | | | Compiler checks correctness of override. | Compiler doesn’t check — might accidentally overload. | | Optional but strongly recommended. | Works fine if method truly overrides, but risky. | | No runtime impact — only compile time validation. | Same runtime behavior if truly overriding. | ✅ Takeaway @Override is not required for overriding, but it’s a best practice — it protects you from subtle bugs caused by typos or signature mismatches. 3️⃣ Difference between final, effectively final, and const | Concept | Meaning in Java | Example | Notes | | | | | | | final | Variable’s reference cannot change after assignment. | final int x = 10; | For objects, the reference is final, not the contents. | | Effectively final | Variable not declared final, but never reassigned after initialization. | Used in lambdas / inner classes. | Compiler treats it as final. | | const (other languages) | Compile time constant (C/C++/C ). | const int x = 5; | Java reserved const but never implemented it — use static final. | Example: 4️⃣ Pass by value vs. reference in Java ✅ Java is always pass by value , but the value can be a reference . 💡 Explanation When you pass an object to a method, Java copies the reference value (the memory address). That means: You can change the object’s state (since both references point to the same object). You cannot change what the caller’s variable refers to. Example: ➡️ The object’s content changed, but the caller’s variable still points to the same object. 5️⃣ Implement an immutable list without using Collections.unmodifiableList() We can make our own immutable class by: Making the internal list final. Wrapping it to prevent external mutation. Exposing only read only methods. ✅ Example: Usage: ✅ Summary Table | Topic | Key Point | | | | | hashCode() without equals() | Breaks hashing contract, leads to wrong behavior in sets/maps | | Overloading vs Overriding | Compile time vs runtime dispatch; v table lookup for overriding | | final vs effectively final vs const | Control mutability of references; no const in Java | | Java parameter passing | Always pass by value (reference value for objects) | | Immutable list | Custom wrapper with defensive copy + blocked mutation | 6️⃣ How does the ForkJoinPool work internally? 💡 Concept ForkJoinPool (introduced in Java 7) is a specialized thread pool designed for divide and conquer parallelism — especially recursive, fine grained tasks . Typical usage: ForkJoinPool manages ForkJoinTasks (RecursiveTask or RecursiveAction). Tasks can split (fork) into subtasks and later join their results. ⚙️ Internal Mechanics 1. Work stealing algorithm Each worker thread has its own deque (double ended queue) . When a thread finishes its own tasks, it “steals” tasks from the tail of another thread’s deque. This minimizes contention and maximizes CPU utilization. 2. Task submission Tasks are placed in a worker’s deque. If submitted externally (pool.submit()), they go into a shared submission queue. 3. Execution Each worker thread repeatedly: Takes a task from the head of its deque. Executes it; if the task forks new subtasks, they are pushed at the head of its own deque. 4. Joining When a task calls join(), it either: Gets the result immediately if already computed. Or suspends until the result is ready. The worker may “help” execute other tasks while waiting — improving throughput. 5. Parallelism control ForkJoinPool maintains a parallelism level (usually Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()). It dynamically manages worker threads for CPU saturation but avoids oversubscription. ✅ Example Under the hood: The pool balances these subtasks across threads via work stealing. 7️⃣ Difference between synchronized, Lock, and StampedLock | Feature | synchronized | Lock (e.g. ReentrantLock) | StampedLock | | | | | | | Type | JVM keyword | Java util class (java.util.concurrent.locks) | Newer lock (Java 8) | | Granularity | Implicit monitor per object | Explicit lock objects | Stamp based locking | | Lock/Unlock | Automatic (enter/exit block) | Manual (lock()/unlock()) | Manual (writeLock()/readLock()/unlock()) | | Fairness | No fairness guarantee | Can be fair/unfair | No fairness, focus on speed | | Reentrancy | Yes | Yes (ReentrantLock) | No | | Read/Write separation | No | Via ReadWriteLock | Yes (readLock, writeLock, and optimisticRead) | | Try/Timeout | No | Yes (tryLock(long, TimeUnit)) | Yes (tryOptimisticRead) | | Performance | Simple but limited | More control | Fast for read heavy workloads | | Typical use | Basic synchronization | Fine grained, flexible control | Optimized read dominated concurrency | 🧩 Example 8️⃣ CompletableFuture vs. traditional Future | Aspect | Future | CompletableFuture | | | | | | Introduced | Java 5 | Java 8 | | Blocking get() | Yes | Optional — can compose non blocking | | Can complete manually | No | Yes (complete(value)) | | Chaining | No | Yes (thenApply, thenCompose, etc.) | | Exception handling | Manual | Built in (handle, exceptionally) | | Async composition | No | Yes — fluent pipeline | | Dependent stages | No | Yes, multiple dependent tasks | ✅ Example CompletableFuture supports asynchronous chaining , combining multiple futures, and non blocking continuations. Internally, it uses the ForkJoinPool by default for async execution. 9️⃣ Design a concurrent cache with Read Write Locks 💡 Goal Allow multiple concurrent readers but only one writer. ✅ Example Implementation 🚀 Optimization Replace HashMap with ConcurrentHashMap for finer granularity. For read heavy workloads: StampedLock with optimistic reads: 🔟 False Sharing and How to Avoid It 💡 Concept False sharing occurs when multiple threads modify different variables that reside on the same CPU cache line (typically 64 bytes). Even though threads access different data, cache coherency protocols (MESI) cause cache invalidations , leading to major performance degradation. 🔍 Example Both a and b are independent, but updates trigger invalidations on the same cache line. 🚫 Effect CPU cache thrashing Reduced throughput on multi core systems ✅ Avoidance Techniques 1. Padding / Contention avoidance Use @sun.misc.Contended (requires JVM flag XX: RestrictContended). Or manually add padding fields to align to cache lines. 2. Separate objects Store heavily updated fields in separate objects to avoid co location. 3. Use LongAdder / LongAccumulator These classes are designed to reduce contention and false sharing by spreading updates across multiple variables internally. ✅ Summary Table | | Topic | Key Takeaway | | | | | | 6 | ForkJoinPool | Work stealing pool for fine grained parallelism | | 7 | synchronized vs Lock vs StampedLock | Increasing flexibility and performance | | 8 | CompletableFuture | Asynchronous, composable, non blocking futures | | 9 | Concurrent cache | Use ReadWriteLock or StampedLock for safe access | | 10 | False sharing | Cache line contention — solved by padding or LongAdder | Junit <https://www.java2novice.com/junit examples/junit annotations/ Junit mockito <https://programmingtechie.com/2020/10/16/spring boot testing tutorial unit testing with junit 5 and mockito/ 7. Filter Even and Odd Numbers using Streams</strong </summary .map() is for transforming elements; to filter, use .filter(). The condition (s/2) == 0 doesn’t check for even numbers — you want s % 2 == 0. The lambda must always return a value (in .map), but here you want to keep or discard items — so .filter() is the right method. Explanation | Operation | Stream Method | Condition | | | | | | Filter even | .filter() | s % 2 == 0 | | Filter odd | .filter() | s % 2 != 0 | </details <details <summary 🧩 Example using <code Runnable</code and <code wait/notify</code </summary ✅ Output (approx): 🧠 Explanation count is shared by both threads. lock ensures synchronization . When one thread is not supposed to print (e.g. even thread sees an odd number), it calls lock.wait() and releases the lock. After printing, the thread increments count and calls lock.notify() to wake up the other thread. This repeats until the count reaches 10. </details <details <summary ⚙️ Alternative using <code Callable</code + <code ExecutorService</code </summary You can also use Callable<Void if you prefer an executor based approach: This behaves the same, but uses an ExecutorService to manage threads. </details cleaner and safer version using Lock and Condition instead of wait/notify. <details <summary 🧩 Using <code Lock</code and <code Condition</code (Recommended Way)</summary ✅ Output: <details <summary 🧠 Why this is better than <code wait/notify</code </summary Condition objects (oddTurn and evenTurn) are more readable than arbitrary wait()/notify() calls. Lock provides fine grained control over which condition to signal. No need for synchronized blocks — the lock ensures mutual exclusion. Avoids accidental wake ups (spurious wakeups) better than plain Object.wait(). </details <details open <summary <strong 🔍 19. String vs StringBuilder Comparison Explained</strong </summary What prints and why? | Line | Output | Explanation | | | | | | System.out.println(s1 == s2); | true | Both refer to the same interned string literal in the String Pool, so references are equal. | | System.out.println(s1.equals(s2)); | true | Contents are the same, so .equals() returns true. | | System.out.println(sb1.toString() == s1); | false | sb1.toString() creates a new String object, so reference comparison is false. | | System.out.println(sb1.toString().equals(s1)); | true | Contents are the same, so .equals() returns true. | Important points: == on Strings compares reference equality (are both variables pointing to the same object?). String literals like "Java" are interned , so identical literals share the same reference. StringBuilder.toString() creates a new String object each time, so reference is different from s1. .equals() compares the content of strings. How to make sb1.toString() == s1 true? You can intern the string explicitly: Because .intern() returns the canonical representation from the String Pool. </details <details <summary <strong ✨ 20. Find Palindromes using Streams</strong </summary Palindrome: a string that reads the same forwards and backwards. To check, compare the string with its reverse. Using streams, you can filter only palindrome words. Explanation | Operation | Stream Method | Logic | | | | | | Convert array | Arrays.stream() | Turn the array into a stream. | | Filter palindromes | .filter() | Keep only words where word.equalsIgnoreCase(reverse(word)). | | Collect results | .collect() | Collect into a List<String . | Example Output </details <details open <summary <strong Check if a given string is palindrome using recursion.</strong </summary </details <details open <summary <strong ⚡ 21. Sort Map by Values (Streams, TreeMap, Comparator)</strong </summary By default, HashMap doesn’t maintain order. We can sort by keys easily using TreeMap, but sorting by values requires: Streams (.sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())) TreeMap with custom comparator Collecting into LinkedHashMap to preserve sorted order Explanation | Method | Approach | | | | | Streams + sorted | Sort by values (comparingByValue), then collect into LinkedHashMap. | | Streams + reverseOrder | Same as above, but descending order. | | TreeMap with Comparator | Sorts by keys , not values (but useful to show difference). | Example Output </details <details open <summary <strong 🌀 22. Swap Values without Using Another Variable</strong </summary Normally, swapping uses a temporary variable: But we can do it without an extra variable using: Arithmetic (Addition/Subtraction or Multiplication/Division) Bitwise XOR Explanation | Method | Logic | | | | | Addition & Subtraction | Add both → subtract back to extract original values. | | Multiplication & Division | Multiply → divide back to extract original values. (⚠️ risky: zero/overflow). | | XOR Bitwise | XOR twice cancels out, restoring swapped values. | Example Output </details <details open <summary <strong 🎯 23. Two Sum using Streams</strong </summary Stream approach: Use IntStream.range to iterate over indices. For each index i, find a matching index j where nums[i] + nums[j] == target. Stop at the first valid pair. Explanation | Operation | Stream API Used | Purpose | | | | | | Generate indices | IntStream.range(0, n) | Iterate over all possible i. | | Pair with next indices | flatMap(IntStream.range) | Generate all pairs (i, j) with j i. | | Filter matching sums | .filter(nums[i] + nums[j] == target) | Keep only pairs that match the target. | | Return first match | .findFirst() | Get first valid pair (since problem guarantees one). | Example Output </details <details open <summary <strong 🗂️ 24. Group Employees by Department & Filter by Year using Streams</strong </summary Group by Department → use Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment). Filter by Joining Year → use getJoiningDate().getYear() 2018. Explanation | Operation | Stream API | | | | | Group by department | Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment) | | Filter by year | .filter(e e.getJoiningDate().getYear() 2018) | | Collect results | .collect(Collectors.toList()) | | Sort by date asc | .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getJoiningDate)) | | Sort by date desc | .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::getJoiningDate).reversed()) | Example Output </details <details <summary <strong Sort by value in Map</strong </summary In Java, a HashMap doesn’t maintain any order. If you want to sort it by values , you can use streams (Java 8+) or a List<Map.Entry<K,V with a comparator. Sort groups by the first occurrence in the input . 3. Flatten each group with flatMap, sorting inside the group so negatives come before positives. </details <details <summary <strong Count how many times each number occurs</strong </summary pair → how many complete pairs (count ÷ 2) odd → leftover count (count % 2) Here’s how you can do it with Java Streams : ✅ Output: </details <details <summary Palindrome Check Using Java Streams</summary ✅ Palindrome Check Using Java Streams 🧠 Explanation replaceAll("[^a zA Z0 9]", ""): removes all non alphanumeric characters. toLowerCase(): makes the comparison case insensitive. IntStream.range(0, cleaned.length() / 2): iterates from start to the middle. allMatch(...): ensures all symmetric character pairs match. Java Fundamentals & JVM 1.1 Core Concepts | Question / Topic | Answer | | | | | What is JVM? | An abstract machine providing a runtime environment to execute Java bytecode. | | Why is Java platform independent? | Programs compile to bytecode (.class), which runs on any OS with a JVM installed — Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA) . | | Is JVM part of JDK or JRE? | JVM is part of JRE; JRE is part of JDK. | | Can Java run without JVM? | No — bytecode execution requires JVM. | | What is bytecode? | Intermediate, platform independent code generated by the Java compiler. | | Is Java 100% object oriented? | No — it supports primitive data types. | | Why is Java compiled and interpreted? | Source → bytecode (compiled) → interpreted/JIT compiled at runtime. | 1.2 JVM / JRE / JDK | Component | Full Form | Purpose | Contains | | | | | | | JVM | Java Virtual Machine | Executes bytecode | Execution engine | | JRE | Java Runtime Environment | Runs Java programs | JVM + Libraries | | JDK | Java Development Kit | Develops Java apps | JRE + Compiler + Tools | 1.3 Top Java Features | Feature | Description | | | | | Platform Independent | Runs on any OS with a JVM | | Object Oriented | Based on classes and objects | | Simple & Secure | No pointers, built in security | | Robust | Exception handling + garbage collection | | Multithreaded | Supports concurrent execution | | High Performance | JIT compiler optimizes at runtime | | Dynamic | Supports dynamic class loading | 1.4 JVM Internal Architecture | Component | Role | | | | | Class Loader | Loads, links, and initializes class files into JVM memory | | Runtime Data Areas | Heap, Stack, Method Area, PC Register, Native Method Stack | | Execution Engine | Interpreter, JIT Compiler, Garbage Collector | | Native Interface (JNI) | Allows Java to interact with native (non Java) code | Class loading phases: Loading → Linking (verify bytecode, allocate memory, resolve references) → Initialization (run static blocks/variables). 1.5 JVM Memory (Runtime Data) Areas | Memory Area | Description | Thread Scope | | | | | | Heap | Stores objects and instance variables | Shared across all threads | | Stack | Stores local variables, method call info | Each thread has its own (thread safe, fastest) | | Method Area (Metaspace) | Class metadata, static variables, method bytecode | Shared | | PC Register | Tracks currently executing instruction | Per thread (supports context switching) | | Native Method Stack | Executes native (non Java) methods | Per thread | 📘 If Method Area runs out of memory → OutOfMemoryError. Since Java 8, PermGen was replaced by Metaspace , which uses native memory and grows dynamically. 1.6 Execution Engine | Component | Role | | | | | Interpreter | Executes bytecode line by line (slow — re interprets repeatedly) | | JIT Compiler | Compiles frequently executed ("hot") bytecode into native machine code for speed | | Garbage Collector | Reclaims memory from unreachable objects | 1.7 ClassLoader Subsystem | ClassLoader | Loads From | | | | | Bootstrap | Core classes (java.lang. ) | | Extension | jre/lib/ext | | Application | Classpath (user defined) | 1.8 main() Method Explained | Modifier | Reason | | | | | public | Accessible by JVM from anywhere | | static | Runs without creating an object | | void | No return value | | String[] args | Command line arguments | 📘 Without static, JVM throws: Error: Main method not found 1.9 Java vs C++ | Feature | Java | C++ | | | | | | Platform | Independent | Dependent | | Memory Management | Automatic (GC) | Manual (delete) | | Multiple Inheritance | Via interfaces only | Supported directly | | Pointers | Not allowed | Allowed | | Compilation | To bytecode | To machine code | | Exception Handling | Mandatory (checked) | Optional | 1.10 Pass by Value | Question | Answer | | | | | Does Java support pass by reference? | No — Java is always pass by value . | | How does this apply to objects? | The object reference is copied by value; the copy still points to the same object, so object state can be modified, but the reference itself can't be reassigned to affect the caller's variable. | 2. Data Types, Variables & Type Casting 2.1 Primitive Data Types | Type | Size | Default | Example | | | | | | | byte | 1 byte | 0 | byte b = 10; | | short | 2 bytes | 0 | short s = 100; | | int | 4 bytes | 0 | int x = 500; | | long | 8 bytes | 0L | long l = 10000L; | | float | 4 bytes | 0.0f | float f = 10.5f; | | double | 8 bytes | 0.0d | double d = 20.99; | | char | 2 bytes | '\u0000' | char c = 'A'; | | boolean | 1 bit | false | boolean flag = true; | Non primitive types: String, Array, Class, Interface, Object. 2.2 Variable Types | Type | Scope | Memory | Default | | | | | | | Local Variable | Inside method | Stack | None — must initialize | | Instance Variable | Inside class, outside method | Heap | Has default | | Static (Class) Variable | Class level, shared | Method Area | Has default | 2.3 Type Casting — Overview | Question | Answer | | | | | What is type casting? | Converting one data type into another. | | Categories? | Primitive type casting and Object type casting. | | Checked when? | Both compile time and runtime, depending on scenario. | 2.4 Widening vs Narrowing (Primitive Casting) | Aspect | Widening (Implicit) | Narrowing (Explicit) | | | | | | Direction | Smaller → Larger | Larger → Smaller | | Safety | Safe, no data loss | Risky — may lose data/overflow | | Syntax | Automatic | Must cast manually: (int) d | | Order | byte→short→int→long→float→double | — | | Example | int i=10; double d=i; | double d=9.8; int i=(int)d; // 9 | 2.5 Upcasting vs Downcasting (Object Casting) | Aspect | Upcasting | Downcasting | | | | | | Direction | Child → Parent reference | Parent → Child reference | | Implicit/Explicit | Implicit | Explicit | | Safety | Always safe (child IS A parent) | Risky — may throw ClassCastException | | Example | Animal a = new Dog(); | Dog d = (Dog) a; | | Safe technique | — | Check with instanceof first | | Enabling principle | Polymorphism | — | | Tricky Question | Answer | | | | | Can we downcast without upcasting first? | No — leads to ClassCastException. | | Does casting change the actual object? | No — only changes the reference type/view, not memory. | | Does instanceof work with interfaces? | Yes. | 2.6 Casting vs Generics | Aspect | Type Casting | Generics | | | | | | Checked | Runtime | Compile time | | Safety | Lower | Higher | | Runtime errors | ClassCastException possible | Mostly prevented | | Explicit syntax | Yes | No (inferred) | | Overhead | Yes (runtime checks) | No (type erasure) | | Works with primitives? | N/A | No — only objects (autoboxing bridges this) | | Tricky Question | Answer | | | | | Can generics fully replace casting? | No — casting still needed for legacy/runtime scenarios. | | Why does casting still exist? | Backward compatibility and runtime polymorphism. | | Do generics add runtime overhead? | No, due to type erasure. | | Framework returns Object — what do you use? | Casting (carefully). | | Building reusable utility classes? | Generics. | 2.7 Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing | Primitive | Wrapper | | | | | byte | Byte | | short | Short | | int | Integer | | long | Long | | float | Float | | double | Double | | char | Character | | boolean | Boolean | | Question | Answer | | | | | Why are wrapper classes needed? JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is a Java API enabling programs to connect and interact with databases — executing SQL and performing CRUD operations. 10.2 JDBC Driver Types | Type | Name | Description | | | | | | Type 1 | JDBC ODBC Bridge | Uses ODBC driver (deprecated) | | Type 2 | Native API Driver | Uses native client libraries | | Type 3 | Network Protocol Driver | Translates JDBC to DB independent network calls | | Type 4 | Thin Driver (Pure Java) | Directly communicates with DB — ✅ most used | 10.3 Connecting to a Database 10.4 JDBC API Components | Component | Purpose | | | | | DriverManager | Manages drivers; establishes connections via getConnection() | | Connection | Represents a session; creates statements; manages transactions | | Statement | Executes static SQL | | PreparedStatement | Parameterized SQL — prevents SQL injection, better performance for repeats | | CallableStatement | Executes stored procedures | | ResultSet | Holds retrieved data; cursor based row traversal | | SQLException | Handles DB access errors | PreparedStatement vs Statement : PreparedStatement is precompiled and parameterized — prevents SQL injection and performs better for repeated execution; Statement is vulnerable to SQL injection. Always prefer PreparedStatement. 10.5 JDBC RowSet | Type | Description | | | | | JdbcRowSet | Connected — requires active connection (like ResultSet) | | CachedRowSet | Disconnected — stores data in memory | | WebRowSet | XML representation for web transfer | 10.6 Handling Large Data (e.g. 1GB Excel Delta) Use streaming parsers (Apache POI SXSSF), compare row hashes, use database staging tables for comparison, and batch processing. Prefer Hibernate for complex relationships, raw JDBC for bulk operations. 11. SQL & Databases 11.1 Core Queries 11.2 Indexing, Joins, Procedures | Concept | Description | | | | | Indexing | Data structure (commonly B tree) improving query speed via sorted references — faster reads, slower writes | | Inner Join | Returns only matching rows from both tables | | Left Outer Join | All left table rows + matches from right (NULL if no match) | | Stored Procedure | Precompiled, reusable SQL block | | Function | Returns a single value, usable inside SELECT | | Trigger | Auto executes on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events (e.g. audit logging) | 11.3 ACID Properties | Property | Meaning | Example | | | | | | A tomicity | Transaction is all or nothing | Debit A succeeds, Credit B fails → entire transfer rolls back, A's balance unchanged | | C onsistency | DB remains in a valid state, honoring constraints/rules | Total bank balance stays ₹10,000 before and after an internal transfer | | I solation | Concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other | Two users booking the last seat simultaneously — only one succeeds | | D urability | Once committed, data survives crashes/failures | Order saved to DB persists even if the server crashes right after | 🧠 Memory trick: "All Cats Ignore Dogs" → Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability 12. Design Patterns | Pattern | Description | | | | | Singleton | Ensures only one instance exists — private constructor, static instance, public getInstance(); thread safe via synchronized or enum singleton | | Prototype | Creates new objects by cloning an existing prototype — useful when object creation is expensive; implements Cloneable and overrides clone() | | Proxy (Hibernate) | Used for lazy loading — Hibernate returns a proxy object; actual data fetched only when accessed, reducing unnecessary DB calls | Hibernate Related Patterns | Pattern | Role | | | | | Proxy | Lazy loading | | Unit of Work | Session tracks changes | | Identity Map | First level cache | | Data Mapper | ORM mapping | | Repository | Data access abstraction | Testability Patterns | Pattern | Benefit for Testing | | | | | Dependency Injection | Mock dependencies | | Factory | Create test doubles | | Strategy | Swap algorithms | | Observer | Test event handling | | Repository | Mock the data layer | 13. Hibernate & ORM | Concept | Description | | | | | First level cache | Session scoped, automatic | | Second level cache | SessionFactory scoped, configurable | | Query cache | Caches HQL/Criteria query results | | Lazy Loading | Associated objects loaded only when accessed, not during initial query — reduces memory usage and improves performance; implemented via proxy objects | 14. Spring Framework 14.1 Stereotype Annotations | Annotation | Layer | Description | | | | | | @Component | Any | Generic Spring bean | | @Service | Business/Service | Specialization of @Component for service logic | | @Repository | DAO/Persistence | Adds exception translation from JDBC to Spring DataAccessException | 14.2 Dependency Injection | Question | Answer | | | | | What is DI? | Dependencies provided externally rather than created inside the class — improves loose coupling, testability, flexibility. | | Types of DI | Constructor Injection (preferred), Setter Injection , Field Injection (least preferred). | | Why prefer Constructor Injection? | Ensures required dependencies, enables immutability, easier testing, fails fast at startup if a dependency is missing. | | Field Injection issue? | Hard to test, generally not recommended. | | Circular dependency? | Constructor injection fails; Setter injection can work around it. | | DI Container? | Manages object creation/lifecycle and resolves dependencies automatically (e.g. Spring IoC Container, Google Guice). | | Service not registered? | Throws exception at injection point — Spring: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. | | DI vs Service Locator? | DI pushes dependencies into objects; Service Locator has objects pull from a central registry — DI is cleaner and more testable. | | @Autowired? | Spring annotation for automatic dependency injection on constructor, setter, or field. | 14.3 Bean Scopes | Scope | Lifetime | | | | | Transient | New instance every request | | Scoped | One instance per scope/request | | Singleton | One instance for the application lifetime | 14.4 Web Layer / REST | Annotation | Used For | URL Pattern | Example | | | | | | | @RequestParam | Query parameters | /users?id=10 | @GetMapping("/users") getUser(@RequestParam int id) | | @PathVariable | URI template variables | /users/10 | @GetMapping("/users/{id}") getUser(@PathVariable int id) | | Comparison | Answer | | | | | @Controller vs @RestController | @Controller returns view names (MVC templates); @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody, returns JSON/XML directly. | | PUT vs POST | POST creates a new resource (non idempotent); PUT updates/replaces the entire resource (idempotent). | | Default embedded server in Spring Boot? | Embedded Tomcat (swappable to Jetty/Undertow). | 14.5 HTTP Response Codes | Code | Meaning | Category | | | | | | 200 OK | Request successful | 2xx | | 201 Created | Resource created | 2xx | | 204 No Content | Empty response body | 2xx | | 400 Bad Request | Invalid request data | 4xx | | 401 Unauthorized | Not authenticated | 4xx | | 403 Forbidden | Authenticated but no permission | 4xx | | 404 Not Found | Resource not found | 4xx | | 500 Internal Server Error | Server failed | 5xx | | 503 Service Unavailable | Server overloaded/down | 5xx | 14.6 Tracing & Batch Processing | Concept | Description | | | | | Tracking multiple REST calls | Correlation IDs in headers, MDC logging context, distributed tracing (Zipkin, Jaeger), Spring Sleuth | | Spring Batch | Framework for batch processing — Job, Step, ItemReader, ItemProcessor, ItemWriter; used for ETL, migrations, reports; supports transactions and restart | 15. Security & Authentication | Concept | Description | | | | | Authentication | Who are you? — e.g. login with username + password | | Authorization | What can you access? — e.g. Admin vs User role based access | | JWT | A self contained token format carrying user info + expiry — used for stateless API auth | | OAuth2 | An authorization framework/protocol (e.g. "Login with Google") — delegated access | | JWT vs OAuth2 | OAuth2 = protocol; JWT = token type/format | | Typical project setup | JWT tokens for stateless auth, Spring Security for config, OAuth2 for third party login, BCrypt for password hashing, RBAC | 16. Microservices | Concept | Description | | | | | Architecture | Small, independent services — components include API Gateway, Service Discovery, Config Server, Load Balancer | | Benefits | Scalability, technology flexibility, independent deployment | | Sync communication | REST APIs, gRPC (for performance) | | Async communication | Message brokers — Kafka, RabbitMQ | | Service mesh | Istio — traffic management and security | | Email routing example | API Gateway routes by path/header → Service Discovery locates the Email Service → message queue for async delivery | | Why not share a DB across services? | Breaks service independence | | Sync vs Async tradeoff | Sync is simple but blocking; Async is scalable but more complex | 17. Misc Java Topics 17.1 Regular Expressions (java.util.regex) | Symbol | Meaning | Example | | | | | | . | Any single character | c.t → cat, cut | | | 0 or more | do g → dg, dog | | + | 1 or more | go+ → go, goo | | ? | 0 or 1 | colou?r → color, colour | | \d | Any digit | \d+ → 123 | | \w | Word char | \w+ → abc123 | | ^ | Start of line | ^Hello | | $ | End of line | world$ | | {n,m} | Between n and m times | \d{2,4} → 12, 1234 | 17.2 Packages & Containers | Type | Description | Example | | | | | | Built in package | Predefined in Java | java.lang, java.util, java.io, java.sql | | User defined package | Created by developers | package com.myapp; | | Container (general) | Object that holds other objects | Collections (List/Set/Map), Servlet containers (Tomcat), Spring IoC container | 17.3 I/O Streams | Aspect | InputStream/OutputStream (Byte) | Reader/Writer (Character) | | | | | | Data Type | Binary (8 bit bytes) | Text (16 bit Unicode) | | Use Case | Images, audio, video | Text files | | Example Classes | FileInputStream, BufferedOutputStream | FileReader, BufferedWriter | | Console Input Method | Example | | | | | Scanner (easiest) | Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in); | | BufferedReader | new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)) | | Console | System.console().readLine() | | print vs println vs printf | Behavior | | | | | print() | No newline | | println() | Adds newline | | printf() | Formatted output with specifiers | 17.4 Logging Typical setup: SLF4J with Logback implementation; log levels (ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG); structured logging with correlation IDs for request tracing. 18. Quick Interview Reference Summary | Topic | Key Point | | | | | Platform Independence | Bytecode runs on any JVM — WORA | | JDK JRE JVM | JDK contains JRE which contains JVM | | 4 OOP Pillars | Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction | | Polymorphism types | Overloading (compile time), Overriding (runtime) | | Interface vs Abstract | Interface: multiple inheritance, no constructor. Abstract: single inherit, has constructor | | final/finally/finalize | Restrict / Cleanup / GC hook | | String Pool | Literals reuse; new String() always creates a new object | | ArrayList growth | 50% increase (oldCapacity + oldCapacity/2) | | HashMap vs Hashtable | HashMap: faster, null allowed. Hashtable: synchronized, no null | | Fail Fast vs Fail Safe | ArrayList = fail fast; CopyOnWriteArrayList = fail safe | | Stream pipeline | Source → Intermediate (lazy) → Terminal (eager) | | Thread creation | Extend Thread OR implement Runnable | | sleep() vs wait() | sleep: no lock release. wait: releases lock | | JDBC Type 4 driver | Pure Java, most commonly used | | Checked vs Unchecked | Checked = compile time. Unchecked = runtime | | GC types | Minor (young gen), Major (old gen), Full (entire heap) | | Generics | Compile time type safety | | Record (Java 14+) | Immutable DTO with auto generated methods | | ACID | Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability | 19. Karat / Live Coding Interview Strategy 19.1 Section 1 — Domain Knowledge / Trivia ( 20 min) Rapid fire questions testing foundational CS literacy — up to 6 questions (200 points). | Topic Area | Specific Concepts | | | | | OOP | Four Pillars: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism | | Databases | ACID properties, LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN | | Operating Systems | Process vs Thread, Deadlocks | What interviewers want: Precise, professional definitions — not lectures. They're checking a box, not looking for deep discussion. 19.2 Section 2 — Coding Problems ( 40–45 min) | Criterion | What They Observe | | | | | Problem Clarification | Did you paraphrase the problem and confirm 1–2 example inputs? | | Approach & Complexity | Stated brute force, then optimal, with time/space complexity before coding? | | Code Completion | How many problems completed? (Expectation: 2–3 total ) | | Code Quality | Clean naming, modularization, edge case handling | | Testing | Dry ran the example? Tested empty/null/large inputs? | ⚠️ Critical insight: Number of problems solved is a key metric. Spending 30 minutes on problem 1 means automatically failing problem 2 — speed is intentionally part of the rubric. 19.3 Section 3 — Communication (Cross cutting) Complexity Statement — stated before coding In Code Monologue — talking through variables and logic Error handling — acknowledge → diagnose → plan 19.4 Why Candidates Fail Despite Feeling Successful | Candidate's Belief | What the Rubric Actually Showed | | | | | "I solved the problem correctly" | Only one problem solved; expectation was 2–3 — Code Completion scored 40%. | | "My solution worked" | Complexity wasn't stated before coding — lost points on Approach & Complexity. | | "I used the internet for help" | Help taken without consent — triggers a Red Flag. | | "I clarified requirements" | Took 5 minutes; rubric expects 2–3 minutes max — ate into time for Problem 2. | | "I explained my thinking" | Explained what the code does, not why that approach or its trade offs. |

title: Javascript Core Concepts
text: JavaScript Core Concepts — Deep Dive Comprehensive explanations of 7 essential JavaScript concepts with ASCII flow diagrams and code examples. Table of Contents 1. Destructuring Assignment 2. Spread Syntax 3. Closures 4. Function Composition 5. Event Delegation 6. Web Workers 7. Event Loop FEPerformance 1. Destructuring Assignment Destructuring lets you unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables — a cleaner alternative to manual indexing. How It Works Array Destructuring Object Destructuring Function Parameter Destructuring Nested + Mixed Destructuring ASCII Flow — Object Destructuring 2. Spread Syntax The spread operator (...) expands an iterable (array, object, string) into individual elements. Core Concept Array Spread Object Spread Spread in Function Calls Spread vs Rest ASCII Flow — Object Spread Merge 3. Closures A closure is a function that remembers the variables from its outer (lexical) scope even after that outer function has returned. Lexical Scope Chain Basic Closure Closure Memory Model Practical Use Cases 1. Data Privacy / Encapsulation 2. Function Factories 3. Memoization Common Pitfall — Loop + Closure 4. Function Composition Function composition is the process of combining multiple functions so the output of one becomes the input of the next — building complex logic from small, reusable pieces. Core Concept ASCII Flow Manual Composition compose — Right to Left pipe — Left to Right (More Readable) Real World Example — Data Pipeline ASCII Flow — Data Pipeline Partial Application & Currying (Enables Composition) 5. Event Delegation Event delegation leverages event bubbling — instead of attaching listeners to every child element, attach a single listener to a parent and determine which child triggered it. Event Bubbling Without Delegation (Inefficient) With Delegation (Efficient) ASCII — Without vs With Delegation Real World Example — Dynamic List Event Flow — Three Phases stopPropagation vs preventDefault 6. Web Workers Web Workers run JavaScript on a background thread , keeping the main UI thread free from heavy computation. The Problem Without Workers With Web Workers Basic Web Worker main.js worker.js Transferable Objects (Zero Copy Transfer) Shared Workers (Multiple Tabs) What Workers Can & Cannot Do ASCII — Worker Communication Loop 7. Event Loop JavaScript is single threaded but handles async operations via the Event Loop — a mechanism that coordinates the call stack, Web APIs, and task queues. Components Event Loop — Execution Order Classic Example — Execution Order Step by Step Trace Microtask vs Macrotask async/await Under the Hood Blocking the Event Loop (What NOT to Do) Full Event Loop ASCII — With Async Example Summary — Priority Order Quick Reference | Concept | One liner | Key Method/Syntax | | | | | | Destructuring | Unpack arrays/objects into variables | const { a } = obj / const [x] = arr | | Spread | Expand iterables into elements | [...arr] / {...obj} | | Closures | Inner function remembers outer scope | Function returning function | | Composition | Chain pure functions, output → input | pipe(f, g, h)(x) | | Event Delegation | One parent listener for all children | e.target.closest() | | Web Workers | Background thread for heavy tasks | new Worker('w.js') + postMessage | | Event Loop | Async coordination: stack + queues | Microtasks before macrotasks | Last updated: March 2026
