Use JOIN FETCH to avoid N+1 ✅ Loads order + items in one query instead of one per item. 2. Batch fetching / entity graph JPA will load related entities in batches instead of one by one. Or use: entityGraph 3. Use projections instead of full entities Returns lightweight DTOs — no persistence overhead. 4. Pagination + streaming Use Pageable or stream results for large tables: Prevents loading millions of rows in memory at once. 5. Disable dirty checking when reading only Avoids JPA overhead for read only queries. 6. Second level cache Enable 2nd level or query cache with providers like Ehcache / Redis for frequently read data. ✅ Rule of thumb: Don’t load objects when you only need data. Use projections, fetch joins, and pagination for large datasets. 22️⃣ What’s the difference between EntityManager.persist() and merge()? | Method | Purpose | Behavior | Return Type | | | | | | | persist() | Insert new entity | Makes entity managed and schedules insert | void | | merge() | Update or attach detached entity | Returns a new managed copy | Returns managed instance | 🔹 Example ✅ Important: After merge(), always use the returned reference (merged), not the original object. 🧠 Notes persist() → only for new entities. merge() → for detached or existing entities. Calling merge() on a transient entity creates a new managed copy with the same state. 23️⃣ How do you handle pagination efficiently in Spring Data JPA? 💡 Use Pageable and Page<T API 🧩 Why it’s efficient: Translates to LIMIT + OFFSET in SQL automatically. Returns metadata: ⚙️ Optimization Tips 1. For large OFFSETs , use keyset pagination : → faster for infinite scrolling. 2. Avoid unnecessary count queries Use Slice<T instead of Page<T when total count not needed. 3. Index pagination columns for efficiency. 4. Project only required columns using DTOs. 24️⃣ How do you manage schema migrations across microservices? 💡 Problem Each service owns its own database — schema versions must evolve predictably across environments. 🧩 Best Practices 1. Use database migration tools Flyway or Liquibase are the standards. Place migration scripts under src/main/resources/db/migration. Example (Flyway): Spring Boot auto runs them at startup: 2. Each microservice manages its own schema Microservices must own their data — no shared schema. 3. Schema versioning per service Maintain Flyway metadata table (flyway schema history) to track applied versions. 4. Pipeline integration In CI/CD: Run migrations before deploying new service version. Rollback strategy: keep backward compatible scripts. 5. Avoid cross service joins Instead use: API calls or Async events (Kafka, CDC via Debezium) ✅ Key idea: Schema migrations are version controlled, automated, and owned by each service independently. 25️⃣ What’s the best approach for auditing (createdBy, updatedBy) in JPA? 💡 Goal Track who created/updated a record and when it happened. 🧩 Option 1: Spring Data JPA Auditing 1. Enable auditing 2. Auditable base class 3. Extend entities 4. Provide AuditorAware ✅ Automatically fills createdBy, updatedBy, createdAt, updatedAt. 🧩 Option 2: Custom entity listener If not using Spring Data: 🧠 Best Practices Store userId instead of username if possible. Use Instant (UTC) for timestamps. Avoid database triggers — keep audit logic in application for portability. ✅ Summary Table | | Topic | Key Takeaway | | | | | | 21 | JPA optimization | Use projections, fetch joins, pagination, batch fetch | | 22 | persist() vs merge() | persist → new, merge → update/reattach | | 23 | Pagination | Use Pageable, Slice, and keyset pagination | | 24 | Schema migrations | Use Flyway/Liquibase per service | | 25 | Auditing | Use Spring Data Auditing or custom entity listeners | ✅ LAZY / EAGER / JOIN FETCH Core Difference | Concept | What it controls | When it applies | Query impact | | | | | | | FetchType.LAZY / EAGER | Default loading strategy | Applies to all queries | Controlled by Hibernate | | JOIN FETCH | Overrides loading for a specific query | Applies to that query only | Explicit SQL JOIN | 🔹 1. FetchType (LAZY vs EAGER) This is defined at entity mapping level . ✅ LAZY (default for collections) Items are NOT loaded initially When accessed → triggers another query 👉 ❌ Leads to N+1 problem 1 query for orders N queries for items ✅ EAGER Items are loaded immediately Hibernate decides how (JOIN or additional query) 👉 ❌ Problems: Loads data even if not needed Can cause performance issues Not flexible 🔹 2. JOIN FETCH (Query level control) ✅ What happens: 👉 ✅ Key advantages: Single query Avoids N+1 Loads only when needed Works even if mapping is LAZY 🔥 Key Difference (Simple Way) | Scenario | Behavior | | | | | LAZY only | Load later → multiple queries | | EAGER only | Always load → may waste data | | JOIN FETCH | Load on demand + efficiently | ✅ Important Insight (INTERVIEW GOLD) 🔥 JOIN FETCH overrides LAZY Even if: This works: 👉 Hibernate forces eager loading for that query only ✅ Real Use Case Bad (N+1 problem): Good (JOIN FETCH): 👉 ✅ Single optimized query ⚠️ Important Notes 1. Use DISTINCT with collections 👉 Avoid duplicate orders due to JOIN 2. Cannot use pagination easily 👉 Because JOIN multiplies rows 3. Only for associations ✅ Works with: @OneToMany @ManyToOne @ManyToMany ✅ Final Mental Model 🔥 When to Use What | Use case | Recommendation | | | | | Default mapping | Use LAZY ✅ | | Always needed relationship | Consider EAGER cautiously ⚠️ | | Avoid N+1 in specific query | Use JOIN FETCH ✅✅✅ | ✅ One line Summary 👉 LAZY/EAGER decides how entity behaves normally 👉 JOIN FETCH decides how this specific query should behave efficiently 📦 AOP in Spring Boot – Explained (with Custom Annotations + Logging) AOP (Aspect Oriented Programming) allows you to separate cross cutting concerns like logging, security, and retry mechanisms from your core business logic. This makes the code cleaner , more modular , and easier to maintain . <details <summary <strong 🔍 What is AOP?</strong </summary AOP stands for Aspect Oriented Programming , and it helps you inject common functionality (like logging, security, transactions) into different parts of the application without duplicating code . 💡 For example: Instead of writing logging code in every method, AOP lets you write one aspect class to handle logging for all methods. </details <details <summary <strong 🧱 Key AOP Terminology</strong </summary | Term | Description | | | | | Aspect | A module that encapsulates a cross cutting concern (e.g., logging) | | Advice | Code that is executed at a join point (before, after, around a method) | | Join Point | A point in the application (like a method execution) where advice can be applied | | Pointcut | An expression to match join points | | Weaving | Linking aspects with the target objects | This Spring Boot AOP Project includes: @LogExecution — a custom annotation to log method execution @Retryable — a custom retry annotation to reattempt failed methods SLF4J + Logback — for structured logging Full aspect classes to intercept and act on methods A working service (MyService) that simulates failures </details <details <summary <strong ⚙️ Setup – Dependencies</strong </summary Add this to your pom.xml: And enable AOP: </details <details <summary <strong 🛡️ Custom Annotation: @LogExecution</strong </summary Purpose Logs method entry , return value , and exceptions centrally. Example usage Corresponding Aspect This helps monitor what's happening in your app without modifying business logic. </details <details <summary <strong 🔁 Custom Annotation: @Retryable</strong </summary Purpose Retries a method if it fails, for a fixed number of attempts. Example usage Retry Logic Aspect Each time the method throws an exception, it retries until success or until the attempt limit is reached. </details <details <summary <strong 📋 Real Example: MyService.java</strong </summary 💡 This simulates a flaky method. AOP handles retries and logging transparently! </details <details <summary <strong 📊 Logging with SLF4J + Logback</strong </summary SLF4J is used for logging with support from Logback 🎯 This is configured automatically with Spring Boot starter logging. Optionally, you can add a custom logback.xml file to control: Log file paths Log levels (INFO, DEBUG, ERROR) Pattern layouts </details <details <summary <strong 🏁 Application Entry Point</strong </summary This runs on app start and triggers the riskyOperation() method. </details <details <summary <strong 🧪 Testing & Output</strong </summary When you run the app, you'll see: 🎉 This shows: Logging worked Retry succeeded after failure No duplicate logging in your service logic </details <details <summary <strong ✅ Benefits Recap</strong </summary ✨ Cleaner Code : No duplicate logic across services 🔄 Reusable : Apply annotations anywhere! 📦 Modular : Central logic for retry, logging, etc. 🔐 Ready for Prod : Easily extend for security, validation, etc. </details Spotless lint Run ./gradlew spotlessCheck ./gradlew spotlessApply Zipkin Traceable 🔎 Elasticsearch in Spring Boot Type : Distributed full text search and analytics engine. Primary Use Case : Searching large volumes of text or documents. Supporting advanced queries: fuzzy search, autocomplete, relevancy ranking. Analytics on logs, metrics, or events (often with ELK stack: Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana). Strengths : Full text search (better than SQL LIKE). Handles complex queries (filters, aggregations, scoring). Distributed and scalable. Spring Boot Integration : Via spring data elasticsearch. Example: ⚡ Redis in Spring Boot Type : In memory data store / cache / message broker. Primary Use Case : Caching frequently accessed data (reduce DB load). Session storage. Message queues / Pub Sub. Rate limiting, counters, leaderboard (sorted sets). Strengths : Extremely fast (in memory). Simple data structures (string, list, set, hash, sorted set, stream). Good for real time use cases. Spring Boot Integration : Via spring boot starter data redis. Example: ✅ When to Use What Use Elasticsearch if: You need search capabilities (full text search, fuzzy search, autocomplete). Your main queries involve finding documents by content rather than by ID. Use Redis if: You need caching to reduce DB load. You need fast lookups (key value). You’re building real time features (leaderboards, queues, session store). 🚀 Combined Usage in Spring Boot Many production systems actually use both : Store data in Postgres/MySQL (source of truth). Use Redis for caching frequently accessed records. Use Elasticsearch for search functionality. 📊 Detailed Comparison Table ✅ Expanded and detailed version for gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ, GraphQL, and REST API | Aspect | gRPC | Kafka | RabbitMQ | GraphQL | REST API | | | | | | | | | Communication style | Remote Procedure Calls (unary, client streaming, server streaming, bidirectional streaming) | Publish/Subscribe via distributed commit log (stream of ordered records) | Message broker with queues and routing (Pub/Sub + work queues) | Query language over HTTP (client defines exact shape of response) | Resource based request/response (CRUD using HTTP verbs: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) | | Transport | HTTP/2 with Protobuf serialization (binary, compact, strongly typed) | Custom TCP protocol, distributed partitions, durable log storage | TCP using AMQP (lightweight messages, acknowledgements, retries) | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (usually JSON), optional WebSockets for subscriptions | HTTP/1.1/2 (JSON, XML, or other formats) | | Coupling | Tight — client must know the server contract and schema (Protobuf definitions) | Loose — producers publish to topics, unaware of who consumes | Medium — producers publish to an exchange, consumers subscribe via queues, some decoupling but not full broadcast | Tight — clients must know schema to form queries, though schema provides strong documentation | Medium — clients must know endpoint structure and request/response format | | Data lifetime | Transient — lives only during the RPC call/stream | Persistent — data stored in partitions for hours/days/weeks (configurable retention) | Transient by default — messages deleted once acknowledged; supports durable queues for persistence | Transient — response exists only during request/response lifecycle | Transient — response delivered per request only | | Scalability | Vertical — efficient multiplexing over HTTP/2 per connection | Massive horizontal scalability — partitioning, consumer groups, distributed brokers | Horizontal — clustering supported, though throughput is lower than Kafka | Horizontal — scales at API gateway level with multiple resolvers | Horizontal — stateless servers behind load balancers | | Best for | High performance microservice communication, real time APIs, strongly typed interactions | High throughput event streaming, event sourcing, analytics pipelines | Reliable task queues, job scheduling, background worker processing | Flexible client facing APIs that minimize over/under fetching | Simple, universal CRUD APIs with broad adoption | 🔑 When to Use (with examples) ✅ gRPC When you need synchronous or near real time interaction between services . Example: a user service calls an auth service to validate credentials. When you need bidirectional streaming communication . Example: a mobile app chats with a backend, both sending and receiving messages continuously. When you want strongly typed contracts across microservices. Example: backend to backend services in a polyglot system (Java, Go, Python). ✅ Kafka When you need an event driven architecture where multiple services react to events. Example: a payment service publishes a “PaymentCompleted” event consumed by shipping service , email service , and analytics service . When you need high throughput pipelines for data streams. Example: real time clickstream data or IoT telemetry processed by multiple analytics consumers. When you need durability and replay . Example: replaying historical events for fraud detection models or audit trails . ✅ RabbitMQ When you need a reliable task queue for job distribution. Example: an order service places tasks in a queue for invoice generation or PDF rendering . When you need message acknowledgement and retries . Example: an email service retries sending if the SMTP server fails. When you need simple pub/sub with routing. Example: log processing where different queues handle different log levels ( info , warn , error ). ✅ GraphQL When you want clients to decide what data they fetch (preventing over/under fetching). Example: a mobile app requesting { user { id, name, avatar } } instead of fetching the full user object. When you have complex relationships and need efficient data fetching. Example: fetching a user’s profile, posts, and comments in one request instead of multiple REST calls. When you want schema first API development with strong tooling. Example: auto generating TypeScript types or frontend codegen from GraphQL schema. ✅ REST API When you need simple CRUD operations with broad adoption. Example: a product service exposing /products, /products/{id} for GET/POST/PUT/DELETE. When you need public APIs where compatibility matters. Example: exposing a payment API for 3rd parties (Stripe, PayPal style). When you want human readable, easy to test endpoints . Example: quick cURL or Postman tests without special tooling. 🌐 Together (Common Architecture) A modern system often combines them: 1. Frontend → Backend Uses REST API (simple endpoints) or GraphQL (flexible queries) for client facing apps. Example: mobile app fetches data via GraphQL. 2. Backend → Internal Services Uses gRPC for synchronous, strongly typed microservice communication. Example: profile service calling auth service over gRPC. 3. Event Backbone Uses Kafka for async event streaming. Example: order service emits OrderCreated → multiple consumers process it. 4. Job Processing Uses RabbitMQ for background tasks. Example: email service or report service processing queued jobs. ✅ Rule of Thumb (Expanded) Use gRPC → For direct, strongly typed, low latency communication (service to service, real time). Use Kafka → For event driven, high throughput, durable event distribution (analytics, pipelines, decoupling). Use RabbitMQ → For task queues, guaranteed delivery, retries, worker jobs (job scheduling, notifications). Use GraphQL → For flexible, client driven APIs (web/mobile apps, complex queries). Use REST API → For simple, standardized, widely compatible APIs (CRUD, public APIs, quick integrations). restGrpcGraphRabitmq.png GraphQL All calls to graphQL are post calls. GraphQlQueryResolver is used instead of JPARepo. ⚔️ REST API vs. GraphQL <details <summary <strong REST API</strong </summary Uses standard HTTP methods like GET , POST , PUT , DELETE for CRUD operations. Works well when you need simple, uniform interfaces between separate services or applications. Caching strategies are straightforward to implement. The downside is it may require multiple round trips to assemble related data from separate endpoints. </details <details <summary <strong GraphQL</strong </summary Provides a single endpoint for clients to query precisely the data they need. Clients specify the exact fields required in nested queries, and the server returns optimized payloads containing just those fields. Supports Mutations (for modifying data) and Subscriptions (for real time notifications). Excellent for aggregating data from multiple sources and adapting to rapidly evolving frontend requirements . However, it shifts complexity to the client and can allow abusive queries if not properly safeguarded. Caching strategies can be more complicated than in REST. </details RestVsGraphQl Multiple DB ✅ 1. When do we use Multiple DB? Microservices connecting to different DBs Read/Write separation (Master–Replica) Multi tenant applications Migration scenarios Integrating legacy + new systems ✅ 2. Core Concept Spring Boot normally auto configures one DataSource . For multiple DBs, you must manually configure: ✅ Multiple DataSource ✅ Multiple EntityManagerFactory ✅ Multiple TransactionManager ✅ 3. High Level Architecture 👉 Each DB has its own config + repo + entities ✅ 4. application.yml Example ✅ 5. DB1 Configuration ✅ 6. DB2 Configuration ✅ 7. Repository Structure (Important) 👉 Each DB must have separate packages ✅ 8. Using in Service Layer ✅ 9. Handling Transactions Across DBs (Important) ⚠️ By default: Each DB has independent transactions ✅ If you need single transaction across DBs : Use JTA / XA Transactions Example tools: Atomikos Narayana (Spring Boot support) ✅ 10. Alternative Approach (Dynamic Routing DB) If DB changes dynamically (like multi tenant): 👉 Use AbstractRoutingDataSource ✅ 11. Common Interview Questions ❓ Why @Primary? Default DB when multiple beans exist ❓ Why separate packages? Spring uses @EnableJpaRepositories to bind repo → DB ❓ Can one entity connect to multiple DBs? ❌ No (one entity = one persistence unit) ❓ What about Spring Boot auto config? Disabled automatically when multiple DataSources defined ❓ How to scale this design? Use: API Gateway CQRS (different DB for read/write) Event driven sync (Kafka) ✅ 12. Common Mistakes ❌ Missing @Primary → Bean conflict ❌ Same package for repos → wrong DB mapping ❌ Forgetting transaction manager → runtime errors ❌ Mixing entities between DBs ✅ Final Summary (Short) In Spring Boot, multiple DBs are configured by defining multiple DataSource, EntityManager, and TransactionManager beans , and linking them using @EnableJpaRepositories with separate packages. API Versioning in Spring Boot Context API versioning is an important design practice in Spring Boot applications because APIs rarely remain unchanged throughout their lifetime. As business requirements evolve, a REST endpoint may need to: Return additional fields Accept a modified request structure Behave differently for new consumers If these changes are introduced directly into an existing endpoint, older clients may break unexpectedly. API versioning provides a safer approach by allowing teams to introduce improved API behavior while keeping earlier contracts available for consumers who have not yet migrated. Traditional Versioning Approaches In earlier Spring Boot projects, developers typically implemented versioning using: Separate URL paths Custom request conditions Filters Header based mappings While these approaches worked, they often resulted in: Repeated code Inconsistent implementation styles across teams Additional maintenance effort API Versioning in Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4 With Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4 , API versioning becomes a first class request mapping feature. Developers can: Declare API versions directly on controller methods Configure how Spring resolves the version Use consistent versioning strategies across applications Spring can read the requested version from: Request Headers Query Parameters Media Types Path Segments Common API Versioning Strategies 1. Path Based Versioning Version is included in the URL path. Example Benefits Easy to understand Highly visible Easy to test Drawbacks URLs change between versions Resource identity becomes coupled with versioning 2. Header Based Versioning Version is provided in a request header. Example Benefits Clean URLs Resource path remains stable Widely used in enterprise systems Drawbacks Harder to test directly in a browser Versioning is not visible in the URL 3. Query Parameter Versioning Version is passed as a query parameter. Example Benefits Easy to test from browsers Simple implementation Drawbacks Clutters URLs Often considered less RESTful 4. Media Type Versioning Version is specified in the requested representation. Example Benefits Keeps URLs stable Aligns with REST principles Supports content negotiation Drawbacks More complex for consumers Additional configuration required Enterprise Recommendation In enterprise APIs, the preferred approaches are usually: Header Based Versioning Media Type Versioning These approaches keep the resource URL clean, stable, and independent of API evolution. Example: Header Based Versioning The following example demonstrates version resolution using a custom request header. Configuration What This Configuration Does Reads the API version from the request header. Uses Version 1 when no explicit version is provided. Automatically falls back to the default version when the header is absent. Controller Implementation Once version resolution is configured, Spring automatically routes requests to the appropriate method. API Response Models Version 1 Response Response Version 2 Response Response Request Examples Version 1 Request Response Version 2 Request Response How Spring Selects the Endpoint The resource URL remains: Only the representation changes according to the requested version. When Should You Create a New Version? A new version should be introduced when changes may break existing consumers. Examples ✅ Create a New Version Removing fields Renaming fields Changing request structure Modifying response contracts Changing business behavior ❌ Usually No New Version Needed Adding optional response fields Performance improvements Internal refactoring Bug fixes that preserve behavior Best Practices 1. Maintain Backward Compatibility Avoid breaking existing consumers whenever possible. 2. Document All Versions Clearly document: Supported versions Request formats Response structures Deprecation timelines 3. Define a Deprecation Strategy Communicate: Deprecated versions End of support dates Migration guidance 4. Avoid Too Many Active Versions Supporting many versions increases: Testing effort Maintenance cost Operational complexity 5. Prefer Clean Migration Paths Provide consumers with: Upgrade guides Side by side documentation Deprecation notifications Key Takeaways API versioning allows services to evolve without breaking existing consumers. Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4 introduce native API versioning support. Common versioning approaches include: Path Based Header Based Query Parameter Based Media Type Based Enterprise APIs often favor Header Based or Media Type versioning to keep URLs clean and stable. Not every change requires a new version; only breaking contract changes typically justify one. Well managed versioning reduces risk, simplifies migrations, and supports long term API evolution. References Spring Framework API Versioning Documentation Native API Versioning Feature in Spring Boot Context API versioning is an essential practice for evolving REST APIs without breaking existing consumers. As business requirements change, APIs often need to introduce new fields, modify request structures, or alter behavior. Without a versioning strategy, such changes can cause compatibility issues for clients that depend on older contracts. Spring Boot's native API versioning support provides developers with a straightforward mechanism for handling multiple API versions while keeping the codebase organized and maintainable. By leveraging version aware request mappings, different versions of the same endpoint can coexist and evolve independently. The primary goals of API versioning are: Maintain backward compatibility Support gradual client migration Reduce breaking changes Simplify long term API evolution Native API Versioning in Spring Boot Spring Boot allows multiple versions of an endpoint to exist side by side by differentiating requests based on version information. A common approach is using request headers to specify the API version. Version 1 Endpoint Version 2 Endpoint How It Works When a client invokes the endpoint, Spring examines the request headers and routes the request to the appropriate handler method. Request Flow Example Requests Version 1 Client Response Version 2 Client Response Benefits of Native API Versioning 1. Backward Compatibility Older applications continue working without modification. At the same time: can access enhanced functionality. 2. Independent Evolution Each version can evolve separately. Example 3. Reduced Risk New features can be introduced without impacting existing consumers. This reduces: Production issues Client side regressions Forced migrations 4. Cleaner Code Organization Each version has its own handler method, making behavior easier to understand and maintain. 5. Better Scalability As APIs grow, versioned endpoints provide a structured approach for introducing breaking changes. Versioning Strategies in Spring Applications Although the example above uses headers, Spring supports multiple versioning approaches. | Strategy | Example | | | | | Header Based | API Version: 2 | | URL Path Based | /api/v2/employees | | Query Parameter Based | /employees?version=2 | | Media Type Based | Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json` | Header Based Versioning Advantages Clean URLs Easy evolution Suitable for enterprise APIs URL Path Versioning Advantages Highly visible Easy to test Easy for external consumers Query Parameter Versioning Advantages Browser friendly Simple implementation Media Type Versioning Advantages REST oriented approach Keeps URLs unchanged Best Practices 1. Document All Versions Clearly document: Available versions Request formats Response formats Migration guidance Example: 2. Use Consistent Versioning Strategy Avoid mixing multiple styles across services. Example: ✅ Consistent ❌ Inconsistent 3. Deprecate Gradually When introducing a newer API version: 1. Announce deprecation. 2. Define support timelines. 3. Provide migration guidance. 4. Remove only after consumers have migrated. 4. Avoid Version Explosion Do not create a new version for every minor change. Usually no new version is needed for: Optional fields Bug fixes Internal optimizations Create a new version when making: Breaking contract changes Field removals Request structure changes Behavioral changes 5. Remove Obsolete Versions Regularly review version usage. Benefits: Lower maintenance costs Reduced testing effort Smaller attack surface Improved security posture Enterprise Example Imagine an Employee API. Version 1 Version 2 Older consumers continue using Version 1 while newer applications adopt Version 2. This enables smooth API evolution without disrupting existing integrations. Key Takeaways Native API versioning simplifies managing multiple API contracts. Different API versions can coexist without code duplication or complex routing logic. Header based versioning provides a clean and enterprise friendly solution. Versioning helps maintain backward compatibility and supports gradual client migration. Not every change requires a new version; reserve version increments for breaking changes. Well documented deprecation and migration strategies are essential for long term maintainability. Regular cleanup of obsolete versions reduces complexity and operational risk. References Spring Blog: API Versioning in Spring

title: Springsecurity
text: Spring Security — Complete Flow Guide (JWT, RSA Key Pair, Class Flow, Latest Features) Current stable line: Spring Security 7.1.0 (Spring Boot 4.x), with 7.0.6 and 6.5.11 also maintained. 1. Core Architecture — How a Request Flows Through Spring Security Every HTTP request to a Spring Security–protected app passes through a chain of servlet filters before it reaches your controller. Key class relationships (the "class flow") 2. RSA Public/Private Key Generation for JWT Two common approaches: generate a KeyPair programmatically (dev/demo) or generate a PEM keypair via OpenSSL and load it (production). Option A — Generate at startup (java.security) Option B — Generate PEM files via OpenSSL (recommended for production) Load them via Spring's RsaKeyConverters or a small utility, then store the private key in a secrets manager (Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager) — never in source control. Wiring the keys into JWT encode/decode beans Why asymmetric (RSA/EC) instead of a shared HMAC secret? The private key signs the token (only the auth server holds it). The public key verifies the signature (any resource server can hold it, even in another language/service). This is what makes JWT/JWKS work cleanly in polyglot microservices — each service just needs the public key or a /​.well known/jwks.json endpoint, never the signing secret. 3. End to End JWT Authentication Flow Minimal SecurityFilterChain for a JWT resource server Exposing a JWKS endpoint (for other microservices to fetch your public key) This is exactly the JWT/JWKS cross language authorization pattern — a Spring Boot auth server signs with its private key, and any consumer (Quarkus, FastAPI, etc.) validates using the public JWKS endpoint without sharing secrets. 4. What's New — Spring Security 7.0 / 7.1 (Latest) | Feature | Version | Summary | | | | | | Multi Factor Authentication (MFA) | 7.0 | Native MFA support after years of requests — AuthenticationManagerFactories.multiFactor(), @EnableMultiFactorAuthentication, factor based authorization via AllRequiredFactorsAuthorizationManager | | AllRequiredFactorsAuthorizationManager.anyOf | 7.1 | Lets you require any one of several MFA factor combinations rather than a rigid all required set | | ConditionalAuthorizationManager | 7.1 | Compose authorization decisions with conditional (if/else style) logic instead of chaining multiple managers manually | | when / withWhen conditions on multiFactor() | 7.1 | Programmatic MFA — dynamically decide when a second factor is required | | MultiFactorCondition.WEBAUTHN REGISTERED | 7.1 | Require MFA conditionally only for users who have registered a WebAuthn/passkey credential | | PreFlightRequestFilter | 7.1 | Cleaner, dedicated handling of CORS pre flight OPTIONS requests | | InetAddressMatcher | 7.1 | IP address based request matching built into core (useful for allow listing internal services) | | RestClientOpaqueTokenIntrospector | 7.1 | Opaque token introspection now built on Spring's modern RestClient instead of legacy RestTemplate | | WebAuthn authentication events | 7.1 | Passkey/WebAuthn logins now publish AuthenticationSuccessEvent / failure events like other auth mechanisms | | OAuth2 for AI agents (MCP) | 7.x | OAuth2 client/resource server enhancements aimed at securing Model Context Protocol (MCP) based AI agent integrations | | More secure defaults | 7.x | Several previously opt in protections became default on; some legacy insecure configs were removed | | Jackson 3 support | 7.x | Full compatibility with Jackson 3 for Authentication/SecurityContext serialization (e.g. for distributed session caches) | | charset in WWW Authenticate header | 7.1 | Small RFC compliance fix for Basic/Bearer challenge headers | | Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) | 7.x | Resource servers can now publish OAuth2 protected resource metadata, improving client auto discovery | | DPoP bound Access Tokens | 7.x | Sender constrained tokens (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) — mitigates stolen bearer token replay | Migration note: 7.x is a major version bump requiring Spring Framework 7 / Boot 4 and Java 17+ (Java 21 recommended). Spring Security officially maintains 6.5.x (LTS style), 7.0.x, and 7.1.x concurrently — CVE only patches keep landing on 6.5/7.0 while new features land on 7.1+. 5. Other Authentication Mechanisms (Beyond JWT) | Mechanism | Class flow highlight | | | | | Form Login | UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter → DaoAuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService | | HTTP Basic | BasicAuthenticationFilter → same provider chain, credentials decoded from Authorization: Basic header | | OAuth2 Login (social/enterprise SSO) | OAuth2LoginAuthenticationFilter → OAuth2LoginAuthenticationProvider → exchanges auth code for tokens → OidcUserService | | OAuth2 Resource Server — Opaque Token | BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter → OpaqueTokenAuthenticationProvider → introspection call to auth server (token itself carries no claims) | | SAML2 | Saml2WebSsoAuthenticationFilter → OpenSaml4AuthenticationProvider → assertion validated against IdP metadata | | Passkeys / WebAuthn | WebAuthnAuthenticationFilter → public key credential challenge/response, no password at all | | One Time Token (magic link) | OneTimeTokenAuthenticationFilter → token generated, emailed/SMS'd, redeemed once | | Multi Factor Authentication | Primary factor authenticates → AllRequiredFactorsAuthorizationManager blocks access until remaining factors complete | | X.509 client certs | X509AuthenticationFilter extracts cert from TLS handshake → maps CN to a UserDetails | | Remember Me | RememberMeAuthenticationFilter — persistent token cookie, kicks in only when SecurityContext is empty | | LDAP | LdapAuthenticationProvider binds against a directory server | 6. Method Level Security Under the hood this is an AOP proxy : AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor / AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor wrap the bean and consult an AuthorizationManager before/after the real method executes — the same AuthorizationManager abstraction used by AuthorizationFilter at the HTTP layer. 7. Quick Reference — Key Interfaces & Classes SecurityFilterChain — the ordered filter list for a given request matcher AuthenticationManager / ProviderManager — orchestrates authentication AuthenticationProvider — pluggable strategy per auth mechanism UserDetailsService / UserDetails — user lookup abstraction PasswordEncoder — BCrypt/Argon2id hashing & verification SecurityContextHolder / SecurityContext — holds the current Authentication SecurityContextRepository — persists context (HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository vs NullSecurityContextRepository for stateless JWT apps) JwtEncoder / JwtDecoder — sign/verify JWTs (Nimbus based by default) JWKSource / JWKSet — key material source, backs the /oauth2/jwks endpoint AuthorizationManager — the single abstraction behind both HTTP and method security decisions AccessDeniedHandler / AuthenticationEntryPoint — customize 403/401 responses Sources Spring Security Reference — What's New in 7.1 (docs.spring.io) Spring Security 7.1.0 release notes, spring.io/blog (June 2026) Spring I/O 2026 session: "New in Spring Security 7: MFA, OAuth2 and more" Default configuration OAuth2 SpringBootWebSecurityConfiguration.java withDefaultPasswordEncoder should not be used in production. Can be only used in sample development. alt text There are two ways to configure username and password for security. application.properties InMemoryUserDetailsManager <details open <summary <strong ADFS, OAuth 1 & 2, JWT</strong </summary 1. ADFS (Active Directory Federation Services) What it is: A Microsoft product/service that provides Single Sign On (SSO) and federated identity across systems and organizations. How it works: Uses claims based authentication and supports standards like SAML, OAuth, and OpenID Connect. Use Case: Enterprises using Active Directory who want employees to log in once and access multiple systems securely (e.g., Office 365, internal apps). Analogy: Think of it as the identity broker from Microsoft, mostly used in corporate IT. 2. OAuth (OAuth 1.0 & OAuth 2.0) What it is: An authorization framework — it lets apps access resources on behalf of a user without sharing passwords. Key point: OAuth itself does not define how the user authenticates, only how access is delegated . Example: When you “Sign in with Google” and an app can access your calendar or contacts without knowing your Gmail password. 3. OAuth 2.0 (Modern Version of OAuth) What it is: The current and most widely used version of OAuth . What it adds: Different grant types (authorization code, client credentials, password, implicit, refresh tokens). Clear separation of Authorization Server and Resource Server . Easier for mobile and web apps. Use Case: Delegating access (e.g., mobile app getting an access token from Google to fetch user’s calendar data). Important: OAuth 2.0 by itself doesn’t define how users authenticate — it just handles access delegation . Authentication is usually layered on top using OpenID Connect (OIDC) . 4. JWT (JSON Web Token) What it is: A token format (JSON object, signed & optionally encrypted) that can be used in OAuth2.0, OIDC, or custom auth systems. Structure: Header + Payload + Signature (Base64 encoded). Use Case: Representing user identity or access rights in a secure, compact, and stateless way. Example: When you log into an app, it gives you a JWT (like eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...) which you send with each API request as proof you’re authenticated. How They Relate ADFS = A service from Microsoft that can issue tokens using standards like OAuth2.0, SAML, and often produces JWTs . OAuth (2.0) = A protocol for authorization (who can access what). JWT = A token format often used inside OAuth 2.0 for carrying claims about the user. OpenID Connect (OIDC) (not in your list, but important) = An authentication layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that uses JWTs to say who the user is . Quick Cheat Sheet ADFS: Microsoft’s implementation for SSO/federation. OAuth 2.0: Framework for delegated authorization (access rights). OIDC: Extension of OAuth 2.0 for authentication (user identity). JWT: Compact token format often used in OAuth2.0 and OIDC. 👉 If you’re thinking from a Java Full Stack project perspective : Use OAuth 2.0 + OIDC (via Keycloak, Auth0, or Azure AD) for modern apps. Use JWTs for stateless authentication across microservices. It sets XSRF TOKEN in a readable cookie (not HttpOnly). Frontend must read it and send it back in the X XSRF TOKEN header. Example frontend code: 🔑 How It All Works Together 1. Login → Backend issues JWTs in HttpOnly cookies . 2. CSRF Protection → XSRF TOKEN cookie issued, frontend sends it back in headers. 3. CORS → Allows credentials: 'include' so cookies can flow between frontend + backend. 4. JWT Filter → Reads access token from cookie, validates, sets user auth. 5. Logout → Deletes cookies by sending them with maxAge=0. Here’s a Mermaid sequence diagram showing the Spring Security + JWT + CSRF flow step by step 🚀 ✅ This shows the full lifecycle : Login → Issue cookies (access token, refresh token, XSRF TOKEN). Protected Request → Send access token (HttpOnly) + CSRF token (header). Refresh → Use refresh token to get new access token. Logout → Server deletes cookies by sending them back with maxAge=0. Perfect 👍 A state diagram is a great way to visualize the JWT lifecycle in Spring Security. Here’s the Mermaid state diagram for JWT authentication with refresh + logout: ✅ Explanation of states: NoToken → User has no JWTs (before login, after logout, or invalid session). Authenticated → User has a valid access token (short lived). Expired → access token expired, but refresh token may still be valid. Refresh → If refresh token valid → new access token issued, user returns to Authenticated . Logout / Refresh token expired → User goes back to NoToken . JWT lifecycle state diagram with the CSRF token lifecycle , since in Spring Security both interact for secure requests. 🔑 Explanation: JWT lifecycle access token short lived → expires → refreshed via refresh token. Both cleared on logout. CSRF lifecycle Issued as XSRF TOKEN cookie on login. Frontend must send it back as a header (X XSRF TOKEN). If mismatch/missing → request rejected → server may re issue a new CSRF cookie. Cleared on logout as well. Youtube Video 👉 This shows that JWT = identity/authentication while CSRF token = request integrity . They work together : JWT proves who you are , CSRF token proves it’s really you making the request from your client . Here’s the enhanced complete Mermaid sequence diagram with both valid ✅ and invalid ❌ flows : 🔑 What’s New Here Login → handles both valid credentials (cookies issued) and invalid credentials (401 Unauthorized). Protected Request → allows valid JWT + CSRF or rejects invalid/expired ones (401/403). Refresh → either issues a new access token (valid) or forces re login (invalid/expired refresh). Logout → clears cookies if active session, otherwise returns OK but does nothing. </details 1️⃣ Central Idea In microservices, authentication is typically done once at the entry point (API Gateway or Auth Service), and authorization/security info is propagated to downstream services using tokens (usually JWT). 2️⃣ How JWT Works Across Microservices 🔹 Step 1: Authentication Client (user/app) logs in via Auth Service (OAuth2, OpenID Connect). Auth Service verifies credentials and returns a JWT (JSON Web Token). 🔹 Step 2: Client Sends JWT Client includes JWT in Authorization header : This token is stateless , digitally signed (HMAC or RSA), so services can verify it without calling the Auth server . 🔹 Step 3: API Gateway Verification API Gateway can verify token signature and extract claims (userId, roles). Optional: issue short lived tokens or propagate refresh tokens . 🔹 Step 4: Downstream Service Communication When Microservice A calls Microservice B: 1. Propagate token in HTTP headers. 2. Microservice B verifies JWT locally (no need for central DB). 3. Service B enforces authorization based on claims in JWT (roles, scopes). 🔹 Step 5: Optional Service to Service Security Mutual TLS (mTLS) between services for transport level security. Combined with JWT, this ensures: 1. Only authorized services can communicate. 2. Identity of the caller is trusted and verifiable. 3️⃣ Best Practices | Practice | Why | | | | | Use short lived JWTs | Limits impact if token is stolen | | Use refresh tokens | To avoid forcing user login frequently | | Propagate token across all downstream calls | Preserve user identity for auditing & authorization | | Central Auth Service / Identity Provider | Easier to manage roles/scopes | | mTLS for service to service | Prevent unauthorized service access | | Avoid session state in services | JWT is stateless → no DB calls for auth | 4️⃣ Architecture Overview API Gateway validates JWT once. Each service can trust and extract claims from JWT . No distributed session or central DB needed per request. ✅ TL;DR 1. Client authenticates → gets JWT. 2. Client sends JWT to microservices. 3. API Gateway & services validate JWT . 4. JWT claims determine authorization . 5. Optional: mTLS + signed JWT → secure service to service communication. Perfect — let’s clarify this because it’s a common microservices interview trap . The short answer is: it depends on your security setup , but best practice is always propagate authentication or use service credentials . Let’s break it down. 1️⃣ Two Scenarios Scenario 1: Propagate User Authentication (JWT) Service A received a request from the client with a JWT token. Service A calls Service B on behalf of the user , passing the same JWT. Service B validates JWT , extracts claims, and enforces authorization. Flow: Pros: Downstream service knows who the user is . Can enforce role based or permission based authorization . Useful for auditing, multi tenant services, or resource ownership checks. Cons: Slightly more complex: token must be passed along HTTP headers. Downstream service must validate JWT. Example: Scenario 2: Internal Service to Service Call (Service Credentials) Sometimes services trust each other and only need to authenticate service identity , not the user. Use service to service credentials : mTLS certificates OAuth2 client credentials flow → Service A gets token from Auth Server as itself Service A calls Service B with its own token , not the user’s. Flow: Pros: Simplifies downstream authorization: services only check trusted service identity. Suitable for internal APIs not exposed to users. Cons: User info is lost unless Service A includes it in the request body/payload. 2️⃣ Best Practices | Practice | When to Use | | | | | Propagate user JWT | When downstream needs user context (e.g., authorization, auditing) | | Service to service token (client credentials / mTLS) | When downstream only needs trusted internal call, no user info | | Mix both | Gateway validates user → service A propagates JWT for user identity + service token for trust | 3️⃣ Typical Patterns in Microservices 1. API Gateway + JWT Client calls API Gateway with JWT. Gateway validates token → forwards to Service A. Service A either: Propagates JWT to Service B (user context needed) Calls Service B with service credentials (user context not needed) 2. Sidecar/Service Mesh (e.g., Istio) Service to service mTLS handled automatically. JWT or OAuth2 tokens can be injected by the mesh for propagation. ✅ TL;DR With JWT → Service B knows the user, enforces user level authorization. Without JWT (service token) → Service B trusts Service A but has no info about the user. Best practice: propagate user token when user context matters; otherwise use service authentication . user JWT propagation and service to service authentication flows: Token Exchange (OAuth2 On Behalf Of) Service A exchanges user token → new token for Service B ✔ Keeps user context ✔ Limits scope ✔ More secure than raw propagation Explanation 1. Option 1 — User JWT Propagation Service A forwards the client’s JWT to Service B. Service B knows who the user is and can enforce authorization or audit logs. 2. Option 2 — Service to Service Authentication Service A calls Service B with its own token or mTLS identity . Service B trusts Service A but does not know the user . ✅ This diagram makes it clear why JWT is needed if user context matters , and why service tokens are sufficient for internal trusted calls. JWT based authentication and propagation across microservices is done in Spring Boot , with a minimal working example . We’ll cover: 1. JWT generation at login 2. Validating JWT in incoming requests 3. Propagating JWT to downstream services 1️⃣ Generate JWT in Auth Service JWT Utility 2️⃣ Validate JWT in Service A Security Filter Register Filter 3️⃣ Propagate JWT to Service B If Service A calls Service B using RestTemplate or WebClient , pass JWT in headers. Using RestTemplate Using WebClient (Reactive) 4️⃣ Service B validates the JWT Service B applies the same filter and JwtUtil to verify incoming JWT. If valid → process request If invalid/expired → return 401 Unauthorized 5️⃣ Summary 1. Auth Service → Generates JWT on login. 2. Client → Sends JWT in Authorization` header. 3. Service A → Validates JWT, optionally sets SecurityContext. 4. Service A → Service B → Pass JWT downstream in headers. 5. Service B → Validates JWT before serving the request. ✅ This ensures user identity and authorization info travels across microservices without a centralized session.

Locking is used to prevent concurrent transaction issues like dirty reads, lost updates, and inconsistent data. 1. Pessimistic Lock Assumes that conflicts will happen , so it locks the data immediately. Example Imagine Account Balance = ₹1000 Transaction T1 T1 acquires a lock. Transaction T2 T2 must wait until T1 commits or rolls back. Types Pessimistic Read Lock Others can read but cannot modify. Pessimistic Write Lock Others cannot read for update or modify. Spring JPA Use Cases Banking transactions Inventory management Seat booking systems 2. Optimistic Lock Assumes conflicts are rare. Instead of locking the row, it checks whether someone modified the row before commit. Table | id | balance | version | | | | | | 1 | 1000 | 1 | T1 and T2 read version = 1. T1 updates: Success ✅ T2 tries: Fails ❌ because version became 2. Spring JPA Use Cases Most enterprise applications Product catalogs User profile updates 3. Shared Lock (Read Lock) Allows multiple transactions to read the same row. ✅ Read allowed ❌ Update blocked 4. Exclusive Lock (Write Lock) Only one transaction can modify the row. ✅ Owner can read/write ❌ Others cannot read for update or write Interview Comparison | Feature | Optimistic Lock | Pessimistic Lock | | | | | | Lock row immediately | ❌ | ✅ | | Performance | Better | Lower | | Concurrent users | High | Low | | Deadlock possibility | No | Yes | | Version column needed | Yes | No | | Best for | Read heavy systems | Write heavy critical systems | Common Problems Locks Solve Lost Update Without lock: T1 update lost ❌ Locks or optimistic versioning prevent this. Interview One Liner Pessimistic locking prevents conflicts by locking data before modification, while optimistic locking allows concurrent access and detects conflicts during update using a version field. Top Ways to Improve Database Performance dbPerformance 1. Indexing Create the right indexes based on query patterns to speed up data retrieval. 2. Materialized Views Store pre computed query results for quick access, reducing the need to process complex queries repeatedly. 3. Vertical Scaling Increase the capacity of the database server by adding more CPU, RAM, or storage. 4. Denormalization Reduce complex joins by restructuring data, which can improve query performance. 5. Database Caching Store frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer to reduce load on the database. 6. Replication Create copies of the primary database on different servers to distribute read load and enhance availability. 7. Sharding Divide the database into smaller, manageable pieces, or shards, to distribute load and improve performance. 8. Partitioning Split large tables into smaller, more manageable pieces to improve query performance and maintenance. 9. Query Optimization Rewrite and fine tune queries to execute more efficiently. 10. Use of Appropriate Data Types Select the most efficient data types for each column to save space and speed up processing. 11. Limiting Indexes Avoid excessive indexing, which can slow down write operations; use indexes judiciously. 12. Archiving Old Data Move infrequently accessed data to an archive to keep the active database smaller and faster.

title: Terraform
text: Terraform Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool by HashiCorp. Instead of clicking around the AWS or GCP console to create resources, you write declarative config files (in HCL — HashiCorp Configuration Language) describing what infrastructure you want, and Terraform figures out how to create, update, or destroy resources to match that description. Since you're already working hands on with sarath study on Cloud Run, Terraform would let you version and automate that setup instead of clicking through the GCP console each time. Core concepts Provider : a plugin that lets Terraform talk to a specific platform (AWS, GCP, Azure, etc.) Resource : a single infrastructure object you want to manage (a VM, a bucket, a Cloud Run service) State file (terraform.tfstate): Terraform's record of what it has actually created, used to compute diffs Plan : a dry run showing what Terraform will change Apply : executes the plan Module : reusable, parameterized bundle of resources Core workflow Example — GCP (Cloud Run, relevant to your setup) This single file replaces manually configuring the service, env vars, and IAM invoker permission in the console — and you get a repeatable, reviewable definition of it. Example — AWS (equivalent idea: ECS Fargate service) Common uses across both clouds | Use case | AWS resources | GCP resources | | | | | | Compute | EC2, ECS, Lambda, EKS | Compute Engine, Cloud Run, GKE, Cloud Functions | | Networking | VPC, subnets, security groups, ALB | VPC, subnets, firewall rules, Load Balancer | | Storage | S3 | Cloud Storage | | IAM | IAM roles/policies | IAM roles/bindings | | Databases | RDS, DynamoDB | Cloud SQL, Firestore/Bigtable | | Secrets | Secrets Manager | Secret Manager | | Multi env | workspaces / separate state per env (dev/stage/prod) | same | Why it matters in practice Version control : infra changes go through git, PRs, code review — same as app code Reproducibility : spin up an identical dev/staging/prod environment from the same config Multi cloud : same tool, same workflow syntax whether it's AWS or GCP (though resource types differ per provider) Drift detection : terraform plan tells you if someone manually changed something in the console Team collaboration : remote state backends (S3+DynamoDB for AWS, GCS for GCP) let teams share state safely For interviews, a good way to frame it: "Terraform lets you declaratively define infrastructure once and apply it consistently across environments and cloud providers, with state tracking so it knows what already exists and what needs to change." GKE (in GCP) & EKS (in AWS) Good question — GKE and EKS are a different layer than Terraform, but Terraform absolutely can provision them. Terraform = the IaC tool that creates infrastructure (VMs, networks, IAM, and yes, clusters themselves). GKE / EKS = managed Kubernetes control planes offered by GCP and AWS respectively — the thing that runs your containers via Kubernetes. So the relationship is: Terraform can create the cluster , but what runs inside the cluster (Deployments, Services, Pods) is normally managed by Kubernetes native tools — kubectl, Helm, or Kustomize — not Terraform, even though Terraform can do it too via its Kubernetes provider. GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine) and EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service, AWS) are both just managed Kubernetes offerings — the control plane is handled for you, you don't run kube apiserver/etcd yourself. Where Terraform fits: Cluster creation — Terraform is a very natural fit. google container cluster for GKE, aws eks cluster for EKS. Same node pools, networking, IAM roles, all as code. What runs inside the cluster — once the cluster exists, you're deploying Kubernetes objects (Deployments, Services, Ingress). That's traditionally kubectl apply or Helm charts, not Terraform. Terraform does have a kubernetes provider and a helm provider so you technically can manage workloads with it too, but in practice most teams split it: Terraform for infra (cluster + node pools + IAM + networking), kubectl/Helm/ArgoCD for what runs on top. So for an interview style answer: "Terraform provisions the cluster infrastructure; Kubernetes native tools manage the workloads running on that cluster — they're complementary, not competing." Given your track is currently Cloud Run on GCP (simpler, no cluster to manage), GKE/EKS would only make sense if you outgrow Cloud Run's constraints — multiple tightly coupled services, need for sidecars, custom scheduling, etc. Flow Design Quick walkthrough of what each stage actually does: Git push → CI/CD trigger : your cloudbuild.yaml (or a GitHub Actions workflow) watches the repo/branch and fires automatically on push. terraform init : pulls the google provider plugin, connects to the remote state backend (GCS bucket, so state isn't lost between runs). plan → apply : plan is a dry run diff against the current state; apply is what actually executes the changes. Many pipelines gate apply behind manual approval for production. Terraform → GCP APIs : Terraform doesn't talk to GCP directly through some proprietary channel — it makes standard GCP API calls (Cloud Resource Manager, Cloud Run Admin API, IAM API, etc.) using a service account's credentials, same as gcloud or the console would. State file : after apply, Terraform writes what it actually created into the state file in GCS — that's how the next plan knows what already exists vs what's new.
